title: Vinyl Cut Files: Turn a Logo Into Clean, Weedable Paths
seoTitle: Vinyl Cut File Requirements: Weedable Paths From a Logo
seoDescription: Vinyl cutting punishes small counters, double paths and stray nodes. Here is the checklist that produces a file you can weed in one pass instead of fighting.
excerpt: Small counters tear, duplicate paths cut twice, stray nodes confuse the blade, and open paths leave incomplete cuts. This checklist produces a weedable vinyl file on the first try.
content:
Vinyl cutting punishes design mistakes: counters smaller than 2mm tear during weeding, overlapping duplicate paths cut the same line twice and lift the vinyl, stray nodes cause the blade to wander, and open paths leave incomplete cuts. This checklist produces a file you can weed in one pass instead of fighting with tweezers and ruined material.

Weedable Design Rules

Weeding is the process of removing unwanted vinyl (the negative space) after cutting, leaving only the design. If counters (holes in letters, interior voids) are too small, they tear when you try to pick them out. If strokes are too thin, they lift or stretch. If shapes overlap, the cutter will cut the overlapping region multiple times, weakening the vinyl and causing it to tear during weeding.

The minimum weedable feature size depends on vinyl type and blade sharpness. For standard calendared vinyl (Oracal 651, Avery 900), aim for a minimum stroke width of 1-1.5mm and counter sizes of at least 2mm. For premium cast vinyl (3M 180, Avery 1105), you can go slightly smaller — down to 0.8mm strokes and 1.5mm counters — but never below that. Anything finer will either fail to cut cleanly or tear during weeding.

Design ElementMinimum Safe SizeWhy It Matters
Stroke / line width1-1.5mm (calendared), 0.8mm (cast)Thinner lines lift, stretch, or tear during weeding
Counters (holes in letters)2mm (calendared), 1.5mm (cast)Smaller voids tear when picked out with a weeding tool
Gap between adjacent shapes1.5mm minimumCloser gaps risk cutting through the backing or merging shapes
Serif thickness (on fonts)0.5mm absolute minimum, 1mm safeThin serifs snap off during weeding or application
Small dot or decorative accent2mm diameter minimumSmaller dots do not stick reliably or lift during transfer

No Overlapping Paths or Duplicate Geometry

If your file contains overlapping shapes with identical outlines, the cutter will cut the overlapping region twice. This weakens the vinyl and causes it to tear during weeding or application. It also wastes time and dulls the blade. Before exporting, inspect the file for duplicate paths: use View → Outline Mode in Illustrator or View → Display Mode → Outline in Inkscape to see all paths without fills or strokes obscuring them.

If you find overlapping paths that should be merged, use a union or weld operation: in Inkscape, select the paths and choose Path → Union (Ctrl++). In Illustrator, use the Pathfinder panel (Window → Pathfinder) and click Unite. This merges overlapping shapes into a single path, eliminating duplicate cut lines.

Stray Nodes and Open Paths

Stray nodes — isolated points with no connecting path — can cause the cutter to make tiny, unwanted cuts or perforations. Open paths (paths where the end node does not connect to the start node) will cut partway, then the blade will lift and travel back to the start, potentially leaving a visible mark or incomplete cut. Before exporting, clean up stray nodes: in Inkscape, use Edit → Select All, then Path → Clean Up. In Illustrator, select all and choose Object → Path → Clean Up, checking all boxes.

Close all open paths that should be closed. In Inkscape, select a path and choose Path → Close Path. In Illustrator, select the path and choose Object → Path → Join (Ctrl+J or Cmd+J). If a path is intentionally open (e.g., a decorative swirl that does not form a closed shape), ensure it has a stroke so the cutter knows to cut along it.

Weld Overlapping Shapes to Eliminate Internal Cut Lines

If two shapes overlap and you want the cutter to treat them as one continuous piece, weld (union) them before export. Unwelded overlaps cause the cutter to cut the intersection line, which weakens the vinyl and makes weeding difficult. For example, if you have two overlapping circles that form a figure-eight, union them so the cutter cuts only the outer perimeter, not the internal intersection.

Welding also applies to text. When letters touch or overlap (e.g., script fonts), weld them into a single path so the cutter does not cut between touching letters. In Silhouette Studio and Cricut Design Space, this is done with the Weld tool. In Inkscape and Illustrator, use Path → Union or Pathfinder → Unite.

Convert Text to Paths and Simplify Fonts

Live text (editable font objects) will not cut because cutting software does not have access to your fonts. Convert text to paths before export: Type → Create Outlines in Illustrator, Path → Object to Path in Inkscape. This converts each letter into a filled shape.

Not all fonts are suitable for vinyl cutting. Script fonts with thin strokes, ornate serifs, or tiny counters often fail. Test-cut a single letter before committing to a full word. If serifs are too thin, choose a bolder font or manually thicken strokes using Path → Outset in Inkscape or Object → Path → Offset Path in Illustrator.

Ensure Counters Are Separate Voids

When you convert text to paths, ensure that counters (the holes in letters like O, P, A, e) are defined as voids, not separate shapes sitting on top. If the counter is a separate shape, it will cut twice: once as the counter and once as part of the outer letter. To fix this, create a compound path: in Inkscape, select the outer and inner paths and choose Path → Compound Path. In Illustrator, choose Object → Compound Path → Make.

Remove Stray Elements, Hidden Layers, and Construction Geometry

Before exporting, delete all construction lines, guides, reference images, and hidden layers. These elements can export invisibly and confuse the cutter or cause it to make unwanted cuts. In Inkscape, delete all guides (Edit → Guides → Delete All Guides) and hidden layers (Layer → Layers → delete hidden layers). In Illustrator, delete all guides (View → Guides → Clear Guides) and check the Layers panel for hidden or locked layers.

Use the Outline view (View → Outline Mode in Illustrator, View → Display Mode → Outline in Inkscape) to inspect the file for stray elements that are not visible in normal view. If you see anything unexpected, delete it before export.

Export Settings for Vinyl Cutters

Most vinyl cutters (Cricut, Silhouette, Roland, Graphtec) accept SVG. Some older models or third-party software (SignMaster, VinylMaster) prefer DXF. Export settings matter: save as Plain SVG in Inkscape to strip metadata, or use Illustrator's Export As → SVG with Styling: Presentation Attributes and Fonts: Convert to Outlines.

Set document units to inches or millimeters before export to avoid scale issues. In Inkscape: File → Document Properties → Display Units. In Illustrator: File → Document Setup → Units. If your cutter software requires DXF, export as DXF R12 or R14 from Inkscape or use Vectorr's SVG to DXF converter.

For workflows on specific machines, see the Cricut Design Space SVG guide, the Silhouette Studio DXF vs SVG comparison, and the Glowforge SVG requirements. For related cut-file principles, check the laser cutting file optimization article.

faqs.question: What is the minimum stroke width for vinyl cutting?
faqs.answer: For standard calendared vinyl (Oracal 651, Avery 900), aim for 1-1.5mm minimum stroke width. Premium cast vinyl (3M 180, Avery 1105) can go down to 0.8mm. Thinner strokes lift, stretch, or tear during weeding. Test-cut a sample before committing to thin details.

faqs.question: Why do overlapping paths cause problems in vinyl cutting?
faqs.answer: The cutter will cut overlapping regions twice, weakening the vinyl and causing it to tear during weeding or application. It also wastes time and dulls the blade. Union (weld) overlapping shapes before export: Path → Union in Inkscape, Pathfinder → Unite in Illustrator, or the Weld tool in Cricut/Silhouette software.

faqs.question: How do I fix counters (holes in letters) that cut twice?
faqs.answer: Counters must be defined as voids in a compound path, not separate shapes on top. Select the outer and inner paths and create a compound path: Path → Compound Path in Inkscape, Object → Compound Path → Make in Illustrator. This defines the inner path as a void, and the cutter will cut it once as part of the outer shape.

faqs.question: Why does my text disappear or cut incorrectly?
faqs.answer: Live text (editable font objects) is ignored by cutting software. Convert text to paths before export: Type → Create Outlines in Illustrator, Path → Object to Path in Inkscape. This converts each letter to a filled shape. Also ensure counters are defined as voids (compound paths) so they do not cut twice.

faqs.question: What file format should I export for vinyl cutting?
faqs.answer: Most modern vinyl cutters (Cricut, Silhouette, Roland) accept SVG. Export as Plain SVG in Inkscape or use Illustrator's Export As → SVG with Styling: Presentation Attributes. Some older cutters or third-party software prefer DXF R12 or R14. Set document units to inches or millimeters before export to avoid scale issues.

title: Laser Cutting File Optimization: Paths, Order and Kerf
seoTitle: Laser Cutting File Optimization: Path Order, Kerf and Nodes
seoDescription: Machine time is dominated by travel and pierce points, not cutting. Optimize path order, node count and kerf offset to cut the same part in half the time.
excerpt: Machine time is dominated by travel and pierce points, not cutting. Optimize path order (cut inner first), reduce nodes, nest tightly, and batch operations by layer to cut the same part in half the time.
content:
Machine time in laser cutting is dominated by travel, pierce points, and acceleration, not cutting. A poorly organized file can double job time: the laser head jumps back and forth across the sheet, pierces the material hundreds of times unnecessarily, and cuts outer shapes before inner details, causing parts to shift mid-job. Optimizing path order, reducing node count, and applying kerf offset last can cut the same design in half the time with no quality loss.

Path Order: Cut Inner Details Before Outer Perimeters

The single most important optimization is cut order. Always cut inner details (holes, slots, engraves, inner shapes) before cutting outer perimeters. If you cut the outer edge first, the part is freed from the sheet and can shift during subsequent cuts, ruining alignment. Inner cuts remain anchored by the outer material, so they stay in place.

For nested parts (e.g., a box with a cutout window inside a panel), cut from innermost to outermost: first the window, then the panel interior details, then the panel perimeter. Most laser control software (LightBurn, RDWorks, LaserCut) lets you assign layer order or manually reorder paths in a cut list. Use this to enforce inside-first cutting.

OptimizationMachine Time SavedHow to Implement
Cut inner shapes before outer perimetersPrevents part shifting; eliminates re-cutsAssign layers by order; reorder in cut list
Minimize travel (nest tightly)10-30% faster for sparse sheetsUse nesting software or manual layout
Reduce node count (simplify paths)5-15% faster for complex curvesSimplify in Inkscape/Illustrator before export
Group by layer (cuts, scores, engraves)Reduces mode changes; 5-10% fasterAssign colors to layers; batch operations
Apply kerf offset lastEasier to adjust; no double-offsettingOffset in laser software, not design software
Common-line cutting (shared edges)Halves cuts for adjacent partsDesign with shared edges; manual or CAM tool

Minimize Travel with Nesting and Layout

Travel time — the laser head moving between cuts with the beam off — is wasted time. Tight nesting (packing parts close together on the sheet) reduces travel. For sparse sheets (parts spread out with large gaps), nesting can save 10-30% of total job time. For dense sheets, the savings are smaller but still measurable.

Manual nesting in design software (Inkscape, Illustrator) is tedious. Automated nesting software (Deepnest, SVGnest, RDWorks' built-in nester) arranges parts to minimize waste and travel. These tools export a nested layout you can import into your laser software. Nesting is especially valuable for production runs where the same parts are cut repeatedly.

Lead-In and Lead-Out Considerations

Lead-ins (short approach paths before the cut starts) and lead-outs (short exit paths after the cut ends) prevent burn marks at the start/end point of a closed path. They also add travel. If every part has a 2mm lead-in and 2mm lead-out, and you have 100 parts, that is 400mm of extra travel. Minimize lead-in/out length when quality allows, or disable them for hidden edges (e.g., internal corners that will be out of sight in the final assembly).

Reduce Node Count to Speed Path Computation

Vector paths with thousands of nodes take longer to compute and send to the laser controller. A path with 500 nodes cut at 20mm/s takes the same wall-clock time to cut as a 50-node path, but the controller spends more time processing the 500-node version, and the motion planning is less smooth. Auto-traced images and CAD exports often have excessive nodes. Simplify them before export.

In Inkscape, select all paths (Ctrl+A), then choose Path → Simplify (Ctrl+L) 2-5 times. In Illustrator, select all and choose Object → Path → Simplify, setting Curve Precision to 95-98%. For decorative elements, node reduction of 50-70% is common with no visible quality loss. For precision mechanical parts, use conservative settings (98-99% precision) to preserve fit.

When Not to Simplify

Do not simplify paths for precision parts with tight tolerances (e.g., gears, snap-fit joints). Simplification introduces small deviations (typically 0.01-0.1mm depending on settings) that can accumulate and affect fit. Simplify only decorative elements, text, and traced graphics where sub-0.1mm precision is not critical.

Layer Strategy: Batch Cuts, Scores, and Engraves

Laser control software assigns different speeds, powers, and modes (cut, score, engrave) to different layers. If your file has cuts and scores mixed on one layer, the laser may switch modes mid-job, slowing down due to mode-change overhead. Organize your file so all cuts are on one layer, all scores on another, and all engraves on a third. The laser will batch each operation type, reducing mode changes.

In LightBurn, assign colors to layers in the import dialog, then configure each layer with the appropriate cut settings. In RDWorks and LaserCut, layers are numbered (Layer00, Layer01, etc.) and you assign operations in the layer list. Plan your design so operation types map cleanly to layers: red = cut, blue = score, black = engrave, for example.

Apply Kerf Offset Last, in Laser Software

Kerf offset (compensating for material removed by the laser beam) should be applied in the laser control software, not in your design software. If you offset paths in Inkscape or Illustrator before export, and then apply kerf offset again in LightBurn, you will double-offset and ruin fit. Apply kerf once, at the last step, and document where you applied it.

LightBurn has a kerf offset feature in cut layer settings: set it to inward for outer cuts (to compensate for kerf widening the part) and outward for inner cuts (to compensate for kerf widening voids). If your laser software does not have kerf offset, apply it manually in design software using Path → Outset / Inset (Inkscape) or Object → Path → Offset Path (Illustrator). For detailed kerf guidance, see the laser kerf and press-fit guide.

Common-Line Cutting for Adjacent Parts

If two parts share an edge (e.g., tiles in a grid, box sides in a flat-pack), you can cut the shared edge once instead of twice by designing them as a single path with the shared edge omitted. This is called common-line cutting. It halves the cut time for that edge and reduces kerf loss (material removed by the beam).

Common-line cutting requires planning at the design stage. Draw adjacent parts so shared edges overlap exactly, then delete one edge. When the laser cuts, it will cut around the perimeter of the group, leaving the shared edge intact. After cutting, snap the parts apart along the shared edge (which was not cut). This technique is common in production laser cutting and CNC routing.

Limitations and Risks

Common-line cutting only works if the shared edge is straight or if both parts have matching curves along the shared edge. It also assumes the parts will be separated by hand after cutting, which may not be practical for small or fragile parts. Use it for large, flat parts (panels, tiles, gears) where the shared edge is easy to snap or cut by hand post-job.

Final Checks Before Cutting

Before sending the file to the laser, run through this checklist: (1) Inner shapes are cut before outer perimeters. (2) All paths are closed (no open paths that will cause backtracking). (3) Node count is minimized (simplified where appropriate). (4) Kerf offset is applied once, either in laser software or design software, not both. (5) Layers are organized by operation type (cut, score, engrave). (6) Lead-ins and lead-outs are set appropriately for the material.

Preview the toolpath in your laser software (LightBurn's Preview mode, RDWorks' Simulation) to confirm cut order and spot any unexpected travel moves. If the preview shows the laser jumping back and forth across the sheet repeatedly, reorder paths or re-nest parts.

For related workflows, see the LightBurn SVG import guide, the Glowforge SVG requirements, and the PNG to laser-ready vector guide. For file format considerations, check SVG vs DXF and the file formats reference.

faqs.question: Why should I cut inner shapes before outer perimeters?
faqs.answer: If you cut the outer edge first, the part is freed from the sheet and can shift during subsequent cuts, ruining alignment. Inner cuts stay anchored by the outer material. Always cut from innermost to outermost: holes first, then details, then perimeters. Most laser software lets you reorder paths or assign layer priority.

faqs.question: How much time does nesting save in laser cutting?
faqs.answer: For sparse sheets (parts spread out with large gaps), tight nesting can save 10-30% of total job time by reducing travel. For dense sheets, the savings are smaller but still measurable (5-10%). Nesting also reduces material waste. Use automated nesting software (Deepnest, SVGnest, RDWorks) for complex layouts.

faqs.question: What is node count and why does it matter for laser cutting?
faqs.answer: Node count is the number of control points on a vector path. High node counts (thousands of nodes from auto-traced images or CAD exports) slow path computation and motion planning. Simplify paths in Inkscape (Path → Simplify) or Illustrator (Object → Path → Simplify) to reduce nodes by 50-70% with no visible quality loss for decorative elements.

faqs.question: Should I apply kerf offset in my design software or laser software?
faqs.answer: Apply kerf offset once, in the laser control software (LightBurn has built-in kerf offset in layer settings). If you offset paths in Inkscape or Illustrator and then again in LightBurn, you will double-offset and ruin fit. If your laser software lacks kerf offset, apply it manually in design software, but document it clearly.

faqs.question: What is common-line cutting and when should I use it?
faqs.answer: Common-line cutting is designing adjacent parts so they share an edge, then cutting that edge once instead of twice. It halves cut time for that edge and reduces kerf loss. Draw parts with overlapping edges, delete one edge, and the laser cuts the perimeter of the group. Snap parts apart by hand after cutting. Use for large, flat parts with straight or matching curved shared edges.

title: SVG vs DXF: Which One Your Machine Wants
seoTitle: SVG vs DXF: Differences, Units and When to Convert
seoDescription: SVG stores presentation, DXF stores CAD geometry and units. Compare what each keeps, how they disagree on scale, and which to send where.
keywords: which is better svg or dxf
excerpt: An SVG stores how artwork looks; a DXF stores where geometry sits and how big it is. That single difference explains the scale bugs, missing layers, and lost strokes that show up when you send a design to a laser, plotter, or CNC mill.
content:
Open a 100 mm SVG square in a CAD program that assumes millimetres and you will often get a 264 mm square. Nothing is corrupted. The file never said how big it was, so the importer guessed, and it guessed in CSS pixels rather than printed millimetres. That one ambiguity is responsible for a large share of wasted material in small shops.

SVG and DXF are both vector formats, both plain text, and both describe shapes with coordinates. Past that surface similarity the two diverge almost completely, because they were designed for different industries with different assumptions.

What each format actually stores

SVG is a presentation format. Its job is to describe what an image should look like when rendered, and it inherits that job from the web. That means fills, gradients, opacity, stroke caps, CSS rules, and typography are all first-class citizens. It also means the format is relaxed about physical size: a document can specify a viewBox with no width and height at all, leaving the renderer to pick whatever size the container offers.

DXF is a CAD interchange format. Its model space is a coordinate system where numbers mean distances, and the appearance of a line is metadata attached to it. Colour in DXF is usually a number (an AutoCAD Color Index value) rather than a hex string, and lineweight is an integer in hundredths of a millimetre. There are no gradients, no opacity, and no fonts in the web sense — text is either geometry or a reference to a font that may not exist on the receiving machine.

The structural difference in practice

An SVG file is XML: elements nest inside each other, transforms cascade down the tree, and a group can carry styling that affects every child. A DXF file is a flat list of entities introduced by group codes — pairs of numbers and values that say "this is a LINE, it has two endpoints, it sits on layer CUT_1." Nesting exists only through blocks and inserts.

The practical consequence: in SVG, grouping is semantic and inherited. In DXF, layers are the organising principle. Most CAM software builds its toolpath list from DXF layers, so a file whose entire geometry sits on layer 0 will import as one undifferentiated mass. That is why converting artwork for a cutting machine almost always involves deciding what belongs on which layer before export. Our laser cutting guide covers what those layers usually need to be.

Where the scale goes wrong

The SVG specification defines a user unit that maps to CSS pixels, and CSS defines 96 pixels per inch. So an SVG element 96 units wide is nominally one inch. Most CAM packages do not read it that way. Since the overwhelming majority of CAD and laser files are metric, importers such as LightBurn, CorelDRAW's DXF filter, and various Inkscape workflows treat bare numbers as millimetres.

One inch of SVG (96 user units) therefore arrives as 96 mm, which is 3.78 inches. That is the classic 2.54× too large result, and it is why the first thing you check when a cut file is the wrong size is the unit assumption, not the geometry.

The DXF side of the same problem

DXF has an answer for this: the $INSUNITS header variable, which declares the drawing unit — 1 for inches, 4 for millimetres, 5 for centimetres, and so on. A well-formed DXF says exactly how big it is. The trouble is that $INSUNITS is optional in older DXF versions, widely ignored by exporters, and frequently ignored by importers even when present. Many tools default to "unitless" and then apply their own assumption at import time.

Some CAD programs also store a $MEASUREMENT flag and a $INSUNITS value that disagree with each other, which is a reliable way to get a file that reads differently in two programs you own.

PropertySVGDXF
Base conceptPresentation / renderingCAD geometry in model space
EncodingXML, nested, tree-structuredGroup-code pairs, flat entity list
Declared unitsNone intrinsic; user units ≈ CSS px$INSUNITS (optional, often wrong)
Physical sizeImplicit via viewBox and width/heightExplicit numbers in the declared unit
CurvesCubic and quadratic Bézier, arcsPolylines, arcs, splines, ellipses
ColourRGB, HSL, hex, gradients, patternsACI index, true colour, or bylayer
TransparencyFull alpha and group opacityNot part of classic DXF geometry
Grouping<g>, transforms cascadeLayers and blocks
TextLive, styled, reflowableTEXT/MTEXT or exploded to outlines
Typical consumerBrowser, Illustrator, Inkscape, cuttersAutoCAD, CAM, CNC, plasma, waterjet
FillsRich, including gradient meshesHatches and solid fills only
Stroke semanticsPainted width, centred on pathLineweight, plotted as a constant width

Strokes, fills, and what a machine does with them

A filled shape and a stroked outline are very different ideas to a cutting machine. In SVG, a stroke is paint applied along a path — the path itself has zero width. A 2 mm stroke on a rectangle is a 2 mm band of ink centred on the outline. Convert that file to DXF without thinking and you can end up with either a bare outline (correct for cutting) or a doubled outline where the stroke was expanded (usually wrong).

A laser cutter, vinyl cutter, or plasma torch wants a single open or closed path per cut. It reads the path, not the paint. That is why good design files for machines use strokes for cut lines and fills for engrave or score regions, and why you should decide before conversion whether a decorative element is going to be outlined or filled.

Text becomes geometry

Text is the other classic failure. SVG text depends on a font being available at render time. If the receiving CAM tool does not have that font, it either substitutes something radically different or drops the text entirely. The same is true of DXF, where TEXT entities reference a style whose font file is a local resource.

For anything going to a machine, convert text to outlines first. This is not lossy in any way that matters — the letterforms become paths and the geometry is identical to what you saw on screen. It does eliminate editability, so keep a working copy of the original.

Choosing which to send

If the receiving party is a browser, a design application, a cutting machine driven by a craft app, or a vinyl cutter, SVG is usually the right answer. It survives Illustrator and Inkscape round-trips, it carries stroke and fill intent clearly, and it is the native language of most hobby cut workflows.

If the receiving party is CAD — Fusion 360, Rhino, AutoCAD, a CAM post-processor, a plasma table, a waterjet, an industrial laser — DXF is expected. Those tools speak DXF, they want layers and explicit units, and they treat a decorative gradient as noise.

Between the two, SVG to DXF conversion is the common direction, because most artwork is authored as SVG and most machines want DXF. The reverse direction, DXF to SVG, is mostly used for preparing CAD drawings for the web or for cutter software that refuses DXF.

A conversion checklist

  1. Set the document to explicit millimetre dimensions before export, not a bare viewBox.
  2. Flatten or bake transforms so nothing depends on cascaded group scaling.
  3. Convert text to paths.
  4. Assign geometry to named layers — one per operation, such as CUT, SCORE, ENGRAVE.
  5. Keep cut paths as unfilled strokes at a consistent width.
  6. Open the resulting DXF in a viewer and measure a known dimension against a ruler.

The conversion edge cases worth knowing

Bézier curves convert to DXF better as polylines with a tight tolerance than as splines, because spline support in older DXF readers is uneven. A tolerance of 0.01 mm is visually exact at cutting scale while keeping file size manageable. If you push to 0.001 mm the file grows by an order of magnitude for no benefit a laser can resolve.

Gradients, masks, and clip paths cannot survive the trip. Flatten them before converting, or accept that they vanish. Filters likewise — a drop shadow in SVG is not geometry and has no DXF equivalent.

Arcs are the one place where DXF has an advantage: native arc entities are smaller and smoother than a polyline approximation, and many CAM tools generate better toolpaths from true arcs. Converters that recognise circular geometry and emit ARC entities produce noticeably cleaner output for mechanical parts.

If you are starting from a raster logo rather than an SVG, the path is longer: trace it first, then convert. PNG to DXF does that in one step by vectorising the bitmap and writing CAD geometry directly, which avoids a manually tuned SVG step you would only throw away.

When to keep both

For anything that will be reproduced — signage, production parts, a design you send to a fabricator repeatedly — keep the SVG as the design master and generate a DXF per machine. DXF files are consumer-specific in a way SVGs are not: layer naming conventions, unit assumptions, and curve tolerances all vary between shops. Regenerating from the master is cleaner than editing the DXF by hand.

If you handle these conversions at volume, our overview of batch conversion workflows covers how to keep unit and layer settings consistent across a folder of files.

If the source is a PDF drawing rather than an SVG — a common situation when a client supplies a CAD export as a PDF — the route is PDF to DXF, which is a geometry transfer for a true vector PDF and a tracing step for a scanned one. For the broader question of which formats carry which information, the format map puts DXF and SVG beside PDF, EPS and the 3D formats.

faqs.question: Why does my SVG import into my laser software at the wrong size?
faqs.answer: The SVG has no intrinsic physical unit, so an importer falls back on an assumption. Because SVG user units map to CSS pixels at 96 per inch, and most CAM tools assume millimetres, a 96-unit drawing becomes 96 mm instead of 25.4 mm. Set an explicit width and height in millimetres in the source file, or scale by 0.2646 after import.

faqs.question: Can DXF store gradients or transparency?
faqs.answer: No. Classic DXF geometry carries no gradient, opacity or filter data — it has hatches, solid fills, colours and lineweights. Anything involving transparency or a gradient must be flattened to solid shapes before conversion, or it will be dropped during the export.

faqs.question: Should I use SVG or DXF for a vinyl cutter?
faqs.answer: SVG for consumer vinyl cutters. Cricut Design Space and Silhouette Studio both accept SVG directly and handle layers through colour or stroke settings. DXF is still a valid fallback for older Silhouette workflows, and the difference is worth understanding before you export.

faqs.question: Does converting SVG to DXF lose my layer structure?
faqs.answer: It depends on the source. SVG has no native layer concept, so a converter must invent layers from groups, colour, or stroke width. If your SVG groups are meaningless, the DXF layers will be too. Name your groups deliberately, or split the artwork into separate paths per operation before conversion.

faqs.question: What curve tolerance should I use for a cutting DXF?
faqs.answer: 0.01 mm is the practical answer for laser and CNC work. It is finer than any consumer machine can resolve and keeps the polyline count reasonable. Going to 0.001 mm multiplies the point count roughly tenfold with no visible benefit on a cut edge.

title: SVG vs EPS: Modern Vector Against Print Legacy
seoTitle: SVG vs EPS for Print: Which Format to Send
seoDescription: EPS is a print-industry institution, SVG is the web standard. Understand what each stores, what printers accept, and when converting between them loses detail.
excerpt: EPS was built for PostScript printers and speaks CMYK and spot colours natively. SVG was built for screens and speaks RGB. If the next stop is a press, that difference decides which file you send.
content:
Four-colour offset presses, screen-print shops that mix ink by hand, and embroidery digitizers all share one demand: the file must state which inks to use. An EPS can name Pantone 032 at 60% tint. An SVG, as specified, can only say a colour is approximately that red. That is the whole argument in miniature.

Both formats are vector, both are text-based, and both can hold essentially identical geometry. What separates them is what they were written to control, and that shows up most sharply in colour and text.

One is a program, the other is a document

EPS stands for Encapsulated PostScript. It is not a data format in the modern sense — it is a small PostScript program, complete with a header comment block, a bounding box declaration, and a body of drawing operators that a PostScript interpreter executes in order. Lines are drawn with moveto and lineto, fills with fill, and the whole thing is wrapped in %%BoundingBox comments so a host application can place it on a page.

SVG is XML. Elements nest, attributes carry values, and a renderer traverses the tree and paints what it finds. There is no execution model in the base language — the tree describes a final image, and the renderer decides how to produce it.

That distinction has a practical consequence for tooling. EPS requires a PostScript interpreter to render, which is why a modern design app can open an EPS and show you a low-resolution preview stored alongside the PostScript data while still getting the geometry right. SVG requires an XML parser and a rendering engine, both of which every browser already has.

Why the age of the format matters

EPS dates from the mid-1980s and has been frozen essentially since PostScript Level 3. It carries no concept of layers, no live transparency model that every consumer understands, and no standardised handling of embedded raster images beyond a preview convention. It works because the printing industry built its entire prepress toolchain around it, and because it can express exactly the things a press needs.

Colour: the decisive difference

SVG 1.1 defines colour in sRGB, and SVG 2 adds CSS colour syntax and ICC-based colour profiles through the color-profile element — but support for embedded ICC profiles in SVG renderers is thin and inconsistent. In everyday practice, an SVG is an sRGB device colour space document. Whatever CMYK interpretation you intended is lost the moment the file is saved.

EPS inherits PostScript's colour model directly. It can set a device CMYK colour with setcmykcolor, a spot colour through a Separation or DeviceN colour space, and a tint of a named ink. A prepress operator can open the file, see that a shape is Pantone 185 C at 80%, and plate it accordingly.

This matters in two concrete places. In offset printing, a client-supplied brand colour specified as a spot ink must survive to the plate — an RGB approximation of a Pantone match will not, because the press does not have that ink loaded. In screen printing, every colour is a physical screen and a physical ink; the file has to say how many and which ones.

Organic separation work on SVG artwork is possible, and tools exist to generate a separated SVG, but the format itself is still RGB at heart. For production work, PDF with Separation colour spaces or an EPS with named inks is the safer carrier.

PropertySVGEPS

Spot / Pantone supportNot in the standard; approximations onlyNative named inks with tints
Font handlingLive text, or converted to pathsReferences PostScript fonts; usually needs outlining
TransparencyFull alpha, group opacity, blend modesLimited; flattened or rasterised in Level 2
Overprint controlNoneYes, via PostScript operators
Raster embedding<image>, PNG/JPEG/WebPEPSI/DCS conventions, awkward
LayersGroups, not true layersNone
File structureXML treePostScript program text
Bounding boxviewBox and width/height%%BoundingBox / %%HiResBoundingBox
What opens itEvery browser, Illustrator, InkscapeIllustrator, Affinity, prepress RIPs
Print industry acceptancePoorUniversal, legacy but expected

Fonts and the outlining rule

Both formats can technically carry font data. In practice neither is dependable for it, and for opposite reasons.

An EPS that references a PostScript font will fail to render correctly on any machine that lacks that font, and the substituted output can shift line breaks and alignment. PostScript Level 3 allows a Type 3 or Type 42 font to be embedded, and some applications do it, but the results are inconsistent and the font licensing may forbid it anyway.

An SVG can carry live text, and the browser will substitute a fallback font of its own choosing if the specified family is missing. It can also reference a web font via CSS or an @font-face rule, but many SVG importers ignore those rules entirely. Illustrator will open the file, notice the missing font, and ask you to resolve it.

The answer is the same in both cases: convert text to outlines before delivery. Letterforms become ordinary paths, they render identically everywhere, and no font licensing question arises. You lose the ability to re-edit the wording, so keep the source document with live text as the master.

Transparency is where SVG wins

SVG handles alpha cleanly, on fills, strokes, groups, and via fill-opacity and opacity. Blend modes are available through mix-blend-mode in SVG 2 and have wide renderer support. Masks and clip paths are part of the base language.

EPS is much weaker here. PostScript Level 3 introduced smooth shading and some transparency support, but the flattened result is what most prepress workflows expect, because older RIPs cannot composite. If your artwork depends on a soft shadow over a gradient, an EPS pipeline will usually rasterise or flatten the region, and the rasterised region will carry an sRGB interpretation.

What print shops actually expect

Most modern commercial printers prefer PDF over either format. A PDF 1.4 file as defined by PDF/X-4 carries CMYK, spot colours, embedded fonts, and a real trim and bleed model. EPS survives as an accepted legacy format, particularly for logos that a client supplies to be placed into a larger layout.

Where EPS is still firmly expected: screen printing separations, some embroidery and apparel workflows, vinyl and sign shops that have used the same RIP for twenty years, and any client who has been sending EPS since 1998. If you cannot produce what the shop asks for, the job does not run, regardless of which format is technically better.

SVG is expected by a completely different audience: web developers, UI designers, cutting machines, and modern design tools. Sending SVG to a press is usually a mistake, and sending EPS to a web developer is a minor nuisance.

A practical conversion path

Converting SVG to EPS is straightforward geometry work: paths come across, and the header is generated around them. What does not survive automatically is colour intent — an sRGB value becomes a device RGB value, and you then have to decide how the shop converts it to CMYK. Ask for their profile rather than letting a generic conversion decide for you.

Our SVG to EPS converter handles the structural side. For a bitmap source, PNG to EPS traces and writes the PostScript in one step, and EPS to SVG runs the direction most people need after discovering that their client's EPS is actually a font-dependent mess.

The reverse trip, and the reason many teams end up in this article, is that a client hands over a 1990s EPS and the design team needs it on the web. That conversion is genuinely lossy in one direction only: colour comes back as sRGB, spot inks get approximated, and any rasterised regions stay raster inside the SVG.

Units, bounding boxes and placement

EPS carries a bounding box in its header comments, and that box is what a layout application uses to place the file on a page. If the bounding box is wrong — larger than the artwork, or offset — the EPS will appear with unexpected white margins or overlapping neighbouring elements. Designers hit this constantly with logos placed on business cards.

SVG's equivalent is the viewBox plus width and height, and it has the opposite failure mode: a missing viewBox means there is no defined extent, so different viewers crop differently. Neither format enforces correctness; both rely on the producer to declare the bounds accurately.

A second placement complication is scale. An EPS is in PostScript units, which are points at 72 per inch. An SVG's user unit maps to CSS pixels at 96 per inch. A shape described identically in both — say 100 units wide — renders at 100 points in EPS and 100 pixels in SVG. If the SVG also declares width in millimetres, the number means something concrete; if it does not, the receiving application picks. When you convert between them, confirm the ratio rather than assuming the numbers carry over unchanged.

What each format does well outside its home ground

SVG's advantage beyond the browser is that it is trivially manipulable. Because it is XML, a script can recolour every path with a given ID, a build step can inline it into a page, and a CMS can store it as text. Nothing about EPS invites that treatment — a PostScript program is not something you safely transform with a regex.

EPS's advantage beyond prepress is that it is a self-contained page fragment with a declared bounding box, which makes it a natural drop-in asset for older page layout tools. QuarkXPress and InDesign both handle EPS placement with predictable results, including the clipping path that hides the raster preview.

The raster preview problem

Many EPS files carry two representations: the PostScript data, and a low-resolution raster preview used for on-screen display. If the PostScript interpreter is unavailable — which is common in newer software — the application shows the preview instead, and the user sees a soft, pixelated image while the file is actually perfect vector.

This is a source of enormous confusion. A blurry EPS on screen does not mean the file is raster. It means you are looking at the placeholder. Print output uses the PostScript data and is sharp. Conversely, a genuinely raster EPS shows a preview that looks identical to the print output, which is one way to tell them apart: if the print is soft too, the vector was never there.

Practical delivery notes

When sending an EPS to a shop, include the ink list explicitly in the accompanying message. The file can carry named inks, but the shop still has to confirm they have them mixed or loaded. Include the intended finished size, because the bounding box alone does not tell a press operator how large the piece should print.

When sending an SVG to a developer, strip the editor metadata. Illustrator and Inkscape both write namespaced attributes and comments that inflate the file and occasionally confuse importers. Our SVG optimisation guide covers what to remove.

Deciding between them

Send EPS when the destination is a press, a screen-print separation workflow, or a shop that names it explicitly. Send SVG when the destination is a browser, an application, a laser or vinyl cutter, or any pipeline that needs to stay editable and CSS-styleable.

If you are unsure what format a print job needs, our comparison of SVG and PDF for print covers what survives a press workflow in more depth, and the file format reference puts EPS in context alongside AI, PDF and DXF.

faqs.question: Can an SVG hold CMYK colour?
faqs.answer: Not natively. SVG 1.1 is defined in sRGB, and SVG 2's ICC colour support is inconsistently implemented. You can place an sRGB approximation of a CMYK value in a file, but the CMYK intent is gone. For press work, use PDF with Separation colour spaces or an EPS with named inks.

faqs.question: Why does my EPS show the wrong font?
faqs.answer: EPS references PostScript fonts rather than reliably embedding them. If the receiving machine lacks the font, it substitutes one, and metrics shift. Convert all text to outlines before sending the EPS and the problem disappears, at the cost of no longer being able to edit the wording.

faqs.question: Is EPS still supported by modern software?
faqs.answer: Yes, but as legacy support. Illustrator, Affinity Designer, CorelDRAW and Inkscape all open EPS. Adobe has pushed PDF as the standard for years, and some newer tools only handle EPS through a PostScript import path that rasterises unrendered previews. Conversion tools and RIPs still parse it reliably, so even where editing support is thin, production support remains widespread.

faqs.question: Does converting SVG to EPS preserve layers?
faqs.answer: No. EPS has no layer model, so everything arrives in a single drawing order. If you need organised structure on the receiving end, PDF is a better carrier, and even then layer support is optional and viewer-dependent. Group structure can survive as drawing order, but nothing in the receiving application will present it as an editable layer stack.

faqs.question: Which format should I send to a screen printer?
faqs.answer: EPS if the shop asks for it, since separations are traditionally built from EPS or PDF with spot colours. Confirm the ink list with the shop before sending, and specify each colour as a named spot rather than an RGB approximation, so the separation step has something unambiguous to work with.

title: SVG vs PDF for Print: Choosing by What Survives
seoTitle: SVG vs PDF for Print: Which Format Keeps Your Artwork
seoDescription: Both are page-description formats with different priorities. See how they handle fonts, spot colors, and vector data before you pick one for a printer.
excerpt: Both describe a page. Only one of them knows where the bleed ends, the trim begins, and which ink is a spot colour. PDF is built for presses; SVG is built for viewports. Here is how to tell which one your job needs.
content:
A commercial printer will ask for a PDF. Almost nobody will ask for an SVG, and the ones who do are usually handing it to a laser cutter. The reason is not fashion: PDF carries a page model with real edges, and SVG does not. Everything else about the comparison follows from that.

Both formats are vector-first, both are text-based, both can embed raster images, and both describe an image rather than storing pixels. They were designed twenty years apart for different destinations.

Pages, boxes, and why trim exists

A PDF page has a /MediaBox, which defines the full physical page; a /CropBox, which is what a viewer displays by default; a /BleedBox, which extends past the trim to the area the printer trims from; and a /TrimBox, which is the finished size of the printed piece. A /ArtBox exists too, for the content area within the page.

Those four boxes solve a problem that every print job has. Artwork must extend beyond the final edge so the cutting tolerance does not leave a white sliver. The file has to say, unambiguously, where the final edge is. Trim is usually 3 mm beyond the finished size in Europe and 1/8 inch in the US, and the bleed area must be filled with artwork.

SVG has viewBox, width, height, and nothing else. There is no bleed element, no trim designation, and no standard way to communicate that the outer 3 mm is extra. A viewBox can define a coordinate window, but nothing in the specification says which part of that window is the finished piece. Prepress software has no way to recover the information, so a human has to be told, or the job is set up wrong.

Crop marks and imposition

PDF workflows also standardise how crop marks, registration marks, and colour bars sit on the sheet, and how multiple pages are imposed onto a press sheet. None of that vocabulary exists in SVG. You can draw crop marks as lines, but they are just lines — the RIP treats them as artwork, not as instructions.

Colour: CMYK and spot ink

PDF has supported device CMYK, ICC-based colour, and Separation and DeviceN spot colour spaces from the beginning of its print-oriented life. A PDF/X-1a, PDF/X-3, or PDF/X-4 file is a contract: the colour is defined in a specific way, fonts are embedded, and no external dependency can change what the output looks like.

SVG is sRGB by specification. SVG 2 allows ICC colour profiles through CSS Color, but renderer support is thin and prepress tools generally ignore it. There is no spot colour concept. If a job specifies Pantone 032, an SVG cannot say so in any way a RIP will read.

Practical consequence: a design house that delivers SVG to a printer forces the printer to guess at colour conversion. That guess may be right, but it is a guess, and it will not be consistent across jobs.

Print requirementSVGPDF
Trim boxNone/TrimBox
Bleed boxNone; bleed drawn by convention/BleedBox
Media boxwidth/height attributes/MediaBox
CMYK colourNot nativeNative device CMYK
Spot / PantoneNot supportedSeparation / DeviceN
ICC profilesTheoretical, poorly supportedFull, via OutputIntent
Font embeddingOptional and unreliableStandard, licenseable as subset
OverprintNoneYes
Prepress standardNonePDF/X-1a, X-3, X-4, Ghent PDF
Multi-pageOne document, one canvasYes, many pages
Best atScreens, UI, cutting machinesPress, proofs, imposition

Fonts and the embedding contract

PDF's font model is mature. A producer embeds a subset of the font, with the licensing bits that declare whether the file may be further extracted, and the RIP uses the embedded data. Text stays sharp at any resolution and the output is byte-identical to the proof.

SVG can carry text and can reference fonts, but the format does not require embedding and most importers do not honour it. Browser rendering substitutes silently. Illustrator prompts. A cutting machine typically ignores text entirely and requires conversion to paths.

For print specifically, embedding either works (a properly built PDF) or you convert all text to outlines. Outlining in a PDF is acceptable but loses searchability and accessibility. Outlining in an SVG is routine.

Rasters inside vector documents

Both formats can hold bitmaps. A PDF embeds images as XObjects with a defined colour space and resolution; a prepress operator can inspect each image and check its effective DPI against the line screen. An SVG embeds or links images with <image>, and linked images are external dependencies that will silently break if the file moves.

For print, 300 DPI at final size is the usual minimum, and 400–600 DPI for line art with fine detail. There is no automatic check in SVG land, so a linked 72 DPI placeholder sitting inside a print-bound SVG is a common and expensive mistake.

Where SVG is the correct answer

Not every print-adjacent job is a press job. Vinyl cutting, laser cutting, Cricut and Silhouette cutting, and craft plotter work all want SVG or DXF, because those machines need paths and they do not care about page boxes. Screen printing a simple one-colour job often works from a vector file with explicit separation layers, and SVG is fine there as long as the shop can convert it.

Web delivery, application UI, icons, and any context where the image must scale with a viewport or be styled with CSS belongs in SVG. That is not a compromise; it is the format's purpose.

There is also a hybrid role: a PDF is often the best source for making an SVG. Vector PDFs from Illustrator or Inkscape carry clean paths that convert into an SVG with no tracing step. PDF to SVG is a lossless geometry transfer for a genuinely vector PDF, and a tracing operation for a scanned one.

Converting between them

Going SVG to PDF is common when a design needs to become a document: an invoice template, a certificate, a proof for a client. SVG to PDF renders the SVG into PDF drawing operators, and the output is sharp and small. What it cannot do is invent a TrimBox, a CMYK colour space, or an embedded font — it converts what is there.

Going PDF to SVG is common when a vector PDF needs to become editable web artwork. A PDF exported from a vector source converts cleanly. A PDF exported from a raster source, or one where the vector content is obscured by a raster overlay, converts to a traced approximation of that raster.

The often-overlooked point is that PDF's content stream and SVG's element tree have a natural mapping: paths, fills, strokes, and transforms all transfer almost one to one. Groups, clipping, and transparency transfer with some care. Gradients and fonts do not always.

Why print tolerances are measured in micrometres

Offset printing runs at a registration tolerance far tighter than most digital work. A misregistration of 0.05 mm between two inks is visible on a solid edge. That precision only works if the file states the intended page geometry exactly, which is what the PDF page boxes provide. A printer can program their imposition software from those values without asking you.

Bleed is the specific case where this becomes expensive. If a full-bleed image carries no bleed and the sheet drifts by a millimetre during trimming, the finished piece has a white hairline along the edge and is discarded. That is a whole run wasted on a file-level detail: whether the artwork extended past the trim line. SVG has no mechanism to declare where the trim line is, so the printer cannot automate the check.

Ink limits and total area coverage

CMYK builds on a press are not just four independent channels. Total area coverage — the sum of the four ink percentages at a given point — has a practical ceiling, typically 300% on coated stock and 240–280% on uncoated. Beyond that, ink does not dry and the sheet sets off. Rich black, built from 60C 40M 40Y 100K, sits around 240% and is standard; a naive conversion of pure RGB black can produce something near 400% and ruin the job.

PDF pipelines can carry a Total Area Coverage limit and prepress tools validate against it. Whether an SVG can even express four-channels-and-a-limit is moot: it cannot express CMYK at all, so the TAC question never arises until someone converts. And the conversion is done blind, because the source gave no guidance.

Multi-page documents and imposition

A brochure, a booklet, a business card grid — all of these are multi-page jobs. A PDF carries page objects and can describe dozens of pages in one file, each with its own boxes. Imposition software then arranges those pages onto a press sheet with the correct creep and gutter adjustments.

An SVG holds one canvas. Representing multiple pages means either separate files or one enormous canvas with the pages laid out — the latter is what some artboards do when exported, and printers complain about it because they have to guess the page divisions.

Long-term archival

PDF/A exists as a defined archival profile with a self-contained, deterministic subset of the format. Nothing equivalent exists for SVG. If a document needs to look identical in thirty years, PDF/A is the format designed for that job. SVG's permanence comes from its simplicity and open specification, which is a different kind of guarantee — the file will always be parseable, but the rendering may depend on which engine reads it.

A checklist before you send a file to a printer

  1. Export as PDF/X-4 if the printer accepts it, otherwise PDF/X-1a.
  2. Set the document bleed to the printer's stated value — usually 3 mm or 0.125 in.
  3. Confirm the TrimBox matches the finished size and the BleedBox includes the bleed.
  4. Embed or outline all fonts.
  5. Confirm spot colours are named and that black is not a rich build unless intended.
  6. Check effective resolution of every raster element at final size.
  7. Flatten or note any transparency that the chosen PDF/X level may not support.

If your file is an SVG and the printer wants a PDF, the conversion is mechanical but the prepress decisions are not. Read our guide to print-ready artwork for the setup side, and the format reference if you are deciding between PDF, EPS, AI and SVG in the first place.

For cutting and crafting destinations rather than presses, SVG versus DXF is the more useful comparison, and the SVG optimisation guide covers trimming a file down before delivery.

faqs.question: Does SVG support bleed and trim marks?
faqs.answer: No. The SVG specification defines a viewBox and width/height, but no TrimBox or BleedBox. You can draw crop marks as ordinary lines, but prepress software treats them as artwork, not instructions. For real print production, use PDF, which defines MediaBox, BleedBox, TrimBox and ArtBox natively.

faqs.question: Can I convert an SVG to a print-ready PDF?
faqs.answer: You can convert the geometry, but not the print setup. SVG to PDF conversion preserves paths, fills and strokes. It cannot add a TrimBox, convert sRGB to CMYK with an output intent, or embed fonts that were not already embedded. Add those parameters in a design application before export.

faqs.question: Why does my printer refuse SVG files?
faqs.answer: Because their RIP workflow expects PDF or EPS with defined page boxes and CMYK colour. An SVG gives them no trim definition and no colour separation, so they would have to reinterpret the job manually. It is a workflow constraint, not a technical limitation of the format.

faqs.question: Is PDF always vector?
faqs.answer: No. A PDF can contain only raster images, only vector content, or a mix. A PDF scanned from paper is a single raster image per page. A PDF exported from Illustrator with only paths is fully vector. Check by zooming in deeply — vector edges stay sharp, raster edges pixelate.

faqs.question: Which is smaller, SVG or PDF?
faqs.answer: For simple flat artwork, SVG is usually smaller because the XML is compact and paths are not wrapped in PDF object structure. For complex artwork with gradients, filters and type, PDF often wins because its compression and font subsetting are more efficient. Neither is dramatically smaller in normal use.

title: PNG vs SVG: Raster and Vector, Explained Without Jargon
seoTitle: PNG vs SVG: When Each Format Wins
seoDescription: PNG stores pixels, SVG stores shapes. That one difference decides whether a file scales, animates, and stays editable. A practical comparison.
excerpt: A PNG is a grid of pixels fixed at one resolution. An SVG is a list of shapes that renders at any size. Which one wins depends less on the artwork than on what happens to it next.
content:
Scale a 400 pixel PNG logo up to a 3 metre banner and every edge becomes a staircase. Scale the same logo as an SVG and it stays crisp because there were never any pixels to enlarge — just coordinates and curves interpreted anew at whatever size you asked for. That is the fundamental difference, and it is decided at authoring time, not at export.

Both formats are well supported in every browser, both can be transparent, and both are reasonable choices for web graphics. They are not interchangeable.

Pixels versus shapes

PNG is a raster format. The image is a rectangular grid of pixels, each holding a colour and an alpha value. The file stores that grid, compressed with DEFLATE preceded by PNG's own row filters. When you display it at 200% you are asking the renderer to interpolate values that do not exist, and it does its best with bilinear or bicubic guessing.

SVG is a vector format. The file holds geometry — paths defined by Bézier curves, rectangles, circles — plus instructions about how to paint them. At render time the renderer converts each path to device pixels at the current scale. A circle stays a circle at 16 pixels or 16000.

That has a second consequence people often miss: an SVG's complexity is measured in path count and node count, not pixel count. A simple logo might have 40 nodes and render instantly at any size. A traced photograph might have 200,000 nodes and render slowly at every size.

What PNG is genuinely good at

PNG excels at images that are inherently pixel-based: photographs, screenshots, scans, textures, gradients with subtle noise, anything with millions of distinct colours. Its lossless compression preserves those exactly, and its alpha channel is a full 8-bit channel, which is why designers reach for PNG when they need a clean transparent cutout.

PNG also handles anti-aliased soft edges naturally. A vector format representing a soft blur must approximate it with a filter or a gradient; a raster records it directly.

PropertyPNGSVG
Data modelPixel gridGeometry and paint instructions
ResolutionFixed at authoringResolution independent
Scales cleanlyNoYes, to any size
TransparencyFull 8-bit alpha channelAlpha per fill and group
Colour depthUp to 16-bit per channelsRGB, typically 8-bit
PhotographsExcellentPoor, needs thousands of paths
Logos and iconsWorkable at one sizeIdeal
EditabilityPixel-levelNode-level, text stays editable
CSS stylingNoYes, via currentColor and CSS
AnimationAPNG onlyNative SMIL and CSS animation
Typical size, flat logo20–200 KB1–10 KB
Typical size, photo1–8 MBSeveral MB, and looks worse

File size is not the simple story

The intuitive claim is that SVG files are always smaller. For flat vector art this is true and can be dramatic: a 512×512 PNG of a two-colour logo might be 60 KB, while the same logo as an optimised SVG might be 3 KB. Browsers render the SVG natively and the network transfer is a rounding error.

For complex artwork the claim collapses. Auto-trace a photograph into SVG and you get hundreds of thousands of tiny paths. The resulting file can easily exceed the JPEG it came from by an order of magnitude, and rendering becomes expensive because the browser has to rasterise every path on every repaint. A 4000×3000 photo saved as a 2 MB JPEG can become a 15 MB SVG that stutters on scroll.

There is a practical threshold. If the artwork has fewer than a few thousand distinct colour regions with clean edges — logos, icons, lettering, line art, flat illustrations — SVG wins on size and quality. If it has continuous tone, noise, or thousands of colours, raster wins on both.

Where each one breaks

PNG breaks when it is scaled up, embedded in a responsive layout that grows it, printed above its native resolution, or sent to a cutting machine that needs outlines. A 96 DPI PNG placed at 300 mm wide in a print layout will be visibly soft, and no amount of sharpening fixes missing detail.

SVG breaks when it contains a raster image inside it, carries an unresolvable font, references an external file, or is auto-traced from a source that never had clean edges. It also breaks in older email clients and some office applications, and in cutting software that expects fills rather than strokes.

Choosing based on destination

If the destination is a browser viewport of unknown size, SVG is the right default for anything that is not a photograph. It responds to CSS, it can be recoloured at runtime with currentColor, and it stays sharp on a 5K display without a second asset.

If the destination is a cutting machine, vinyl plotter, or laser, SVG is required. Those machines cut paths, and a PNG has to be traced first. PNG to SVG conversion is the standard route, and the quality of the result depends entirely on the source — a high-contrast, clean-edged PNG traces well; a blurry JPEG-style PNG does not.

If the destination is a photo gallery, a texture, a screenshot, or social media, PNG or JPEG is appropriate. SVG simply is not the tool for continuous-tone imagery.

If the destination needs a raster of a vector — a PNG for an email, a fallback, an app icon, or a social preview — then SVG to PNG renders at a chosen pixel size, and picking that size correctly is the whole game. Rendering at 4× the display size and letting CSS scale down is a common defensive choice.

Transparency behaviour differs

Both support transparency, but reliability differs. A PNG's alpha channel is unambiguous and universally supported. An SVG's transparency can depend on which renderer is reading it, and some email clients and document writers flatten or ignore it. If you need a transparent image in an environment you do not control, PNG is safer.

Conversely, SVG transparency composites at render time, so a soft drop shadow stays sharp at any scale, which is not true of a PNG's baked-in shadow.

Decoding cost and rendering budget

There is a rendering difference that rarely shows up in benchmarks but matters on long pages. A PNG decodes once into a bitmap and then composites cheaply on every scroll frame. An SVG is re-interpreted and rasterised whenever it repaints at a new scale or size, which costs real CPU for complex artwork.

For a single icon this is nothing. For a page with thirty complex traced illustrations, it becomes visible as scroll jank on lower-powered devices. The usual mitigation is to keep SVGs simple, cache the rasterisation where possible, and avoid animating SVG properties that force re-layout.

Print and physical output

Neither format is ideal for print on its own, but they fail differently. A PNG carries a DPI tag, and print software divides pixel dimensions by that number to derive a physical size. A 3000-pixel image tagged at 72 DPI becomes 41 inches wide, which is probably not what you wanted. Retagging to 300 DPI makes it 10 inches, and the pixel data is unchanged.

An SVG carries its physical size directly when width and height are in millimetres or inches, so there is no DPI to argue with. That is a genuine advantage for vector artwork bound for print, subject to the CMYK and bleed caveats in SVG versus PDF.

For a cutter or plotter, the difference is not close: an SVG is a set of paths the machine can follow, and a PNG is a picture of those paths that has to be traced first. If the destination is a vinyl cutter or laser, see the format map for the routes out of each format.

Metadata, text and accessibility

An SVG can carry a title and a description element, which screen readers and search engines can use. It can also carry live text that remains searchable and selectable. A PNG has no such structure — any text inside it is pixels, invisible to assistive technology unless you add alt text in the surrounding markup.

That makes SVG the better format for anything containing words that matter: a logo with a tagline, a chart with axis labels, a diagram with annotations. It also makes it preferable for anything that must be indexed. A PNG of a chart is a picture of information; an SVG of a chart is the information.

The conversion question

Converting PNG to SVG is not a format swap; it is a tracing operation. The tracer looks at pixels, finds boundaries between colour regions, and fits curves to them. The result is a genuine vector, but it is an interpretation of the raster, not a recovery of whatever vector authored the original.

Three factors decide quality: source resolution, source contrast, and colour count. A clean 2000 px PNG of a two-colour logo traces near-perfectly. A 300 px JPEG of the same logo, full of compression artefacts, traces into ragged blobs. If you are starting from a poor source, upscaling before vectorising can help, and there is more detail in how image tracing actually works.

Converting SVG to PNG is a simpler operation: rasterise at a target size. The main decisions are pixel dimensions, background colour, and whether to render at 1×, 2×, or higher for retina displays.

A note on SVG for photography

It is technically possible to embed a JPEG inside an SVG and call the result an SVG. That is a wrapper, not a vectorisation, and the resulting file inherits every raster limitation. Useful for keeping an asset pipeline consistent; useless for scaling a photo to billboard size.

For format context across the whole landscape, see the file format map and the format reference.

faqs.question: Is an SVG always smaller than a PNG?
faqs.answer: No. For flat artwork with few colours and clean edges, SVG is often ten to twenty times smaller. For auto-traced photographs, SVG can be several times larger than the equivalent JPEG or PNG because it stores thousands of individual paths. Complexity, not format, determines size.

faqs.question: Can I convert a PNG to SVG and get infinite quality?
faqs.answer: No. Conversion traces the existing pixels into paths, so it reproduces the detail that is present, not detail that never existed. A sharp source traces to sharp curves. A low-resolution or blurry source traces to rough approximations of its blur. The result is scalable, but it is a scalable version of the source.

faqs.question: Which format should I use for a website logo?
faqs.answer: SVG. It stays sharp on any display density, it is typically far smaller than a high-resolution PNG, and it can be recoloured with CSS. Keep a PNG fallback only if you must support an environment that cannot render SVG, which as of modern browsers is rare.

faqs.question: Does SVG support transparency?
faqs.answer: Yes, through alpha in fill and stroke, plus group opacity, masks and clip paths. The rendering model is flexible and composites at any size. A PNG's alpha channel is simpler and slightly more universally supported, so use PNG if the environment is unpredictable.

faqs.question: Why do my traced SVGs look worse than the original PNG?
faqs.answer: Tracing fits curves to colour boundaries, and photographic sources have noisy, anti-aliased boundaries. The tracer has to make decisions about which pixels belong to which region, and those decisions produce jagged or wobbly paths. Clean up the source and simplify the palette before tracing, or accept a stylised result.
