title: Vector File Formats Explained: A Practical Map
seoTitle: Vector File Formats Explained: SVG, DXF, EPS, PDF, AI, DST
seoDescription: Every vector format exists because one machine or program needed something the others could not provide. Here is the whole map in one place.
excerpt: Ten file formats show up in vector work, and each one encodes a different part of the truth: geometry, appearance, or machine instruction. Knowing which is which tells you what will survive a conversion and what will quietly disappear.
content:
Send an SVG to a laser cutter and it works. Send the same SVG to an embroidery machine and nothing happens. Send a DST to Illustrator and it opens as a pile of ungrouped line segments with no colour. The formats are not competing flavours of the same thing — they encode different information, and some of them discard almost everything about how the artwork looked.

The most useful way to organise the landscape is by asking two questions of any format: does it store geometry, and does it store appearance? Everything else — which software opens it, what the extension means, whether it is text or binary — follows from those two answers.

The master map

Here is the whole set on one page. Read it as a table of capabilities, not a ranking.

FormatTypeGeometryAppearanceTypical consumer
SVGXML vectorPaths, curves, textFull: fills, gradients, filters, CSSBrowsers, cutters, design apps
DXFCAD text/binaryExact, with unitsMinimal: layers, colours, lineweightsCAD, CAM, CNC, laser
EPSPostScript programExact, BézierCMYK and spot colour, no transparencyPrepress, screen print, legacy shops
PDFPage descriptionExact, plus page boxesCMYK, spot, embedded fonts, transparencyPrinters, proofing, archiving
AINative Illustrator (PDF-based)ExactFull, plus live layers and effectsIllustrator, some RIPs
DSTEmbroidery stitch fileStitch coordinates onlyNone: no colour, no thread order meaningTajima and compatible machines
PESEmbroidery (Brother)Stitch coordinatesThread palette referenceBrother and compatible machines
STL3D meshTriangles, no unitsNone: colour lostSlicers, 3D printing
3MF3D package (ZIP + XML)Mesh with unitsColour, materials, multiple objectsModern slicers
G-codeMachine instructionsNone: toolpath commandsNoneFirmware on the machine itself
PNGRasterNone: pixel gridExact, with alphaWeb, screenshots, photos
JPEGRaster, lossyNoneApproximatePhotography, web

Three families, not one

Look at the appearance column and the split becomes obvious. SVG, PDF, EPS and AI are presentation formats — they carry geometry and describe how to paint it. DXF, DST and PES are process formats — they carry geometry in a form a specific machine can execute, and appearance is either reduced to a token (a layer name, a thread number) or discarded. STL, 3MF and G-code are manufacturing formats, where geometry becomes a mesh or a toolpath.

Conversion within a family is usually lossless or close to it. Conversion across families is where information disappears, and knowing which direction loses what prevents most unpleasant surprises.

The presentation formats: SVG, PDF, EPS, AI

These four are the ones a designer works in. They share a geometry model based on paths and Bézier curves and they all care about how the result looks.

SVG is the web-native one. XML, CSS-styleable, resolution independent, and the only one of the four that a browser renders natively. Its weakness is print: no CMYK, no spot inks, no bleed or trim boxes. SVG versus PDF covers that gap in detail.

PDF is the print-native one. Page boxes, ICC profiles, embedded fonts, spot colour spaces — everything a press needs. It is the expected delivery format for commercial printing and the most reliable long-term archive for a vector document.

EPS is the legacy print one. PostScript-based, CMYK-capable, universally accepted by older prepress workflows. It predates transparency and has no layer model, and it is still requested by screen printers.

AI is Illustrator's native format. Modern AI files are PDF-compatible, which is why some tools open them at all, but the editable structure — live effects, symbols, artboards, appearance attributes — only reconstructs correctly inside Illustrator. Saving an AI with PDF compatibility enabled produces a file that other programs read as a PDF, which is often what you actually want to send.

What survives between them

Paths, fills, strokes, transforms and clipping generally move cleanly between all four. Gradients move but may be redefined. Transparency moves between PDF and AI, less reliably into EPS. Fonts only move reliably when embedded or outlined. Spot colours survive PDF and EPS, and vanish into SVG.

The process formats: DXF, DST, PES

These carry geometry for a specific class of machine, and each machine imposes its own constraints.

DXF is CAD interchange. Explicit units through $INSUNITS, layers as the organising principle, entities like LINE, ARC, POLYLINE and SPLINE. A DXF is what a laser, plasma table, waterjet or CNC router expects. There are no gradients and no opacity; a colour is a layer index or a true-colour integer.

DST is a Tajima embroidery stitch file. It does not store a design; it stores the order in which the needle enters and leaves the fabric, with jump and trim commands. Colour is not in the format — a DST is read against a machine's thread chart, and the colour order is a convention rather than data. Converting artwork to DST requires a digitizing step that decides stitch type, density, underlay and travel, because a fill path and a satin path produce different stitch sequences from the same outline. Our embroidery file format reference covers the family.

PES is Brother's version of the same idea, with a bit more metadata: thread palette index and some object structure. Still a stitch format, not a vector format, and still unreadable as geometry by a design app.

Why vector-to-embroidery is not a format conversion

Because embroidery is not a printing process. A 20 mm satin column stitches differently from a 20 mm fill, and a letter at 4 mm tall needs different density than the same letter at 40 mm. The conversion from SVG to DST is a digitizing operation with heuristics, not a transcription. Expect to adjust the output.

The manufacturing formats: STL, 3MF, G-code

STL is a triangle soup. Every surface is a mesh of triangles, normals optional, units unspecified. It cannot represent colour, multiple materials, or even a reliable sense of inside and outside for broken meshes. It is universal and minimal.

3MF is the modern replacement: a ZIP archive with XML inside, carrying units, colour, materials, multiple build items, and metadata. Most current slicers prefer it. The difference is covered in 3MF versus STL.

G-code is the finished instruction set. It is not geometry at all — it is a list of moves, feed rates, temperatures and fan speeds for one specific machine. Once you have G-code, the design intent is gone. You cannot meaningfully convert G-code back to a vector; you can only try to reconstruct paths from the toolpath, which is lossy and usually pointless.

Extrusion from a 2D outline — taking a flat logo and giving it height — is the bridge from vector work into this family. SVG to STL extrudes paths into a mesh, and a 3MF export keeps colour and units where STL would discard them.

You haveYou needRouteWhat is lost
PNG logoCut fileTrace to SVG, then to DXFPhotographic detail, gradients
SVG designPrint-ready PDFDesign app, CMYK + bleedNothing in geometry; colour intent must be set
PDF (vector)Editable SVGDirect conversionPage boxes, CMYK, some gradients
SVG outlineEmbroidery DSTDigitizing, not conversionEverything about appearance; stitch plan added
Customer artworkAny of the aboveDepends on sourceUnknown until inspected

How to identify what you were given

Extensions lie. A file named logo.ai may be a PDF, a TIFF, or an EPS. A logo.eps can be a PostScript wrapper around a single huge bitmap. Before planning any conversion, inspect the actual content.

Three quick checks work without specialist tools:

  • Open it in a text editor. Files starting with <?xml and containing <svg are SVG. Files starting with %PDF are PDF. Files starting with %!PS are PostScript, usually EPS. Files starting with PK are ZIP containers — which could be 3MF, or a modern AI or Office document.
  • Zoom in far. If edges stay sharp, it is vector. If they break into blocks, there is a raster inside, possibly hiding under vector clothing.
  • Count colours in the relevant region. A logo that should have three colours and shows anti-aliased thousands is a raster trace, not clean art.

The single most common failure

It is the bitmap wearing a vector extension. A designer exports a JPEG to a file named .eps, a client sends it along, and everyone downstream assumes it is vector until someone tries to scale it. Every conversion attempt then produces soft, fuzzy output because the source never had vector data in it.

The fix is to trace it properly first. PNG to SVG is the usual entry point, and how tracing works explains what the output will and will not be.

Choosing deliberately

Ask what the next consumer is before picking a format. A browser wants SVG. A press wants PDF. A laser wants DXF or SVG. An embroidery machine wants DST or PES. A slicer wants 3MF or STL. There is no universal export, and a file that opens everywhere usually compromises the thing its consumer needed most.

Where two work, pick the one that stores more information. SVG over DXF for design masters, because SVG retains appearance and DXF does not. PDF over EPS for anything with transparency. 3MF over STL for anything multicolour. Keeping the richer file as the master means you can always regenerate the poorer one.

For the detailed reference version of this map, see the Vectorr file format reference. Our SVG versus DXF comparison goes deeper on the geometry-versus-presentation split that drives most unit bugs.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a vector and a raster file?
faqs.answer: A vector file stores geometry — coordinates, curves and paint instructions — and renders at any size. A raster file stores a grid of pixels fixed at one resolution and blurs when enlarged. SVG, PDF, EPS, DXF and AI are vector. PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and TIFF are raster.

faqs.question: Why can't an embroidery machine read an SVG?
faqs.answer: Because embroidery needs stitches, not outlines. The machine requires an ordered sequence of needle penetrations with stitch type, density and underlay decisions. An SVG supplies only the boundary of a shape. Converting it to DST or PES is a digitizing step that decides what those stitches are, not a format swap.

faqs.question: Is an AI file the same as a PDF?
faqs.answer: Modern AI files saved with PDF compatibility contain a PDF stream, so many programs can open them as if they were PDFs. But the editable structure — live effects, symbols, layers, appearance — only reconstructs in Illustrator. If you need universal compatibility, export a PDF rather than relying on the AI file.

faqs.question: Which format should I keep as my master file?
faqs.answer: Keep the richest one your workflow produces, usually SVG for screen and cutter work or PDF for print. Everything else can be regenerated. Never keep only a low-information derivative like DXF or STL as the master, because the appearance data is gone and cannot be recovered.

faqs.question: Can I convert G-code back into a vector file?
faqs.answer: Not usefully. G-code holds machine moves with feed rates and tool commands, not the original geometry. Reconstructing paths from toolpath produces lines along the tool centreline, which lose the distinction between cut contours, fill lines and travel moves. Always keep the source vector alongside the G-code.

title: What Is an SVG, Really? Inside the Markup
seoTitle: What Is an SVG File? Anatomy of Vector Markup
seoDescription: An SVG is XML describing paths, not pixels. Read a real file's structure, learn what viewBox does, and see why it is both powerful and fragile.
excerpt: Strip the branding and an SVG is a short XML document full of coordinates. Understanding the root element, the viewBox, and how shapes nest explains most of the behaviour that surprises people when a file reaches a machine.
content:
A minimal SVG that draws a red circle is about eighty bytes of text. Open it in a text editor and you can read every decision that produced the image: the canvas size, the coordinate window, the shape, and the paint. No other common image format offers this, and that transparency is both why SVG is so useful and why it confuses people who expect an image file to be opaque.

SVG stands for Scalable Vector Graphics. It is a W3C recommendation, currently at SVG 2 with SVG 1.1 as the widely implemented baseline, and it is an XML application — its syntax rules come from XML, and its rendering model is defined separately in the specification.

What is actually inside the file

Every SVG begins with an XML declaration and a root <svg> element that carries the xmlns namespace. Inside, the document is a tree of elements: shapes, groups, definitions, and paint references. Nothing is stored as an image; everything is stored as instructions.

Here is the anatomy, shape by shape.

ElementPurposeWhat commonly goes wrong
<svg>Root; establishes canvas and coordinate systemNo width/height, so size is inferred by the viewer
<path>Arbitrary outline defined by d commandsUnclosed subpaths render with an unintended chord
<rect>Axis-aligned rectanglerounded corners via rx/ry are forgotten on export
<circle> / <ellipse>True curves, not polygonsConverters approximate them as polylines
<polygon> / <polyline>Straight-segment shapesLarge node counts from raster tracing
<line>Single segment with strokeInvisible when stroke is not set
<g>Group; attributes inherit to childrenNested transforms multiply unexpectedly
<defs>Container for reusable definitionsNothing in it renders until referenced
<use>Instantiates a definition by referenceCutting software may ignore it entirely
<text>Live, editable typeMachine software drops it; needs outlining
<image>Embedded or linked rasterLinked files break when the SVG moves
<style>CSS rules applied to the documentStripped by importers that only read attributes

Why shapes are not the same as outlines

A <circle> with radius 50 is a mathematically perfect circle. A <path> that looks like a circle is four cubic Bézier segments approximating one. Visually identical at normal sizes, but not identical objects. Cutters and CAM tools care about this because a circle can be cut as a single arc move, while an approximated circle becomes a dense polyline.

The same holds for stroked versus filled geometry. A 1 mm stroke is paint applied along a zero-width path, not a 1 mm wide band of geometry. Software that reads strokes as cuts behaves differently from software that reads fills as cuts, which is why layer conventions matter so much. Our laser cutting guide explains the conventions in detail.

The coordinate system and the viewBox

This is the part that causes nearly every scaling problem. Two things define the geometry-to-canvas mapping.

width and height describe the canvas — the box the SVG occupies in its container. They can be in user units, or in real units such as mm, cm, in, pt, px. When expressed in real units they are tied to the CSS definition of that unit: one inch equals 96 CSS pixels.

viewBox describes the internal coordinate window, as four numbers: minimum x, minimum y, width, and height. It says "the drawing inside this document lives between these coordinates." Everything in the file is positioned relative to that window.

The viewBox is then fitted to the canvas using the preserveAspectRatio rule, which by default is xMidYMid meet — scale uniformly to fit, centre it, and add empty space if the aspect ratios differ.

Why this matters for machines

A document with a viewBox of 0 0 100 100 and no width or height has no physical size at all. A browser will size it to its container. Illustrator will open it at 100 points. A laser cutter's importer will often assume 100 millimetres.

A document with width="100mm" height="100mm" and the same viewBox is unambiguous: 100 millimetres, with one user unit equal to one millimetre. That version behaves correctly almost everywhere.

The recommended pattern for anything destined for a machine is therefore explicit dimensions in the physical unit plus a viewBox with matching numbers, so the user-unit-to-millimetre ratio is exactly 1:1. Our SVG versus DXF comparison covers what happens when a file without that is handed to CAD.

Presentation and structure

SVG separates content from style in the same way HTML does. A shape's fill can be set as a presentation attribute, presented as CSS in a <style> block, or applied by inline style attribute. All three are valid; the cascade decides the winner, with the inline style highest priority after important declarations.

That flexibility is a problem in practice. Many importers — cutting software, CAD tools, some office suites — read only presentation attributes and ignore CSS entirely. If your file's colours come from a <style> block, those importers may render everything black or drop it. For machine-bound files, prefer presentation attributes on the elements themselves.

Groups, transforms and inheritance

A <g> element groups children and applies its attributes to them. If a group has fill="red", every child without its own fill is red. If a group has transform="translate(10 20) scale(2)", every child coordinate is scaled and offset by that matrix, and transforms nest multiplicatively.

Nested transforms are the second most common source of surprise after missing units. A shape may say it is 5 units wide, but three ancestor transforms can make it 200 units wide on screen. Most conversion tools flatten transforms before writing other formats, which is correct — but only if the flattening respects the whole ancestor chain. Optimising an SVG usually includes exactly this step.

Using <use> to instance repeated definitions is elegant in a browser and poorly supported in CAD and cutting software, which may render every instance from the original position — stacking copies on top of each other. For machine output, expand <use> before export.

Painting: fills, strokes, gradients

Fills can be a solid colour, a gradient, or a pattern. Both linearGradient and radialGradient live in <defs> or anywhere else and are referenced with url(#id). Patterns work the same way.

Strokes add width, linecap, linejoin, dasharray and dashoffset. A dashed stroke is an instruction to the renderer, not geometry. Convert a dashed line to DXF and you get either a solid line or a long series of individual dashes, depending on the converter, and only one of those is what you wanted.

Filters — blur, drop shadow, displacement maps — are also part of the language, backed by SVG filter primitives. They are expensive to render and unsupported by almost every non-browser consumer. Rasterise anything that depends on a filter before sending it anywhere that is not a browser.

Nesting and the coordinate stack

Every element that can hold children can establish a new coordinate system, and those systems stack. A translate on the root shifts everything below it; a scale on a group inside multiplies everything below that; a rotate on a single path applies only to that path. The transform attribute takes a list of matrix operations applied left to right, which contradicts most people's intuition about order until they work through an example.

The transform translate(50 0) rotate(30) means: first rotate the coordinate system by 30 degrees, then translate 50 units along the rotated x axis. Reverse the order and the shape lands somewhere entirely different. Design tools hide this, but exporters write it out literally, and any tool that reads the file sees the matrices as given.

Most converters flatten transforms before writing another format, which resolves the ambiguity. It also means the output has no structure left, so if you need machine-readable groups in the destination, name them before flattening.

Clipping and masking

A clipPath restricts where a shape can paint. It takes any shape as a boundary and clips children to the region inside it. A mask does the same thing but with alpha, so a gradient mask fades content out rather than cutting it hard. Both are structural and neither survives most machine-bound conversions, because a cutter has no notion of a region that partially shows artwork.

In practice, a design file with four clip paths and two masks will convert to either flattened geometry, if the tool is good, or to visibly wrong geometry, if it is not. Check before sending.

Text, fonts and control

The text element places glyphs at coordinates and lets the layout engine do the rest. Characters can be positioned precisely with x and y lists, spaced with dx and dy lists, or rotated with a rotate list. Combined with text-anchor, alignment works reasonably.

That flexibility is exactly why text is the most fragile part of an SVG. The font is a reference, not data, unless it has been converted to paths. A browser substitutes, an application prompts, and a cutting machine ignores it. Designers who deliver files for production almost always convert type to outlines at the last step — which keeps a working copy with live text elsewhere.

Accessibility considerations

An inline SVG is part of the document tree, so its title and desc elements can be announced by assistive technology, and shapes can receive focus and ARIA roles. That makes SVG materially better than a PNG for any graphic that conveys information. Use a title as the accessible name and desc for a longer explanation; leave decorative graphics without them so screen readers skip them.

Storage and delivery

SVG compresses well because it is repetitive text, and most servers gzip it automatically. A 20 KB raw SVG often arrives as 5 KB over the wire. That, combined with caching, makes it the cheapest way to ship sharp artwork over a network — a point worth weighing against the tracing-size caveat in PNG versus SVG.

What SVG deliberately does not do

There is no CMYK colour space, no spot inks, no bleed box, and no page model beyond the single canvas. That is not an oversight; the format was specified for the web, where those concepts do not apply. When a job needs them, PDF is the format — see SVG versus PDF for print.

SVG also has no built-in notion of layers. Grouping is the closest equivalent, and some applications read inkscape:groupmode="layer" or data-name attributes, but the specification knows nothing about them.

For the surrounding landscape, see the practical map of vector file formats. If you have a bitmap rather than an SVG, PNG to SVG is the entry point, and SVG to PNG produces a raster at a size you choose.

One more practical note: because SVG is XML, it can carry scripts and external references. That is legitimate for interactive graphics and a genuine risk for upload pipelines — covered in SVG security.

faqs.question: Is SVG just XML?
faqs.answer: Structurally yes. An SVG file is a well-formed XML document whose elements come from the SVG namespace. That is why you can open one in a text editor, validate it with an XML parser, and transform it with XSLT. The rendering behaviour is defined separately by the SVG specification, not by XML.

faqs.question: What does the viewBox attribute actually do?
faqs.answer: It defines the internal coordinate window — the rectangle of user-space coordinates that the drawing occupies. The renderer scales that window to fit the element's width and height. If width and height are omitted, the viewer chooses a size, which is why the same file can render at wildly different physical sizes in different programs.

faqs.question: Why does my SVG have no units?
faqs.answer: Because SVG user units are a device-independent concept tied to CSS pixels, at 96 per inch, and physical units are optional. Many design tools export with only a viewBox. For machine work, set width and height explicitly in millimetres so the file states its physical size unambiguously.

faqs.question: Can an SVG contain a raster image?
faqs.answer: Yes, via the image element, either embedding base64 data or linking to an external file. A linked image makes the SVG dependent on that file staying put. An embedded one makes the SVG self-contained but is no longer purely vector.

faqs.question: Do browsers support SVG 2?
faqs.answer: Partially. Chrome, Firefox and Safari implement a large subset of SVG 2 alongside the SVG 1.1 baseline, but several SVG 2 features remain unimplemented or inconsistent. For production use, target the shared 1.1 behaviour plus widely supported convenience features. Features such as mesh gradients and some paint servers remain unimplemented after years, so test anything unusual in your actual target browsers.

title: 3MF vs STL: Why the Newer Format Prints Better
seoTitle: 3MF vs STL: Format Differences for 3D Printing
seoDescription: STL stores triangles and nothing else. 3MF stores color, units, materials and structure. Compare them and see where STL quietly costs you prints.
excerpt: STL stores only triangle meshes with no units, color, or material data. 3MF embeds units, per-object materials, print settings, and thumbnails in a compressed ZIP archive. Use STL for universal compatibility, 3MF for multi-material prints and modern slicers. Convert losslessly via PrusaSlicer or Bambu Studio.
content:
STL has been the standard 3D printing format for three decades, yet it encodes only triangle meshes with no material, color, or unit information. Every time you export an STL, you lose metadata — the slicer guesses whether the model is in millimeters or inches, and multi-color prints require separate files per extruder. 3MF solves these problems by embedding units, materials, colors, print settings, and support structures into a single compressed archive. The question is not whether 3MF is better — it objectively is — but whether your slicer, printer firmware, and workflow support it yet.

This guide explains what each format encodes, when to use STL for compatibility versus 3MF for fidelity, and how to convert between them without losing critical data.

What STL Contains (and What It Doesn't)

An STL file is a list of triangles defined by three vertices and a normal vector per triangle. That is the entire specification. No units, no color, no texture coordinates, no material properties. When you open an STL in a slicer, the software assumes the coordinates are in millimeters unless told otherwise. If the model was exported in inches, it prints 25.4 times too large.

STL comes in two flavors: ASCII (human-readable, 5–10× larger) and binary (compact, the default for most exporters). Binary STL has a 50,000-triangle file size around 2 MB. ASCII STL for the same model is 10–15 MB. Use binary unless you need to edit the file in a text editor for debugging.

STL Advantages

STL is universal. Every slicer, CAD tool, and mesh repair utility reads it. Firmware written in 1995 for industrial SLA machines reads it. If you send a model to a service bureau or share it with a client who uses unknown software, STL is the safest choice.

STL is simple. Parsers are trivial to write, and the format has no versioning issues. A file written in 1990 opens identically in 2026 software.

STL Failures

STL cannot encode multiple shells (separate disconnected meshes) in a meaningful way. Each shell becomes part of the same triangle list with no identifier. Slicers treat multi-shell STLs as single objects, which breaks when you need to assign different materials to different parts.

STL has no color data. Multi-material printers require one STL per extruder, manually aligned in the slicer. If alignment is wrong by 0.1 mm, the print has visible seams.

STL does not store normals consistently. Some exporters compute normals from vertex order; others write explicit normals that contradict vertex winding. Slicers recompute normals on import, which occasionally flips faces inside-out.

What 3MF Contains

3MF is a ZIP archive containing an XML manifest, one or more mesh files (in a triangle format similar to STL), and optional textures, thumbnails, and metadata. The manifest declares units (millimeters, inches, microns), materials (PLA, ABS, TPU with color), and build instructions (which extruder, which object goes where on the bed).

Rename a 3MF file to .zip and unzip it. You will find:

  • [Content_Types].xml — declares the archive structure
  • 3D/3dmodel.model — the main mesh and metadata file
  • Metadata/thumbnail.png — preview image for slicer libraries
  • Textures/*.png — color maps for full-color prints

3MF Advantages

3MF stores units explicitly. A model designed in millimeters prints at the correct size even if opened in a slicer set to inches. No manual scaling needed.

3MF supports multiple objects with per-object materials. A multi-color print is one file, not five STLs. The slicer reads which extruder to use for each part from the manifest.

3MF includes print settings as optional metadata: layer height, infill percentage, support placement. When you open a 3MF in PrusaSlicer or Bambu Studio, it auto-populates settings from the file. For print farms or shared models, this reduces setup errors.

3MF is compressed. A model that is 50 MB as ASCII STL or 8 MB as binary STL is typically 1–2 MB as 3MF.

FeatureSTL3MF
Mesh geometryYes (triangles)Yes (triangles)
Units (mm, inches)No (assumed)Yes (explicit)
Multiple objectsNo (all merged)Yes (per-object materials)
Color / materialNoYes
Print settingsNoYes (optional metadata)
File size2–10 MB (binary/ASCII)1–2 MB (compressed)
CompatibilityUniversalModern slicers only (2016+)

When to Use STL

Use STL when the recipient's software is unknown or old. Service bureaus, CNC shops, and industrial SLA operators often use software that predates 3MF. If you are sending a file to a third party, ask which format they prefer. If they don't specify, send STL.

Use STL for single-material prints where color and units are already agreed upon. If you designed a part in millimeters and the printer operator knows that, STL is adequate.

Use STL for mesh repair workflows. Tools like Meshmixer, Netfabb, and Microsoft 3D Builder expect STL input. After repair, you can convert back to 3MF.

When to Use 3MF

Use 3MF for multi-material or multi-color prints. Pack all parts into one file with material assignments in the manifest. The slicer handles extruder switching automatically.

Use 3MF when sharing models on Printables, Thingiverse, or MakerWorld. The thumbnail embedded in the 3MF displays in the file browser, and users see the recommended print settings when they open the file.

Use 3MF for print farms or batch production. Export the model with layer height, infill, and support settings baked in. Operators load the file and print without manual configuration.

Converting Between STL and 3MF

Most slicers convert both directions: import STL, export 3MF (or vice versa). The conversion is straightforward in one direction and lossy in the other.

STL to 3MF (Lossless)

Open the STL in PrusaSlicer, Bambu Studio, or Cura. Set the units if the model imported at the wrong scale (Edit → Scale, or set units in the import dialog). Assign materials if the model has multiple parts. Export to 3MF (File → Export → Export as 3MF).

The resulting 3MF contains the same mesh as the STL plus metadata: units, materials, and optionally print settings. If you save the slicer project before export, settings embed automatically.

3MF to STL (Lossy)

Open the 3MF in a slicer and export to STL (File → Export → Export as STL). The mesh geometry is preserved, but units, materials, and settings are lost. If the 3MF contains multiple objects, the slicer may merge them into one STL or export each as a separate file (behavior varies by slicer).

For multi-part 3MFs, manually select each object in the slicer and export individually. Name each STL descriptively (e.g., body.stl, cap.stl) so you can reassemble them later.

3MF Compatibility in 2026

As of 2026, most modern slicers support 3MF: PrusaSlicer, Cura, Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer, Simplify3D v5+, and Creality Print. Older firmware (pre-2018 Marlin, Repetier) does not read 3MF directly — the slicer must convert it to G-code first.

Some CAD tools still export STL by default (Fusion 360, SolidWorks) but offer 3MF as an option. Enable it in export settings: look for "Save as type → 3MF" or "Export format → 3D Manufacturing Format."

If a tool does not support 3MF, use a slicer as a format converter: import the STL, export as 3MF. PrusaSlicer and Bambu Studio handle this cleanly.

Best Practices for Each Format

For STL

  • Always export binary STL unless you need to debug in a text editor.
  • Set units explicitly in the export dialog (millimeters for most prints, inches for imperial-dimensioned parts).
  • Include scale or unit information in the filename (widget_100mm.stl) to avoid ambiguity.
  • Check mesh integrity before exporting: no flipped normals, no open edges, no self-intersections.

For 3MF

  • Embed a thumbnail so the model previews in file browsers and slicer libraries.
  • Assign materials and colors to each object in the manifest.
  • Set print settings (layer height, infill) if the model has recommended values.
  • Test the 3MF in the target slicer before sharing — not all slicers parse metadata identically.

The Future: OBJ, STEP, and glTF

3MF is not the end of the format story. OBJ supports vertex colors and texture coordinates, making it suitable for full-color resin prints. STEP is a CAD interchange format that preserves parametric history, useful for remixing designs. glTF is a web-native 3D format with PBR materials and animations, increasingly used for AR/VR previews of 3D prints.

For now, 3MF is the best balance of features and compatibility for FDM and SLA printing. Use STL when you need absolute universal compatibility, and export both if unsure.

faqs.question: What is the main difference between STL and 3MF?
faqs.answer: STL stores only triangle meshes with no units, color, or material information. 3MF is a ZIP archive containing meshes, units (mm/inches), per-object materials, colors, and optional print settings. 3MF is better for multi-material prints and modern workflows; STL is better for universal compatibility.

faqs.question: Can I convert STL to 3MF without losing data?
faqs.answer: Yes. Open the STL in PrusaSlicer or Bambu Studio, set units and materials, and export as 3MF. The mesh geometry is preserved and metadata is added. Converting 3MF to STL is lossy — units, materials, and settings are discarded, leaving only the mesh.

faqs.question: Why is my STL printing at the wrong size?
faqs.answer: STL does not store units — slicers assume millimeters by default. If the model was exported in inches, it prints 25.4× too large. In the slicer, scale the model by 25.4 (inches→mm) or 0.0394 (mm→inches) before slicing.

faqs.question: Which format is better for multi-color 3D printing?
faqs.answer: 3MF. It supports per-object material assignments in one file. STL requires one file per extruder, manually aligned in the slicer. Misalignment by 0.1 mm causes visible seams. Use 3MF for multi-material or multi-color prints.

faqs.question: Do all slicers support 3MF in 2026?
faqs.answer: Most modern slicers (PrusaSlicer, Cura, Bambu Studio, OrcaSlicer, Simplify3D v5+) support 3MF. Older firmware (pre-2018 Marlin) does not read 3MF directly — the slicer must convert it to G-code. For unknown recipients, send STL for safety.

title: Converting an SVG to STL for 3D Printing
seoTitle: SVG to STL: Extrude 2D Art Into a Printable Mesh
seoDescription: An SVG is a flat outline. Getting it to print means extruding it, orienting it, and checking it is watertight. Walk the full path from artwork to slicer.
excerpt: Convert 2D SVG to 3D STL by extruding closed paths. Prepare the SVG: convert text to paths, close all paths, simplify nodes, merge overlapping shapes. Use Blender for control, Tinkercad for speed, OpenSCAD for batch processing. Check STL in slicer for non-manifold errors before printing.
content:
Converting a 2D SVG logo or design into a 3D printable STL mesh requires extrusion — pulling the flat vector paths into the third dimension by a specified height. The process is conceptually simple, but the execution depends on which tool you use, whether your SVG has open paths or overlapping shapes, and how you intend to handle details smaller than your printer's nozzle diameter. A conversion that works perfectly in Blender may fail in OpenSCAD, and a file that previews correctly in Tinkercad may slice with errors in PrusaSlicer.

This guide explains the SVG-to-STL pipeline, shows how to prepare SVG files for clean extrusion, and compares the three most reliable tools: Blender, Tinkercad, and OpenSCAD.

Understanding the Conversion Process

SVG describes 2D vector paths — Bézier curves, lines, arcs — with no concept of depth. STL describes 3D triangle meshes with vertices, edges, and faces. To convert between them, a tool must:

  1. Parse the SVG and extract closed paths (open paths cannot become solid meshes).
  2. Triangulate each closed path into a 2D face.
  3. Extrude the face along the Z-axis by a user-specified height.
  4. Generate side walls connecting the top and bottom faces.
  5. Export the resulting mesh as STL.

Each tool handles step 1 differently. Blender imports SVG directly as curve objects. Tinkercad rasterizes the SVG first, then traces it. OpenSCAD requires you to convert SVG to a specific path format manually. The tool you choose depends on how clean your SVG is and how much control you need over the output.

Preparing the SVG for Extrusion

Before converting, clean the SVG to remove features that break extrusion: open paths, text, raster images, and overlapping shapes with ambiguous boolean intent.

Convert Text to Paths

Text in SVG is stored as <text> elements with font references, not outlines. Most 3D tools cannot extrude text directly. In Inkscape or Illustrator, select all text and choose Path → Object to Path (Inkscape) or Type → Create Outlines (Illustrator). This converts each character into vector outlines.

Close All Paths

Open paths (lines, arcs that do not form closed loops) cannot extrude into solid meshes. In Inkscape, select all paths and choose Path → Close Path. Open the XML editor (Edit → XML Editor) and check that every <path> element ends with a Z or z command (which closes the path). If not, manually close the path by connecting endpoints or delete the open path if it is decorative.

Simplify Complex Paths

SVG paths with thousands of nodes produce STL meshes with millions of triangles, which slow slicing and increase file size. Simplify paths before conversion: select all, choose Path → Simplify (Ctrl+L in Inkscape), and run it twice. This reduces node count by 30–50% with minimal visual change. For logos and icons, set a low smoothing threshold to preserve sharp corners.

Merge Overlapping Shapes

If your SVG has overlapping shapes (e.g., a logo with a letter inside a circle), decide whether the overlap is a union (merge) or a subtraction (cut). In Inkscape, select the shapes and use Path → Union, Difference, or Exclusion to resolve ambiguity. This prevents the 3D tool from extruding both shapes independently, which creates non-manifold geometry that slicers cannot handle.

SVG FeatureEffect on STL ConversionFix
Text elementsIgnored or rasterizedConvert to paths (Object to Path / Create Outlines)
Open pathsFail to extrude or produce gapsClose Path in Inkscape, verify Z command in XML
Overlapping shapesNon-manifold mesh, slicer errorsUse Union, Difference, or Exclusion to resolve
Excessive nodesBloated STL, slow slicingPath → Simplify (Ctrl+L) before conversion
Raster imagesIgnoredRemove or trace with Trace Bitmap first

Method 1: Blender (Best Control, Steeper Learning Curve)

Blender imports SVG as curve objects and offers precise control over extrusion depth, beveling, and mesh topology. It is the best choice for complex logos with fine details or for models where you need to adjust geometry after extrusion.

Importing SVG into Blender

Open Blender and delete the default cube (select it, press X, confirm). Go to File → Import → Scalable Vector Graphics (.svg) and select your file. Blender imports the SVG as curve objects in the 3D viewport. If the import scale is wrong, select all curves (A), press S to scale, and type a numeric factor (e.g., 0.1 for 10% size).

Extruding Curves

Select a curve object (click it in the viewport or outliner). In the Properties panel, open the Curve Properties tab (icon: Bézier curve). Under Geometry, set Extrude to the desired height (e.g., 5.0 for 5 mm). The curve becomes a 3D mesh in the viewport. Adjust the extrusion value until the depth looks correct.

For beveled edges, set Bevel → Depth to 0.1–0.5. This rounds the top edges, which improves printability by preventing sharp overhangs. Set Resolution to 3–6 for smooth bevels.

Converting Curves to Mesh and Exporting

With the curve selected, press Alt+C (or Object → Convert To → Mesh). Blender converts the curve into a triangle mesh. Repeat for all curve objects. Select all meshes (A), then Object → Join (Ctrl+J) to merge them into one object.

Export to STL: File → Export → STL. In the export dialog, enable Selection Only if you merged everything, set Scale to 1.0, and choose Binary format. Save the file. Open it in your slicer to verify the mesh is manifold and the size is correct.

Method 2: Tinkercad (Easiest, Limited Control)

Tinkercad is a browser-based CAD tool that imports SVG and extrudes it with one button click. It is the fastest method for simple logos and icons, but it rasterizes the SVG before tracing, which introduces stair-stepping on curves.

Importing SVG into Tinkercad

Open Tinkercad and sign in (free account required). Create a new design. Click Import in the top-right and select your SVG. Set the import scale (mm or inches) and height. Tinkercad traces the SVG and drops the extruded shape onto the workplane.

The trace quality depends on the SVG complexity. Simple shapes (logos, text, icons) work well. Intricate details (filigree, hairlines) may vanish or become blocky.

Adjusting and Exporting

Select the imported shape and adjust its height in the properties panel (right side). Use the Align tool to center it on the workplane if needed. Once satisfied, click Export → .STL in the top-right. Download the file and open it in your slicer.

Tinkercad STLs are typically larger (more triangles) than Blender or OpenSCAD exports because Tinkercad does not optimize mesh topology. For small prints (keychains, badges), this is acceptable. For large models, use Blender for leaner meshes.

Method 3: OpenSCAD (Scriptable, Best for Automation)

OpenSCAD reads SVG via the linear_extrude() function, but only for SVG files with clean path syntax. It is the best choice for batch processing or parametric designs where you want to extrude the same SVG at multiple heights.

Preparing SVG for OpenSCAD

OpenSCAD requires SVG paths in absolute coordinates with no transforms. Export your SVG from Inkscape as Plain SVG (not Inkscape SVG) with Path → Object to Path and Path → Simplify applied. Open the SVG in a text editor and verify that <path> elements have a d attribute with commands like M, L, C, Z. If you see transform= attributes, remove them or apply them manually.

Writing the OpenSCAD Script

Create a new OpenSCAD file (.scad) and write:

linear_extrude(height=5) import("logo.svg");

Replace 5 with your desired height in millimeters and "logo.svg" with the path to your SVG file (relative or absolute). Press F5 to preview or F6 to render. If the preview is empty, check the console for errors — usually "path not found" or "invalid SVG syntax."

Exporting STL from OpenSCAD

Once the render finishes, go to File → Export → Export as STL. OpenSCAD writes a binary STL. Open it in your slicer to verify size and geometry.

For batch processing, write a shell script that generates multiple STLs at different heights:

for h in 3 5 10; do echo "linear_extrude(height=$h) import(\"logo.svg\");" | openscad -o logo_${h}mm.stl /dev/stdin; done

Fixing Common Conversion Failures

Three problems appear frequently: non-manifold geometry, inverted normals, and incorrect scale.

Non-Manifold Geometry (Slicer Errors)

Non-manifold meshes have edges shared by more than two faces, or faces with holes. Slicers cannot process them. The cause is usually overlapping shapes in the SVG that were not merged. Open the STL in Blender, enter Edit mode (Tab), select all (A), and run Mesh → Clean Up → Merge by Distance. Set the threshold to 0.001 and click OK. Then run Mesh → Normals → Recalculate Outside. Re-export the STL.

Inverted Normals (Inside-Out Mesh)

If your model slices with walls missing or the interior filled, the normals are inverted. In Blender, select the mesh, enter Edit mode (Tab), select all (A), and choose Mesh → Normals → Recalculate Outside (Shift+N). Re-export.

Incorrect Scale

If the STL imports into the slicer at 0.1 mm or 10 meters instead of 100 mm, the units are wrong. SVG uses user units (typically pixels or points), not millimeters. In Blender, scale the object before exporting: select it, press S, type the scale factor (e.g., 0.1 or 10), and press Enter. In OpenSCAD, multiply the extrude height by the scale factor: linear_extrude(height=5*0.1).

Best Practices for SVG-to-STL

  • Always convert text to paths before extrusion.
  • Close all open paths and simplify complex geometry.
  • Merge overlapping shapes with Union or Difference to avoid non-manifold errors.
  • Set extrusion height to at least 2× your nozzle diameter (e.g., 0.8 mm for a 0.4 mm nozzle) for structural strength.
  • Check the STL in a slicer before printing — preview mode shows non-manifold errors as red regions.

faqs.question: Can I convert any SVG to STL for 3D printing?
faqs.answer: Only SVG files with closed paths can extrude into solid meshes. Text, open paths, and raster images must be converted or removed first. In Inkscape, convert text to paths (Path → Object to Path) and close all paths (Path → Close Path) before converting to STL.

faqs.question: What is the easiest way to convert SVG to STL?
faqs.answer: Tinkercad. Upload your SVG at tinkercad.com, set height and scale, and export as STL. It works well for simple logos and icons. For complex designs with fine details, use Blender for better control over extrusion depth and mesh topology.

faqs.question: Why does my STL have holes or slicer errors?
faqs.answer: The SVG had overlapping shapes that were not merged, producing non-manifold geometry. Open the STL in Blender, enter Edit mode (Tab), select all, run Mesh → Clean Up → Merge by Distance (threshold 0.001), then Mesh → Normals → Recalculate Outside. Re-export.

faqs.question: How do I set the correct size when converting SVG to STL?
faqs.answer: SVG uses user units (pixels/points), not millimeters. In Blender, scale the object before export: select it, press S, type the scale factor (e.g., 0.1 or 10). In OpenSCAD, multiply the extrude height by the scale factor. Check the size in your slicer after conversion.

faqs.question: Can I batch-convert multiple SVGs to STL?
faqs.answer: Yes, with OpenSCAD. Write a script: for f in *.svg; do echo "linear_extrude(height=5) import(\"$f\");" | openscad -o "${f%.svg}.stl" /dev/stdin; done to extrude all SVGs in a directory at 5 mm height.

title: How to Optimize an SVG Without Breaking It
seoTitle: SVG Optimization Guide: Cut File Size, Keep Fidelity
seoDescription: Most SVGs ship with editor debris. Learn which savings are free, which change rendering, and how to verify a file still looks right after optimization.
excerpt: Optimizing an SVG is not one job. Some passes delete nothing but editor debris; others silently move curves and change how a file cuts. Here is what each pass actually does, what it typically saves, and how to prove the file still looks right.
content:
Every SVG that leaves Illustrator, Inkscape, or a print portal carries baggage: XML namespaces from the editor that made it, metadata blocks, hidden layers, clip paths nobody references, and coordinate values written to twelve decimal places. All of that is weight. None of it is drawing. Optimizing an SVG means deleting the weight without changing the drawing — and the honest version of that sentence is that it means deleting the weight without changing the drawing enough that anyone notices.

The second half of that sentence is where files break. A pass that strips metadata is provably safe. A pass that rounds coordinates to whole numbers is not. Both of them live in the same tool under the same button, which is why people who optimize a cut file and hand it to a laser sometimes find open paths where there were closed ones. This guide separates the passes by risk, then shows how to verify the result instead of trusting it.

What actually lives inside a bloated SVG

Before trimming, it helps to know what you are looking at. Open a freshly exported SVG in a text editor and read the first few lines. On an Illustrator export you will usually find three things stacked on top of each other.

  • Namespace declarations. The root element typically declares the SVG namespace plus any others the editor needs. Adobe Illustrator adds xmlns:x and xmlns:i so it can store round-trip data for reopening the file. Inkscape declares xmlns:inkscape and xmlns:sodipodi. None of these matter to a rendering engine unless an actual attribute or element in the SVG body uses that namespace prefix.
  • Metadata blocks. Illustrator embeds XMP metadata carrying the file creation date, editor version, and license. Inkscape embeds metadata with RDF and Dublin Core tags. When a renderer sees metadata inside a standard SVG, it ignores it. So does a laser.
  • Unused definitions. The defs section holds gradients, clip paths, patterns, filters, and symbols that the document references by ID. Over time, a file accumulates defs that were once used, were never used, or were used on a layer that was later deleted. The renderer will ignore any def that nothing references.

These three categories make the easiest targets because you can delete them without changing what the file draws. Then there are the passes that actually touch the path data: rounding numeric precision, merging consecutive path commands, collapsing nested groups, converting shapes to paths, and simplifying curves. Each of these can shave another 10–40% off the file size, but each one also changes numbers that ultimately control where a cut line lands. The question is whether the change is small enough that it does not matter.

Free savings: metadata, namespaces, and unused definitions

These passes remove data that has no effect on rendering. Run them first, and run them every time.

Removing editor namespaces

If no actual element or attribute in the body of the SVG uses a namespace prefix, the declaration can go. SVG-to-PDF converters and laser software do not care about xmlns:sodipodi or xmlns:i because they never parse tags in those namespaces. The hard part is making sure that an attribute like inkscape:label or i:knockout is not hiding somewhere deep in a layer group. A good optimizer will check before it strips the namespace.

Stripping metadata and comments

The metadata block, any XMP data, and all XML comments can be deleted unconditionally. The metadata holds information for humans and asset management systems, not renderers. Comments are a similar story: helpful in a hand-authored SVG, meaningless to a machine.

Cleaning unused definitions

A def that nothing references is dead code. An optimizer walks the document tree, collects every ID that is cited in a URL reference, then deletes any def whose ID is not in that set. The same logic applies to gradients, clip paths, masks, patterns, and symbols. One edge case: some editors write defs that reference other defs. The optimizer must run the check recursively, keeping any def that is reachable from a live shape.

Expected savings

A file exported from Illustrator with embedded metadata and a few unused gradients typically shrinks by 10–20% when these passes run. An Inkscape file with Sodipodi-specific layer attributes and verbose RDF blocks can shrink by 30%. The output is still pixel-identical to the input because nothing that affects rendering has changed.

Numeric precision: when decimal places matter and when they do not

SVG path data uses real numbers for coordinates, control points, and radii. Most editors write those numbers to six or twelve decimal places by default. The question is how much precision you can drop before the error becomes visible or functional.

Two decimal places is usually safe; zero is not

A coordinate rounded to two decimal places moves by less than 0.01 units in SVG user space. In a file whose viewBox is 500 units wide, that is 0.002% of the canvas. Most laser cutters and vinyl cutters measure position to 0.001 inch, which maps to roughly 0.1 SVG units at typical DPI. Rounding to two decimals leaves you an order of magnitude below the machine's resolution. Rounding to zero decimals — whole numbers — moves points by up to 0.5 units, which is enough to turn a closed path into an open one when two endpoints that were once 10.9 and 11.1 both round to 11.

Compound errors on Bezier curves

A cubic Bezier is defined by four points: two endpoints and two control points. If you round all four independently, the resulting curve can drift from the original by more than the per-point error, especially at the middle of the curve. A safe optimizer checks the visual difference after rounding and rolls back the change if the error exceeds a threshold.

Decimal placesTypical file size reductionRisk of visible change
6+ (editor default)baselinenone
3−10%none for print or cut
2−15%safe for most use cases
1−20%can misalign snapped edges
0 (integers)−25%often breaks closed paths

When to keep extra precision

Small decorative details — hairline accents, tiny logo elements — can shift noticeably when rounded. If the original coordinate is 5.12 and the design calls for that element to sit exactly between 5 and 6, rounding to 5 will make it look off-center. For files with sub-pixel features, keep three decimal places.

Merging paths and collapsing groups

An SVG exported from a design tool often wraps every shape in its own group, even when the group has no transform and no shared attributes. Collapsing those groups saves bytes. Merging consecutive paths of the same color into a single path saves more. Both passes are safe as long as the shapes do not overlap.

Collapsing empty groups

A group that carries no transform, no ID, no class, and no style attribute is pure container overhead. An optimizer can lift its children up one level and delete the group tag. This is always safe. The one exception: if the group has an ID that is referenced by a use element or animation elsewhere in the document, the optimizer must leave it alone.

Merging paths of the same stroke and fill

If two consecutive path elements have identical stroke, fill, stroke-width, and no transforms, the optimizer can concatenate their path data into a single path. This works well for cut files where every shape is an independent outline. It breaks badly when the paths overlap and rely on painter order to control which one appears on top. A conservative optimizer will only merge paths when they do not intersect.

Converting shapes to paths: when it helps and when it hurts

SVG defines convenience elements like rectangle, circle, ellipse, line, and polygon. An optimizer can convert these to path elements, which sometimes allows further path-merging passes. The trade-off: a rectangle becomes a path with four line commands, which is more verbose. Conversion usually saves space only when the optimizer can then merge the resulting path with another, or when the shape-specific attributes are longer than the equivalent path data.

Circles and ellipses lose semantic meaning

A circle is mathematically a circle. A path that approximates a circle with four cubic Bezier segments is not mathematically a circle; it is four curves that look round to the human eye. If you later want to scale the file non-uniformly or apply a shear transform, the circle will remain a perfect ellipse, but the path-based circle will distort. For cut files that never change, this does not matter. For design assets that might be edited later, keep the semantic shapes.

How to verify that an optimized file still looks right

The only reliable way to confirm that an optimization pass did not break a file is to compare the before and after visually or functionally.

Visual diff

Open both the original and optimized SVG in a viewer that supports layers or tabs — or render both to PNG at high resolution and overlay them in an image editor with a difference blend mode. If the difference image is solid black, the files are pixel-identical. If you see colored fringes along edges, the optimizer moved curves. Decide whether the error is acceptable for your use case.

Functional test for cut files

Load the optimized SVG into the laser or vinyl cutter software and check the path preview. Look for open paths where there should be closed ones, duplicate overlapping cuts, and shapes that have shifted relative to each other. For press-fit joinery or precise registration, measure the distance between two known features before and after. If it has changed by more than the machine's tolerance, roll back the pass that caused it.

What to optimize and what to leave alone

Every optimization pass is a trade-off between file size and some other property: fidelity, editability, or semantic clarity. The right choice depends on what you plan to do with the file next.

PassTypical savingRisk
Remove metadata and comments10–30%None (always safe)
Strip unused namespaces and defs5–15%None (always safe)
Collapse empty groups5–10%None (always safe)
Round to 2–3 decimal places10–20%Low (safe for print/cut)
Merge same-color paths10–25%Medium (can break overlaps)
Convert shapes to paths−5% to +10%Medium (loses semantic meaning)
Round to 1 decimal place20–30%High (can misalign edges)
Round to integers25–35%High (often breaks closed paths)

Recommended profile for cut files

Strip metadata, unused defs, and empty groups. Round coordinates to two decimal places. Do not merge paths unless you have verified that they do not overlap. Do not convert shapes to paths unless you need to merge them afterward.

Recommended profile for web or print assets

Strip metadata and unused defs. Round to three decimal places. Collapse groups. Keep shapes as shapes if the file might be edited later. Convert shapes to paths if the file is final and you need to shave every possible byte for web delivery.

Tools that do this work

The industry-standard tool is SVGO, a Node.js command-line optimizer with a plugin architecture. By default it runs a safe set of passes; you can enable or disable individual plugins in a config file. PNG-to-SVG converters often include a post-processing step that calls SVGO or a similar library on the traced output.

Adobe Illustrator has a built-in Save for Web export that applies a fixed optimization profile. Inkscape has Optimized SVG under the Save As dialog, with checkboxes for individual passes. Both are less configurable than SVGO but easier to use if you do not want to write a config file.

For laser and vinyl cutting workflows, some users prefer to skip optimization entirely and trust the machine software to ignore extraneous data. That works until the file is too large for the machine's memory or the upload times out. A one-minute optimization pass that cuts file size by 40% solves both problems.

Related resources

For more on SVG structure and how converters handle traced output, see Image Tracing Explained. For guidance on choosing the right source resolution before tracing, see Best Resolution for Vectorizing. For laser-specific file preparation, see Laser Cutting Guide. For design system token workflows, see SVG Optimization Guide in the resources section.

faqs.question: Will optimizing an SVG change how it looks?
faqs.answer: Some optimization passes are safe and will never change rendering: removing metadata, stripping unused definitions, and collapsing empty groups. Other passes — rounding coordinates, merging paths — can introduce small visual differences. The key is verifying the output by comparing the optimized file to the original at the resolution you care about.

faqs.question: How many decimal places should I keep in SVG coordinates?
faqs.answer: Two decimal places is safe for nearly all print and cut workflows. Three decimal places preserves more fidelity for small details. One decimal place can misalign snapped edges. Zero decimal places (integers) often creates open paths where there were closed ones, so avoid it unless you have verified the output.

faqs.question: Can I merge all paths of the same color into one path?
faqs.answer: Only if the paths do not overlap. When two paths overlap, SVG uses painter order to determine which one appears on top. Merging them into a single path collapses that order into a single shape, which can change the visual result. A safe optimizer checks for intersection before merging.

faqs.question: Should I convert circles and rectangles to paths?
faqs.answer: For final cut files, it usually makes no difference. For design assets that might be edited later, keep semantic shapes like circles and rectangles because they preserve geometric meaning. A circle stays round under non-uniform scaling; a path-based circle built from Bezier curves does not.

faqs.question: Why did my optimized file break in the laser cutter?
faqs.answer: The most common cause is rounding coordinates to integers, which moves endpoints enough that closed paths become open. Another cause is merging overlapping paths, which changes cut order. Always verify the optimized file in your machine software before committing to it, and dial back the numeric precision if you see issues.

title: Image Tracing Explained: Thresholds, Corners and Nodes
seoTitle: Image Tracing Explained: How Raster Becomes Vector
seoDescription: Tracing is a decision process, not a button. Understand color reduction, corner detection and node tolerance so the result is editable instead of a pile of points.
excerpt: Image tracing is not one algorithm. It is a pipeline: quantize the colors, trace the boundaries, fit curves to the edges, then simplify the result. Here is what each stage actually does and where the common tracing mistakes come from.
content:
When you load a raster image into a tracer and click the button, the software does not magically know which pixels are part of a logo and which are part of the background. It does not understand that the black pixels form letters or that the white pixels are supposed to stay white. All it sees is a grid of color values. Image tracing is the process of turning that grid into vector paths — and every tracer on the market uses roughly the same pipeline to do it.

The pipeline has four stages: preprocess the image to make the edges cleaner, quantize the colors so there are fewer of them, trace the boundaries between color regions, then fit curves to those boundaries and simplify the result. Each stage has settings that control how aggressive it is, and most tracing failures come from pushing one stage too hard. This guide walks through the pipeline in order, explains what each stage does, and shows which settings matter.

Stage one: preprocessing

Before a tracer can find edges, it needs clean edges to find. Real-world images rarely have them. A photo has continuous tone and soft gradients. A scanned document has JPEG compression artifacts, sensor noise, and uneven lighting. A logo saved as PNG might have anti-aliasing halos where the designer tried to make it look smooth on a white background.

Desaturate or convert to grayscale

Most tracers work in grayscale or indexed color, not full RGB. If you feed in a color photo, the tracer converts it to grayscale before processing. You can often get better results by doing this step yourself in an image editor, where you have control over which channel to use or how the luminance is weighted. For a logo that is mostly red on white, extracting the red channel gives you higher contrast than a standard grayscale conversion.

Adjust contrast and brightness

A tracer finds edges by looking for sharp changes in brightness. If the image is low-contrast or unevenly lit, the edges will be mushy and the tracer will either miss them or put the boundary in the wrong place. Boosting contrast before tracing sharpens the decision. The trade-off: too much contrast turns gradients into hard steps, and too much brightness adjustment clips detail in the highlights or shadows.

Blur or sharpen

Blurring suppresses noise and small details, which can make the traced output cleaner. Sharpening accentuates edges, which can help the tracer find faint boundaries. Most users should leave this alone and let the tracer handle it, but if your source image is unusually noisy or soft, a light blur or sharpen can help.

Stage two: quantization

A photograph has millions of possible colors. A traced vector file typically has between two and twenty. Quantization is the process of reducing the input to a fixed palette. The tracer groups similar colors together, then treats each group as a single flat color. The number of colors in the palette determines how many distinct shapes the tracer will create.

Number of colors

This is the single most important setting in the whole pipeline. Set it too low and the tracer merges regions that should be separate. Set it too high and the tracer creates a separate shape for every subtle gradient or shadow, which produces a bloated file full of overlapping paths. For a logo or line art, two to five colors is typical. For a photo-style illustration, eight to sixteen. Beyond that you are usually tracing noise.

Color mode: full color vs. black and white

Most tracers offer a black-and-white mode that skips quantization and instead thresholds the image at a single brightness cutoff. Pixels brighter than the threshold become white; pixels darker become black. This is the right choice for scanned line art, text, or any image that is genuinely monochrome. It is the wrong choice for anything with gradients or multiple colors, because you lose all the intermediate tones.

Threshold value

In black-and-white mode, the threshold determines where the boundary between black and white lands. A threshold of 128 (middle gray) treats anything brighter than half-white as white. For a clean logo on a white background, this usually works. For a scanned document with uneven lighting, you might need to lower the threshold to capture faint text, or raise it to suppress page texture.

SettingWhat it controlsTypical mistake
Number of colorsHow many distinct shapes the tracer createsToo many colors = bloated file, overlapping paths
Black/white thresholdBrightness cutoff in monochrome modeFixed at 128 when image has uneven lighting
Palette modeAutomatic palette vs. custom colorsLetting tracer pick colors when source has gradients

Stage three: boundary tracing

Once the image is quantized, the tracer walks the edge between each pair of colors and records the boundary as a sequence of points. The algorithm is usually a variant of marching squares or a contour-following method. The output at this stage is a polygon — a path made of straight line segments, one segment between each pair of adjacent pixels.

Speckle suppression

Noise in the source image produces tiny isolated regions in the quantized version. A single stray pixel becomes a one-pixel square. A cluster of three pixels becomes a three-pixel blob. These are almost never intentional shapes. A good tracer offers a speckle suppression setting that discards regions smaller than a threshold. Measured in pixels, this determines the smallest feature the tracer will keep.

Corner detection

A polygon from the boundary trace follows the pixel grid, which means every edge is either horizontal, vertical, or stair-stepped at 45 degrees. Real artwork has corners at arbitrary angles. The tracer looks for places where the polygon changes direction sharply and marks them as corners. These corners will later become corner nodes in the final curve, while the smooth sections will become smooth nodes.

Stage four: curve fitting

A polygon made of hundreds of short line segments is not a useful vector. The next stage fits cubic Bezier curves to the polygon, replacing long runs of line segments with a single smooth curve. The algorithm is usually a least-squares fit that tries to minimize the distance between the original polygon and the fitted curve.

Curve tolerance or fitting error

This setting controls how closely the fitted curve must match the original polygon. A tight tolerance produces curves that hug the polygon closely, which means more control points and a larger file. A loose tolerance allows the curve to deviate further, which means fewer control points and a smaller file. The right value depends on what you plan to do with the output. For a logo that will be scaled to billboard size, you want tight tolerance. For a decorative illustration that will only ever be seen at thumbnail size, you can get away with loose.

Corner threshold

When the tracer finds a corner in the polygon, it needs to decide whether to create a sharp corner node or a smooth node. A sharp corner has independent control handles on each side; a smooth node has aligned handles. The corner threshold sets the angle below which a corner is considered sharp. A threshold of 90 degrees means any corner sharper than 90 degrees gets a corner node. A threshold of 180 degrees means all corners are smooth, which produces a very fluid result but loses hard edges.

Simplification: node reduction

After curve fitting, the tracer runs a simplification pass that looks for consecutive Bezier segments that can be merged into a single segment without exceeding the fitting error. This is where most of the file-size savings happen. The trade-off: aggressive simplification loses fine detail. For technical drawings, you usually want minimal simplification. For organic shapes, you can push it further.

StageKey settingWhat it controls
PreprocessContrast/brightnessHow sharp the edges are before tracing
QuantizeNumber of colorsHow many shapes the tracer creates
TraceSpeckle suppressionSmallest feature size in pixels
Fit curvesCurve toleranceHow closely curves match pixel edges
SimplifyNode thresholdHow many nodes survive simplification

Layer by color vs. single silhouette

Most tracers offer two output modes: one path per color, or a single merged silhouette. The layer-by-color mode creates a separate path for each color in the quantized palette, stacked in painter order. This is the right choice when you want to edit individual colors later or when you need to send the file to a process that expects separated layers, like screen printing. The single-silhouette mode traces only the outermost boundary and discards interior detail. This is the right choice for a stencil or a shape that will be cut from a single material.

When to use layer-by-color

Use this mode when the source has multiple distinct regions that you want to keep separate. A logo with a colored icon and colored text. A map with different regions colored differently. A schematic with color-coded lines. The output will have one path per color, and you can change the colors or rearrange the layers in a vector editor afterward.

When to use single silhouette

Use this mode when you only care about the overall shape. A profile silhouette. A rubber stamp. A stencil for spray paint. The output will be a single path, possibly with holes for interior cutouts, and all the color information is discarded.

Common tracing problems and how to fix them

Most tracing failures come from a mismatch between the source image and the tracer settings. Here are the patterns that come up over and over.

Too many paths, file size is huge

The color count is set too high, so the tracer is creating a separate path for every subtle gradient or shadow in the source. Lower the color count to 4–8 and see if the output still captures the important features. If it does, you are done. If it does not, the source image might not be suitable for tracing.

Edges are jagged or stair-stepped

The curve tolerance is set too loose, so the fitted curves deviate from the pixel boundaries by more than one pixel. Tighten the tolerance until the curves follow the edges. If that makes the file too large, the source resolution might be too low. See Best Resolution for Vectorizing.

Small details are missing

Speckle suppression is set too high, so the tracer is discarding features you wanted to keep. Lower the speckle threshold to zero and see if the details reappear. If they do, you can dial the threshold back up until it only removes noise. If they do not, the details might be below the resolution of the source image.

Corners are too round or too sharp

The corner threshold is wrong for the subject matter. For geometric shapes and technical drawings, lower the threshold to 60–90 degrees so corners stay sharp. For organic shapes and hand-drawn artwork, raise it to 120–150 degrees so the curves flow smoothly.

Tools and software

Adobe Illustrator has a built-in Image Trace feature that runs the full pipeline and gives you sliders for most of the settings. Inkscape has Trace Bitmap under the Path menu, with a simpler interface and fewer options. Both are good for interactive work where you can preview the result and tweak settings until it looks right.

For batch processing, command-line tracers like Potrace or AutoTrace offer scriptable interfaces and fine-grained control. PNG-to-SVG converters often wrap one of these libraries and expose a subset of the settings. For photos and complex illustrations, specialized tools like Vector Magic or Adobe Capture use machine learning to improve the boundary detection, but they still run a similar pipeline under the hood.

Related resources

For guidance on preparing a source image before tracing, see Best Resolution for Vectorizing. For advice on whether to upscale a low-resolution image first, see Upscaling Before Vectorizing. For optimizing the traced output, see SVG Optimization Guide. For production workflows that involve tracing, see Batch Conversion Workflows.

faqs.question: What is the difference between image tracing and vectorization?
faqs.answer: They are the same thing. Image tracing is the process of converting a raster image into vector paths. Vectorization is the general term for that process. Both describe the same pipeline: quantize colors, trace boundaries, fit curves, and simplify.

faqs.question: How many colors should I use when tracing a logo?
faqs.answer: For a simple logo, two to five colors is typical. For a more complex icon or illustration, six to ten. Beyond that you are usually tracing gradients or shadows that will bloat the file. If the traced output has dozens of overlapping paths, lower the color count.

faqs.question: Why does my traced image look jagged?
faqs.answer: The curve tolerance is set too loose, so the fitted Bezier curves deviate from the pixel edges by more than one pixel. Tighten the tolerance setting until the curves follow the edges. If that makes the file too large, the source resolution might be too low.

faqs.question: Can I trace a photograph and get a good result?
faqs.answer: Depends on what you mean by good. If you want a posterized or stenciled version with flat colors, yes. If you want something that looks like the original photo, no. Tracing discards continuous tone and replaces it with hard edges. For photo-realistic results, keep it raster or use a different technique.

faqs.question: How do I remove noise and small specks from the traced output?
faqs.answer: Raise the speckle suppression threshold. This tells the tracer to discard any region smaller than a certain number of pixels. Start at 2–4 pixels and increase until the noise disappears. If you also lose details you wanted to keep, the source image needs cleaning before tracing.

title: The Resolution That Actually Satisfies a Vectorizer
seoTitle: Best Image Resolution for Vectorization: PPI, Edges and Artifacts
seoDescription: Too low and edges are guesses; too high and noise becomes paths. Here is how to pick source resolution and pre-clean an image before tracing.
excerpt: Vectorizers need clean edges, not huge files. Practical guidance: 300–600 PPI at final reproduction size is the sweet spot. Beyond that, you are usually tracing JPEG artifacts and anti-aliasing halos, not actual shapes.
content:
Vectorizers need clean edges, not huge files. The common belief is that more resolution is always better, but that is only true up to a point. Beyond 600 PPI at the final reproduction size, you are usually tracing JPEG artifacts, anti-aliasing halos, and sensor noise rather than the actual shapes. The real constraint is not resolution but edge quality: a 300 PPI scan of a clean logo will trace better than a 1200 PPI scan of a blurry photo.

This guide explains how resolution, compression artifacts, and edge softness interact with the tracing pipeline, and gives practical rules for choosing the right source resolution before you hit the trace button.

What vectorizers actually see

A vectorizer does not understand your logo or your photograph. It sees a grid of color values and looks for boundaries between regions of different colors. The quality of those boundaries — how sharp they are, how much noise surrounds them, whether they land on a single pixel or blur across three — determines whether the vectorizer produces clean paths or jagged, oversimplified ones.

Resolution is one factor that affects boundary quality, but it is not the only one. A 150 PPI scan of a crisp printed logo has better-defined edges than a 600 PPI photo of a hand-painted sign shot in low light. The vectorizer cannot create detail that was not in the source, so the first question is always: does the source have clean edges?

The practical target: 300–600 PPI at reproduction size

For most vectorization tasks, 300–600 PPI at the final reproduction size is the sweet spot. Below 150 PPI, edges become blocky and the vectorizer has to guess where corners land. Above 600 PPI, you start tracing compression artifacts and anti-aliasing instead of actual shapes. The exception: technical drawings and CAD exports, which have mathematically sharp edges and can benefit from higher resolution if the source was rendered at high DPI.

How to calculate effective resolution

If you have a 1500×2000 pixel image and you plan to reproduce it at 5×6.67 inches, the effective resolution is 1500÷5 = 300 PPI horizontally and 2000÷6.67 = 300 PPI vertically. If the reproduction size is unknown, assume the size at which the image looks sharp on screen when viewed at 100%. That is usually close to the intended reproduction size.

For web graphics and icons that will only ever be displayed on screen, think in pixels rather than inches. A 512×512 icon does not need to be scanned at 1200 PPI; it needs to be 512 pixels wide.
