If you are tracing a 128×128 favicon, upscaling it to 2048×2048 before tracing will not add detail — it will only make the vectorizer trace the upscaling algorithm's interpolation artifacts.

Common source quality problems and their symptoms

Most vectorization failures come from source images that look acceptable to the human eye but contain artifacts the vectorizer cannot ignore. Here are the patterns that show up in the traced output.

JPEG compression artifacts

JPEG compresses images by dividing them into 8×8 pixel blocks and applying a discrete cosine transform to each block. The result: sharp edges acquire ringing artifacts — faint oscillations on both sides of the edge. When a vectorizer traces a JPEG at high magnification, those oscillations become separate paths. The solution is to avoid JPEG as a source format for vectorization. If JPEG is all you have, apply a light blur or noise reduction filter before tracing to smooth out the block boundaries.

Anti-aliasing halos

Anti-aliasing makes raster graphics look smooth by blending the foreground color with the background at edges. A black logo on a white background gets a row of gray pixels along every edge. When you save that logo as PNG and later try to vectorize it on a different background, the gray pixels become visible as a halo. The vectorizer sees them as a separate color region and traces them as a thin outline around the main shape. The fix: before tracing, use the original background color or expand the logo slightly to push the anti-aliased pixels outside the final shape.

Soft focus and motion blur

A photograph taken out of focus or with motion blur has edges that span multiple pixels. The vectorizer has to choose where to place the boundary, and there is no single correct answer. If the blur spans five pixels, rounding to the nearest pixel moves the traced edge by up to two pixels from the center of the blur gradient. For logos or text, this is usually unacceptable. The solution is to re-shoot or re-scan the source with better focus, or to manually sharpen the image before tracing and accept that the result is an approximation.

Source problemSymptom in traced outputFix
JPEG artifactsExtra paths near edges, ringingUse PNG or TIFF source, or blur before tracing
Anti-aliasing haloThin outline around shapesMatch original background or expand shape
Soft focusEdges land in wrong placeRe-scan or sharpen before tracing
Low resolutionBlocky stair-stepped edgesRe-scan at 300+ PPI or accept approximation
Over-sharpenedOvershoot halos treated as separate shapesApply gentler sharpening or skip it

When higher resolution helps and when it does not

Higher resolution helps when the source has fine detail that would otherwise fall below the sampling threshold. A logo with 1-point hairlines, a map with thin boundary lines, a schematic with closely spaced traces — these all benefit from 600 PPI or higher. The detail is real, and the vectorizer needs enough pixels to distinguish it from noise.

Higher resolution does not help when the source is already soft or noisy. Scanning a blurry photograph at 1200 PPI gives you a larger file full of blur, not more detail. The vectorizer still has to guess where the edges are, and now it has more pixels to guess across. For continuous-tone images like photographs or watercolor paintings, resolution above 300 PPI rarely improves the traced result unless you are deliberately trying to capture texture.

The noise threshold

Digital sensors and scanners introduce noise — random variation in pixel values. At 150–300 PPI, noise is usually smaller than the features you care about, so the vectorizer ignores it. At 1200 PPI, noise can be larger than the smallest features, and the vectorizer starts tracing it as if it were intentional detail. The solution: if you must scan at high resolution, apply light noise reduction before tracing.

Preparing the source image before tracing

Most source images benefit from light preprocessing before they reach the vectorizer. The goal is to make the boundaries between regions as clean and unambiguous as possible.

Cropping and rotation

Crop the image to the region of interest. A vectorizer that sees a 4000×3000 photograph of a logo sitting in the center will waste time tracing the background. Rotate the image so edges are axis-aligned if possible. A perfectly horizontal line traces better than a line at 3 degrees, because the pixel stair-stepping is more predictable.

Levels and curves adjustment

Adjust levels so the white background is truly white and the black foreground is truly black. A scanned document that looks white on screen might actually be light gray, which means the vectorizer sees two colors instead of one. Stretching the histogram so the background hits 255 and the foreground hits 0 makes the color quantization step simpler.

Despeckle and median filter

A light despeckle or median filter removes isolated stray pixels without blurring edges. This is especially useful for scanned line art, where dust on the scanner glass shows up as black specks. The vectorizer will trace every speck as a separate shape unless you clean them first.

Resolution vs. file size trade-off

Higher resolution means larger files, which means longer upload times, more memory usage during tracing, and larger traced outputs if the vectorizer does not simplify aggressively. A 300 PPI source at 8.5×11 inches is about 8 megapixels. A 600 PPI source at the same size is 32 megapixels. A 1200 PPI source is 128 megapixels. Most vectorizers slow down noticeably above 20–30 megapixels.

For batch processing, the time difference compounds. A PNG-to-SVG converter that handles 300 PPI sources in two seconds might take twenty seconds per file at 1200 PPI, and the traced output might not be any better. If the source quality is good, 300–400 PPI is almost always enough.

Special cases: text, technical drawings, and high-DPI displays

Text and technical drawings have a special requirement: edges must land exactly where the designer intended, because even a one-pixel shift can make the text less readable or the drawing dimensionally incorrect. For these sources, 400–600 PPI is the practical target, and you should verify the traced output against the source at high zoom.

For high-DPI displays (Retina, 4K, etc.), the same rules apply: resolution is measured at the final display size. A logo that will be displayed at 256×256 CSS pixels on a 2x Retina display needs 512×512 physical pixels, which is 512 pixels in the source image, not 1024.

Testing: trace at multiple resolutions and compare

The best way to confirm that your source resolution is sufficient is to trace the same image at two or three different resolutions and compare the output. If the 300 PPI version and the 600 PPI version produce paths that differ by less than one pixel when scaled to the same size, the 300 PPI version is good enough. If the 600 PPI version captures features the 300 PPI version missed, you needed the higher resolution.

A quick visual test: overlay the two traced outputs at the same scale in a vector editor. If the paths align, you are done. If they diverge, zoom in to the areas where they differ and decide whether the extra detail in the higher-resolution trace is worth the larger file size.

Related resources

For advice on the tracing pipeline itself, see Image Tracing Explained. For guidance on whether to upscale a low-resolution source before tracing, see Upscaling Before Vectorizing. For optimizing the traced output, see SVG Optimization Guide. For converter-specific resolution recommendations, see the help pages for PNG to SVG and JPG to SVG.

faqs.question: What resolution should I scan a logo at before vectorizing it?
faqs.answer: 300–400 PPI at the size you plan to reproduce it is sufficient for most logos. If the logo has very fine detail like 1-point hairlines, go up to 600 PPI. Beyond that, you are usually tracing scanner noise and compression artifacts rather than real detail.

faqs.question: Will scanning at a higher resolution give me a better vector?
faqs.answer: Only if the source has real detail that would otherwise fall below the sampling threshold. Scanning a blurry photo at 1200 PPI gives you a larger file full of blur, not more detail. Clean edges at 300 PPI trace better than soft edges at 1200 PPI.

faqs.question: Why does my high-resolution scan produce a worse traced result than a low-resolution one?
faqs.answer: At very high resolution, JPEG compression artifacts, anti-aliasing halos, and sensor noise become visible to the vectorizer, and it traces them as if they were intentional shapes. A 300 PPI clean source often traces better than a 1200 PPI noisy source.

faqs.question: How do I know if my source image has enough resolution?
faqs.answer: Trace it at the current resolution and at 2x the current resolution, then compare the outputs. If the higher-resolution trace does not capture features the lower-resolution one missed, the lower resolution is sufficient. If it does, you needed the extra pixels.

faqs.question: Can I just upscale a low-resolution image before tracing?
faqs.answer: Upscaling with an AI tool can help if the source is uniformly soft, but it can also introduce hallucinated detail that the vectorizer will trace as real features. See the Upscaling Before Vectorizing guide for when to upscale and when to trace the low-resolution source as-is.

title: Upscale First or Vectorize First? The Order Changes Everything
seoTitle: Upscale Before Vectorizing: When It Helps and When It Hurts
seoDescription: Upscaling invents detail. Tracing documents it. Do them in the wrong order and you turn soft edges into jagged noise. Here is the decision rule.
excerpt: AI upscalers hallucinate detail. If you trace hallucinated detail, you get wavy paths where the true edge was straight. Rule: upscale only when the source is uniformly soft, not when it has compression artifacts or already-clean edges.
content:
AI upscalers promise to recover detail from low-resolution images, and they can be impressive on photographs. But vectorization is not photography. When a vectorizer traces an upscaled image, it is tracing the upscaler's best guess at what the edges should look like — and that guess can include hallucinated detail that was never in the original. The result: wavy paths where the true edge was straight, extra nodes where the original had none, and corners that shift by several pixels from their real location.

This guide explains when upscaling before vectorizing helps, when it makes things worse, and how to tell the difference.

What AI upscalers actually do

Modern AI upscalers are trained on millions of high-resolution images and learn to predict what detail should exist at scales the source image does not contain. When you feed in a 100×100 icon and ask for a 400×400 output, the upscaler does not simply interpolate between pixels — it guesses what edges, textures, and fine details would be present if the image had been captured at higher resolution in the first place.

For photographs, this is often a good trade. The upscaler adds plausible detail that makes the image look sharper to the human eye. For logos, line art, and anything with mathematically straight edges, it is a problem. The upscaler does not know that the edge is supposed to be perfectly straight; it only knows what natural images usually look like. So it adds tiny wobbles, sub-pixel shifts, and smoothing that a human would not notice but a vectorizer will trace as real geometry.

When upscaling helps: uniformly soft sources

Upscaling before vectorizing makes sense when the source image is uniformly soft — low resolution, out of focus, or heavily compressed — and there is no higher-quality version available. In this case, the upscaler can sharpen edges and make the boundary between foreground and background clearer, which gives the vectorizer a better target to trace.

Old scans and low-resolution downloads

A 150 PPI scan of a printed logo from the 1980s. A 72 DPI screenshot of a web graphic. A thumbnail downloaded from a stock image site. These sources all have blocky, stair-stepped edges because the original resolution was too low. An AI upscaler can smooth those stair-steps into curves, which the vectorizer can then fit more cleanly.

Soft focus and motion blur

If the source image has edges that blur across three or four pixels, an AI upscaler trained on sharp images will try to sharpen them. This can help the vectorizer decide where the boundary lands, especially if the blur is uniform across the whole image. The trade-off: the upscaler might sharpen some edges correctly and hallucinate others incorrectly, so you need to inspect the traced output carefully.

When upscaling hurts: compression artifacts and clean edges

Upscaling makes things worse when the source image has JPEG compression artifacts, anti-aliasing halos, or already-clean edges that do not need help. In these cases, the upscaler amplifies the artifacts or introduces new ones, and the vectorizer traces the amplified noise as if it were real detail.

JPEG compression artifacts

JPEG compression creates 8×8 pixel blocks with ringing artifacts near edges. An AI upscaler sees those artifacts and tries to make sense of them, often by turning them into textured regions or wavy lines. The vectorizer then traces those hallucinated features. The result: a logo that was a simple four-path shape becomes a 40-path mess. For JPEG sources, clean up the artifacts before tracing, do not upscale.

Already-clean edges at moderate resolution

A 300 PPI scan of a printed logo has clean edges. Upscaling it to 1200 PPI does not add real detail; it adds the upscaler's interpretation of what a 1200 PPI version might look like. If the original edges were straight, the upscaled version might have micro-wobbles that the vectorizer will trace. The rule: if the source already has clean edges at 250–400 PPI, trace it as-is.

ScenarioUpscale before tracing?Why
Low-res scan (150 PPI or less)YesEdges are blocky; upscaler smooths stair-stepping
Soft focus photoMaybeUpscaler sharpens edges, but might hallucinate detail
JPEG with compression artifactsNoUpscaler amplifies artifacts; clean source first
Clean 300+ PPI sourceNoEdges are already good; upscaling adds noise
Screenshot at 72 DPIYesVery blocky; upscaler helps

How to test whether upscaling helped

The best way to know if upscaling improved the traced result is to trace both the original and the upscaled version, then compare the outputs. Open both traced SVGs in a vector editor at the same scale and overlay them. If the upscaled version has cleaner paths with fewer nodes and straighter edges, the upscaling helped. If it has more nodes, wavy paths, or shifted corners, it hurt.

Node count as a proxy for quality

A simpler test: count the number of nodes in each traced output. For logos and line art, fewer nodes usually means cleaner tracing. If the upscaled version has 50% more nodes than the original, the upscaler probably hallucinated detail. If it has the same number of nodes or fewer, it might have helped.

Spot-check straight edges

Zoom in on a section of the traced output that should be a perfectly straight line. If the line is made of three or four Bezier segments with control points that deviate from a straight path, the source had noise or the upscaler added wobbles. If the line is a single segment or two segments that form a clean straight edge, the source was good.

Upscaling settings that matter for vectorization

Most AI upscalers offer settings for sharpness, noise reduction, and detail enhancement. For vectorization, you want moderate sharpness and aggressive noise reduction. High sharpness settings can create overshoot halos that the vectorizer will trace as separate shapes. Low noise reduction leaves specks that become extra paths.

Recommended settings

Use the photo or standard preset if available, not the illustration or artwork preset. The illustration preset is trained to preserve hand-drawn lines and textures, which is the opposite of what you want. Set noise reduction to medium or high. Set sharpness to low or medium. Avoid any setting labeled texture enhancement or detail recovery, because those add synthetic detail the vectorizer will trace.

Alternatives to upscaling: preprocessing the low-res source

Before reaching for an upscaler, try preprocessing the low-resolution source to make its edges cleaner. These techniques do not add resolution, but they can make the existing resolution more useful.

Bilateral filter

A bilateral filter smooths regions of similar color while preserving edges. This removes noise and compression artifacts without blurring the boundaries the vectorizer cares about. Most image editors have this filter under Noise Reduction or Surface Blur. Apply it lightly before tracing a noisy source.

Unsharp mask

An unsharp mask accentuates edges by boosting contrast at boundaries. For a soft-focus source, a light unsharp mask can make edges clearer without introducing the hallucinations an AI upscaler might add. Keep the radius small (1–2 pixels) and the amount moderate (50–100%).

Levels adjustment

Stretch the histogram so the brightest pixels are white and the darkest pixels are black. This maximizes contrast and makes color quantization simpler during tracing. For a scanned document with gray instead of white background, this step alone can eliminate a whole layer of spurious paths.

Special case: pixel art and low-bit graphics

Pixel art is intentionally low resolution. Each pixel is part of the design. Upscaling pixel art before vectorizing defeats the purpose, because the upscaler smooths the hard pixel boundaries into curves. For pixel art, either trace it at the original resolution and accept the blocky result, or use a nearest-neighbor upscale (not AI) to make the pixels bigger without adding anti-aliasing.

Tools and workflows

Popular AI upscalers include Topaz Gigapixel, waifu2x, Real-ESRGAN, and the upscaling features built into Photoshop and GIMP. For vectorization, avoid upscalers trained specifically on anime or illustrations, because they add stylistic artifacts. Use general-purpose photo upscalers with noise reduction enabled.

For batch processing, command-line tools like Real-ESRGAN or waifu2x-ncnn can upscale folders of images before handing them to a PNG-to-SVG converter. Test the pipeline on a few sample images first to confirm that upscaling improves the traced output before committing to a large batch.

Related resources

For guidance on choosing the right source resolution before tracing, see Best Resolution for Vectorizing. For the tracing pipeline itself, see Image Tracing Explained. For optimizing the traced output, see SVG Optimization Guide. For preparing sources with compression artifacts, see File Formats Guide.

faqs.question: Should I upscale a low-resolution logo before vectorizing it?
faqs.answer: Only if the logo is uniformly soft or very blocky (below 150 PPI). If it already has clean edges at 250–300 PPI, upscaling will add micro-wobbles the vectorizer will trace. Test by tracing both the original and upscaled versions and comparing node counts.

faqs.question: Why does my upscaled image produce a worse vector than the original?
faqs.answer: The upscaler is adding detail that was not in the original, and the vectorizer is tracing those hallucinated features as real geometry. For logos and line art, this usually makes things worse. Upscale only when the source is so low-resolution that edges are blocky.

faqs.question: What upscaling settings should I use before vectorizing?
faqs.answer: Use moderate sharpness and high noise reduction. Avoid detail enhancement or texture recovery settings, because those add synthetic detail the vectorizer will trace. Use a general-purpose photo upscaler, not one trained on illustrations or anime.

faqs.question: Can I use an AI upscaler to fix JPEG compression artifacts?
faqs.answer: No. Upscalers amplify JPEG artifacts rather than removing them. Clean up compression artifacts with a bilateral filter or noise reduction tool before tracing, and avoid upscaling JPEG sources unless you have already removed the block boundaries.

faqs.question: How do I know if upscaling helped my traced result?
faqs.answer: Compare the node count and visual quality of the traced SVG before and after upscaling. If the upscaled version has significantly more nodes or wavy paths where the original had straight ones, the upscaling hurt. If it has fewer nodes and cleaner edges, it helped.

title: Vectorizing a Painting: When Vector Art Helps and When It Lies
seoTitle: Vectorize a Painting or Photo: What Survives and What Changes
seoDescription: Painting is continuous tone and texture; vector is flat geometry. Learn the styles that vectorize well and what you lose by converting.
excerpt: Continuous tone, layered transparency, and brush texture do not translate to vectors. Styles that work: flat poster art, ink wash, stencil designs. What is lost: impressionist blending, watercolor softness, impasto texture. The honest result is stylized, not photorealistic.
content:
Vectorizing a painting is not the same as vectorizing a logo. Paintings have continuous tone, layered transparency, brush texture, and subtle gradients — none of which translate cleanly to the flat fills and hard edges that vector formats expect. The question is not whether you can vectorize a painting, but what you are willing to lose in translation.

This guide explains which painting styles vectorize well, which do not, and how to approach the conversion when the goal is a stylized or posterized interpretation rather than a photorealistic reproduction.

What gets lost: continuous tone and texture

A painting is continuous tone. The artist mixes colors on the canvas, blends edges with a brush, and builds up layers of translucent paint. A vector file is discrete: each shape has a single fill color, a single stroke, and a hard boundary. When you vectorize a painting, the tracer quantizes all that continuous variation into a fixed number of flat colors.

Brush texture disappears entirely. The tracer sees texture as noise and either smooths it out or traces it as thousands of tiny shapes. Layered transparency flattens into opaque fills. Subtle gradients become hard steps. If the goal is to preserve the look of the original painting, keep it raster. If the goal is to extract the composition and color palette for a stylized interpretation, vectorization can work.

Painting styles that vectorize well

Some painting styles are closer to vectors to begin with. They rely on flat shapes, limited palettes, and hard edges rather than continuous blending. These styles translate more cleanly.

Flat color and poster-style art

Paintings done in a poster style — flat fills, limited palette, no gradients — vectorize almost perfectly. Each color region becomes a path, and the result looks close to the original because the original was already flat. Think Soviet propaganda posters, WPA-era illustrations, or modern flat-design artwork.

High-contrast ink and line art

Ink wash paintings, sumi-e, and other styles that use black ink on white paper with limited intermediate tones vectorize well in black-and-white mode. The tracer treats the image as a threshold and produces clean silhouettes. Fine linework and calligraphic strokes become paths that can be scaled without losing crispness.

Stencil and cut-paper styles

Paintings that mimic stencils or cut-paper collages — distinct shapes with no blending, each shape a single color — map directly to vector fills. Matisse cutouts, Kara Walker silhouettes, and similar styles are already conceptually vector-like, so the traced output looks intentional rather than posterized.

Art styleVectorization resultWhat to expect
Flat poster artExcellentNearly 1:1 reproduction
Ink wash, sumi-eGoodClean silhouettes, lost gradations
Stencil/cut-paperExcellentPerfect match if source is clean
Impressionist (Monet, Renoir)PoorLoses all brush texture and subtlety
Watercolor with soft edgesPoorHard edges replace soft blends
Oil with thick impastoPoorTexture becomes noise or is lost

Painting styles that do not vectorize well

Styles that rely on continuous tone, subtle blending, or visible brush texture do not survive vectorization. The traced output will look like a bad posterization of the original, not a stylized interpretation.

Impressionism and soft blending

Impressionist paintings (Monet, Renoir, Pissarro) use thousands of small brush strokes and subtle color variations to create the illusion of form and light. A vectorizer sees those variations as distinct regions and either merges them all into mush or creates thousands of overlapping paths. Neither result looks like the painting.

Watercolor with soft edges

Watercolor relies on soft edges where pigment bleeds into wet paper. A vectorizer has to decide where each color region ends, and there is no correct answer. The result: hard-edged shapes that look nothing like watercolor. If you want a vector watercolor effect, use gradient meshes or leave it raster.

Thick oil paint with impasto

Oil paintings with thick impasto — visible texture from brush strokes or palette knife work — have three-dimensional surface variation that a photograph flattens into a 2D image. The vectorizer sees the highlights and shadows of that texture as separate colors and traces them as shapes. The result is a mess. For impasto work, photograph it under controlled lighting and accept that the output will be an abstraction.

How to vectorize a painting: the tone-separation workflow

If the goal is a stylized vector version of a painting, the approach is not to trace the raw photograph. Instead, posterize the image first, manually or with a filter, then trace the posterized version. This gives you control over how many colors survive the conversion and where the boundaries land.

Step one: clean up the photograph

Start with the best photograph of the painting you can get. Even lighting, no glare, color-corrected. Crop to the painting itself, removing the frame and wall. Adjust levels so the highlights are white and the shadows are black, which maximizes the usable range.

Step two: posterize to N colors

Apply a posterize or tone-separation filter to reduce the image to a fixed number of color levels. For a simple composition, 4–6 levels. For a complex one, 8–12. The filter groups similar colors together and replaces them with flat fills. This is what the vectorizer will do anyway, so doing it manually first lets you preview and adjust the result.

Step three: trace each tone as a separate layer

Trace the posterized image with the layer-by-color setting enabled. This creates one path per color, stacked in painter order. You can then edit individual colors, rearrange layers, or delete regions that did not posterize cleanly. The result is a vector file that looks deliberately stylized rather than accidentally posterized.

Dealing with gradients: when to use gradient meshes

If the painting has large areas of smooth gradients — a sky that fades from blue to white, a shadow that transitions from black to mid-tone — flat fills will look stepped and artificial. For these areas, consider using SVG gradients or gradient meshes instead of solid fills.

A PNG-to-SVG converter will not create gradients automatically; you have to add them by hand after tracing. Identify regions that should be smooth, delete the posterized paths, and replace them with linear or radial gradients. This is manual work, but it produces a cleaner result than tracing with 50 color levels.

Alternative: keep it raster and optimize for web or print

For many paintings, the honest answer is that vectorization is the wrong tool. If the goal is to reproduce the painting on the web, optimize a high-quality JPEG or WebP and serve it at multiple resolutions. If the goal is large-format printing, keep the painting as a high-resolution raster TIFF or PNG and send that to the printer. Vectors are not always better; they are better only when scalability or editability matters more than fidelity.

Special case: extracting silhouettes and shapes from paintings

Sometimes the goal is not to vectorize the whole painting but to extract a specific shape or figure from it. A portrait silhouette. A botanical illustration. A single object from a still life. For this, use a selection tool to isolate the shape, delete the background, then trace just the isolated region. The result: a clean vector silhouette that can be used in logos, icons, or graphic design.

Tools and workflows

Adobe Illustrator Image Trace and Inkscape Trace Bitmap both have poster-art presets that work well for tone-separated sources. For manual posterization, use Photoshop's Posterize filter or GIMP's Posterize tool before exporting to SVG. For gradient meshes, Illustrator and Inkscape both support them, but creating good meshes is manual work.

For paintings with soft edges and complex blending, consider exporting to PDF with embedded raster images rather than fully vectorizing. This gives you scalable text and graphics layered over a high-resolution raster reproduction of the painting.

Related resources

For the tracing pipeline itself, see Image Tracing Explained. For choosing the right source resolution before tracing, see Best Resolution for Vectorizing. For optimizing the traced output, see SVG Optimization Guide. For color separation workflows in screen printing, see Color Separation Guide.

faqs.question: Can I vectorize an oil painting and keep it looking realistic?
faqs.answer: No. Vectorization replaces continuous tone with flat fills and hard edges. For realistic reproduction, keep the painting as a high-resolution raster image. Vectorize only if you want a posterized or stylized interpretation, not a faithful reproduction.

faqs.question: What painting styles vectorize best?
faqs.answer: Flat poster art, ink wash, sumi-e, stencil designs, and cut-paper styles vectorize well because they already use limited palettes and hard edges. Impressionism, watercolor with soft blending, and oil paintings with thick impasto do not vectorize well.

faqs.question: How many colors should I use when vectorizing a painting?
faqs.answer: For a simple composition, 4–6 colors. For a complex one, 8–12. Beyond 12, the file becomes bloated with overlapping paths and the result looks like a bad JPEG artifact rather than a stylized vector. Posterize manually first to preview the color reduction.

faqs.question: Can I trace just one object from a painting instead of the whole thing?
faqs.answer: Yes. Use a selection tool to isolate the object, delete the background, then trace just the isolated region. This works well for silhouettes, botanical illustrations, or extracting a single figure from a complex composition.

faqs.question: Should I use gradients when vectorizing a painting?
faqs.answer: If the painting has large smooth gradients (a sky, a shadow transition), flat fills will look stepped. Add linear or radial gradients manually after tracing to replace posterized regions. This is extra work but produces a cleaner result than tracing with 50 color levels.

title: Logo Vectorization: Turning a Supplied Logo Into Clean Paths
seoTitle: Logo Vectorization: From Raster Supplier File to Clean SVG
seoDescription: You receive a logo as a screenshot and need a cut-ready file. Follow the cleanup sequence that produces a logo with clean curves and correct colors.
excerpt: The production sequence for a raster logo: get the largest source, trace at high res, delete background, merge same-color shapes, fix straight edges, rebuild type, check counters at final size, verify color count. Each step prevents a failure mode that shows up in production.
content:
A raster logo is a liability. It cannot scale without losing quality, it cannot be edited without redrawing it, and it cannot be sent to a vinyl cutter or laser without conversion. Vectorizing a logo is the production workflow that turns that liability into a scalable, editable asset — but only if you do it correctly. Trace a logo badly and you get wavy edges, open paths, and type that looks worse at large sizes than the original raster.

This guide walks through the production sequence for converting a raster logo to vector: from finding the best source to rebuilding type and verifying the result at final size.

Step one: get the largest, cleanest source you can

Before tracing anything, exhaust every option for finding a larger or cleaner version of the logo. Check the company website for a press kit or brand assets page. Search for high-resolution versions on the Internet Archive or Google Images filtered by size. Ask the client if they have the original file, even if they say they do not — sometimes an old employee has it on a backup drive.

A 300 PPI source will always trace better than a 72 PPI one, and a PNG will always trace better than a JPEG. If the only source you have is a 100×100 favicon, the vectorized result will be an approximation, not a faithful reproduction. Set expectations accordingly.

Step two: trace at high resolution

Trace the logo with tight tolerance settings: low curve tolerance, high speckle suppression, corner threshold around 80–90 degrees for geometric logos and 120–140 degrees for organic ones. The goal is to capture the true edges as accurately as possible. Do not simplify aggressively at this stage; you can reduce nodes later.

Check the trace in outline mode

After tracing, switch to outline mode (wireframe view) in your vector editor and inspect the paths. Look for stair-stepping along edges that should be smooth, extra nodes in the middle of straight segments, and open paths where endpoints did not snap together. These are the artifacts that will show up when the logo is scaled large.

Step three: delete the background

If the logo was on a white or colored background, the tracer will have created a background shape. Delete it. For logos with interior cutouts (the counter in an O, the hole in an A), verify that the cutouts are real holes and not overlapping shapes. In SVG, holes are made with path winding rules or compound paths; overlapping shapes look fine on screen but can cause problems in cut files or print separations.

Step four: merge shapes of the same color

If the logo has multiple shapes that are all the same color and do not overlap, merge them into a single path. This reduces file size and makes the logo easier to edit. In Illustrator, select the shapes and use Pathfinder → Unite. In Inkscape, use Path → Union. Do not merge overlapping shapes unless you are certain about painter order.

Step five: fix straight edges and align corners

Logos often have edges that are supposed to be perfectly horizontal, vertical, or at 45 degrees. A traced edge might be off by 0.5 degrees, which is invisible at small sizes but obvious when the logo is printed at 24 inches. Zoom in and check every edge that looks like it should be aligned. Use the Align tools to snap edges to the pixel grid or to each other.

Round coordinates for clean output

After aligning edges, round all coordinates to two decimal places. This removes sub-pixel jitter and makes the file smaller. In Illustrator, this is part of the Simplify command. In Inkscape, use Extensions → Modify Path → Round Coordinates. Do not round to integers unless you have verified that it does not break closed paths.

Step six: rebuild or replace type

If the logo includes text, the traced version will be outlines, not live type. That is fine for production, but it means the text cannot be edited later. More importantly, traced type often looks worse than the original font because the tracer smooths details that were intentional — the sharp serifs on a Times New Roman A, the flat terminals on a Helvetica S.

Identify the font and replace the outlines

Use a font identification tool (WhatTheFont, Identifont) to find the font used in the logo. If you can identify it, recreate the text as live type, convert it to outlines, then replace the traced letterforms. This gives you the true letterforms instead of an approximation. If the font is proprietary or unavailable, keep the traced version but inspect it carefully at large sizes.

Rebuild custom lettering

If the logo uses custom lettering or a modified typeface, you cannot replace it with a stock font. In this case, redraw the letters by hand on top of the traced paths. Use the traced version as a guide, but build clean Bezier curves with minimal nodes. This takes longer but produces a result that will scale cleanly to any size.

StepWhat to checkCommon mistake
Get best sourceResolution, format, compressionTracing a 72 DPI screenshot when a 300 DPI PDF exists
TraceTight tolerance, outline mode inspectionAccepting the default trace without checking paths
Delete backgroundReal holes vs. overlapping shapesLeaving a white background shape in the file
Merge same-color shapesNon-overlapping onlyMerging overlapping paths and breaking painter order
Align edgesHorizontal, vertical, 45-degree linesLeaving a 0.3-degree skew that shows at large sizes
Rebuild typeFont match, serifs, terminalsUsing traced letterforms that look mushy at 24 inches
Verify at scaleZoom to 500%, check counters and small textOnly previewing at thumbnail size

Step seven: check counters and small details at final size

Zoom in to 500% or print a test at the largest size the logo will be reproduced. Check that counters (the holes in O, P, R, A) did not close up, that small text is still readable, and that hairline details did not disappear. A logo that looks fine at 200 pixels wide can fall apart at 2000 pixels if small features were traced imprecisely.

Step eight: verify color count and separate spot colors

Count how many distinct colors the logo uses. A two-color logo should have exactly two fill colors in the vector file, not three because the tracer picked up an intermediate anti-aliasing shade. If the logo will be printed with spot colors (Pantone), assign the correct spot color values now rather than relying on CMYK approximations.

Fixing intermediate shades from anti-aliasing

If the source logo had anti-aliased edges, the tracer might have created shapes in an intermediate color. A black logo on white background might have gray outlines. Select all shapes of the intermediate color and either delete them (if they are thin outlines) or merge them into the main color (if they are part of the intended fill).

Production formats: SVG, EPS, PDF, or AI

Once the logo is vectorized and cleaned, export it in the formats your downstream processes need. For web use, SVG. For print production, EPS or PDF. For vinyl cutting or laser engraving, SVG or DXF. Keep the native Illustrator or Inkscape file as the master so you can re-export in other formats later.

For each export, verify that the file opens correctly in the target application. Some vinyl cutters do not handle compound paths correctly and need all shapes to be separate. Some printers expect spot colors to be named exactly as they appear in the Pantone library. Test the export rather than assuming it will work.

Common logo vectorization pitfalls

Here are the failures that show up in production after the vectorization is done, sorted by how often they happen.

Open paths in a shape that should be closed

The most common failure. Two endpoints that were 0.3 pixels apart in the raster became paths that do not quite meet in the vector. When sent to a laser or vinyl cutter, the machine sees an open path and does not cut a closed shape. The fix: zoom in to every corner and verify that endpoints snap together. Use a small snap tolerance (0.1 units or less) to catch near-misses.

Wavy edges on geometric shapes

A rectangle with 20 nodes per side instead of one node per corner. The tracer followed anti-aliasing or JPEG artifacts and created micro-wobbles. The fix: rebuild geometric shapes by hand with the rectangle, ellipse, and polygon tools, then use Pathfinder to combine them. Do not trace a rectangle; draw a rectangle.

Type that looks worse at large sizes

Traced letterforms lose the crispness of the original font. Serifs become rounded, terminals become soft, and the whole thing looks mushy when printed at 24 inches. The fix: identify the font and replace the traced letters with outlined type, or redraw the letters by hand.

Related resources

For the tracing pipeline itself, see Image Tracing Explained. For choosing the right source resolution, see Best Resolution for Vectorizing. For optimizing the traced output, see SVG Optimization Guide. For converter recommendations, see Logo to Vector and PNG to SVG. For preparing files for vinyl cutting, see Cricut Design Guide.

faqs.question: What resolution do I need to vectorize a logo?
faqs.answer: 300–400 PPI at the final reproduction size is sufficient. Higher resolution helps if the logo has very fine details like hairlines, but beyond 600 PPI you are usually tracing noise. If the only source is a low-resolution screenshot, the vectorized result will be an approximation.

faqs.question: Should I rebuild the text in a logo or keep the traced outlines?
faqs.answer: If you can identify the font, replace the traced text with outlined type from the original font. Traced letterforms often look mushy at large sizes because the tracer smooths details that were intentional. If the font is custom or unavailable, keep the traced version but inspect it carefully at 500% zoom.

faqs.question: Why does my vectorized logo have open paths when the original looked closed?
faqs.answer: The tracer created endpoints that are close but do not snap together. At raster resolution the gap is invisible, but when sent to a cutter the machine sees an open path. Zoom in to every corner and verify that endpoints meet. Use a small snap tolerance to catch near-misses.

faqs.question: How do I fix wavy edges on a geometric logo?
faqs.answer: The tracer followed anti-aliasing or JPEG artifacts. Rebuild geometric shapes by hand with the rectangle, ellipse, and polygon tools, then use Pathfinder to combine them. Do not trace a rectangle; draw a rectangle and align it to the traced reference.

faqs.question: Can I vectorize a logo from a business card photo?
faqs.answer: Only if the photo is high resolution, well-lit, and in focus. A phone photo of a business card is usually too low-resolution and has perspective distortion. If that is the only source, the vectorized result will be an approximation. Set expectations with the client before starting.

title: SVG Security: Why the Format Can Carry Scripts
seoTitle: SVG Security Risks: Scripts, External References and Safeguarding
seoDescription: SVG is XML and can carry script, external references and event handlers. Learn which vectors are real, how to sanitize, and what to check in user uploads.
excerpt: An SVG is not an image in the way a JPEG is an image. It is an XML document that browsers will happily execute, fetch and evaluate. That makes it a useful file type and a hostile one to accept blindly.
content:
Upload an SVG to a web application and you may have handed the server a document that can run script, fetch external URLs, expand an entity bomb, and phone home to a tracking pixel. Upload a JPEG and the worst case is a decoder bug. The difference is structural: SVG is executable markup, not a bitmap.

This matters most in three places — a browser rendering an untrusted SVG, a server-side upload or conversion pipeline, and a CDN serving user files from the same origin as the application.

What an SVG can contain beyond shapes

The XML root can hold child elements that are not drawing instructions at all. The SVG specification allows a <script> element, and it allows event attributes such as onload, onclick, and dozens of others on almost any element. These are the same JavaScript event attributes HTML has.

That is intended behaviour. Interactive SVG documents — diagrams with clickable regions, animated explainers, charts with tooltips — depend on it. But it means opening an SVG in a browser is closer to opening an HTML page than to opening a PNG.

Most importantly, when an SVG is loaded as a top-level document rather than through an <img> tag, any script it contains runs in the origin that served it. If your application serves user-uploaded SVGs from its own domain, script inside those files runs with your domain's privileges and can read cookies, call your APIs, and read local storage.

External references

An <image> element can point at a remote URL. So can a <use> element, a filter reference, a gradient reference, and CSS url() values inside a <style> block. Every one of those triggers an outbound HTTP request when the document is rendered.

Two attacks live here. The first is a tracking beacon: an image reference to an attacker-controlled host with a unique identifier in the query string tells the attacker when and where the file was opened. The second is server-side request forgery: if your backend rasterises SVGs, the rasteriser may follow those URLs from inside your network, reaching internal metadata endpoints or admin interfaces that are not publicly reachable.

VectorWhere it bitesImpactMitigation
<script> elementBrowser, same-origin servingStored XSS; session theftStrip in sanitiser; serve from a separate origin
on* event attributesBrowserXSS on interaction or loadAllowlist attributes; never pass through unchanged
javascript: hrefBrowserExecution on clickReject non-safe URL schemes
External <image href>Browser, server rasteriserTracking, SSRF, IP leakInline or block remote references
XXE entity definitionsServer-side XML parserFile disclosure, SSRFDisable external entities and DTDs
Billion laughs entity expansionServer-side parserMemory exhaustion, DoSLimit entity expansion; cap input size
Deeply nested groupsRenderer, rasteriserCPU/memory DoSLimit nesting depth and node count
Huge filter regionsRasteriserMemory exhaustionStrip filters or cap output pixels
Oversized viewBoxRasteriserMassive raster allocationClamp target dimensions server-side

What matters for a browser

A browser treats a top-level SVG as a document. Script runs, external requests fire, and same-origin policy applies to the serving origin. If you serve user SVGs from https://yourapp.com, the script inside them runs as yourapp.com.

Three defences reduce this to near zero, and they are independent:

  1. Serve user-uploaded content from a separate origin or a cookie-less subdomain, so script cannot reach your session cookies or call your authenticated APIs.
  2. Send Content-Disposition: attachment for direct downloads, so a navigation to the file downloads rather than renders it.
  3. Send a strong Content Security Policy with script-src 'none' on the response that serves the file.

The <img> element has different rules. When an SVG loads through <img src=\"file.svg\">, browsers disable scripting and do not run external resource loads the same way. That is why referencing untrusted SVGs via <img> is much safer than inlining them into the page or navigating to them. Inline SVG — pasting markup into the HTML — is the most dangerous pattern, because the markup lands in the page's own DOM.

What browsers already protect against

Modern browsers disable external entity resolution in XML, so classic XXE against a browser is largely historical. They also apply origin boundaries to SVG served cross-origin. These protections do not extend to your server-side tooling, which is where the remaining risk concentrates.

What matters for a server-side pipeline

If your application accepts an SVG upload and then parses, sanitises, measures, or rasterises it, the XML parser itself becomes an attack surface. The classic vulnerabilities are well documented and still reproducible in libraries configured with defaults.

XXE. A DTD declares an entity that points at a local file or a URL. When the parser expands it and the content is echoed or embedded in output, the file is exfiltrated. Disabling DTD processing entirely is the clean fix; there is no legitimate reason for an SVG from an untrusted source to define custom entities.

Entity expansion. The billion laughs pattern nests entity references so that a tiny document expands into gigabytes. Limits on total expansion, or rejection of any internal DTD, close it.

Rasteriser resource exhaustion. Converting a vector to a bitmap is proportional to target pixel count, not input file size. A one-kilobyte SVG with a viewBox the size of a billboard and a request to render at 300 DPI can ask for several gigabytes of memory. Cap the target dimensions on the server and reject anything beyond a sane maximum.

Filters and nested groups. A small document with deeply nested groups each carrying a blur filter causes multiplicative work. Depth limits and a filter allowlist are the defence.

The sanitisation approach that works

Use an allowlist, not a blocklist. Blocklists lose because the SVG specification and browser behaviour keep adding attributes, and because parsers accept spelling variants and namespace tricks that a naive string match misses.

A working allowlist for image-oriented SVGs:

  • Elements: svg, g, path, rect, circle, ellipse, line, polyline, polygon, defs, linearGradient, radialGradient, stop, use, title, desc.
  • Excluded entirely: script, foreignObject, style, iframe, audio, video, animate variants that set href.
  • Attributes: geometry and paint only — d, x, y, width, height, rx, ry, cx, cy, r, points, fill, fill-opacity, stroke, stroke-width, stroke-linecap, stroke-linejoin, opacity, transform, viewBox, preserveAspectRatio.
  • Always rejected: any attribute beginning on, any href or xlink:href that is not a same-document #id fragment, and any value beginning javascript: or data:text/html.

foreignObject deserves special mention. It allows arbitrary HTML — including script — inside an SVG. Almost no legitimate logo file needs it, and it defeats most naive filters because the payload is not in an SVG element at all.

Content sniffing and MIME types

Browsers decide how to render a file from its Content-Type header, with some sniffing. If your server labels a user-uploaded SVG as text/plain, most browsers will not execute it and the risk drops. If it serves it as image/svg+xml, the file becomes an active document. That header is a security control, not a formality.

Serving with Content-Type: text/plain plus Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff produces a file that a browser downloads rather than renders. Users who want to preview it see a stored raster instead. This combination closes the browser-side attack surface for user uploads more completely than any sanitiser written in-house.

Sanitiser libraries and their limits

Maintained libraries exist for the purpose and generally do the job well, provided they are configured with a strict policy rather than a permissive one. The pattern in practice is to run the library with the same conservative profile you would use for HTML, then to additionally block foreignObject, which most HTML sanitisers permit because HTML needs it and SVG does not.

The failure mode to watch for is a sanitiser applied to a parsed DOM and then the original file written back. If the clean output is not what gets stored, the sanitiser did nothing but use CPU. Verify by re-parsing what was persisted and checking that the document contains only allowlisted elements.

Chain of custody for converted files

Conversion is a trust boundary. An untrusted SVG that has been converted to PNG is no longer dangerous, but the intermediate file and the conversion process are. Keep the original quarantined, never let it reach a path that will eventually be served, and treat the rasterised output as a new artifact with its own integrity checks.

If you offer conversion as a product feature — taking customer artwork and returning a cleaned vector, for instance — the safest architecture is to convert into a raster, display that for approval, and only generate the vector output from geometry your own pipeline produced. That way no untrusted markup ever leaves your infrastructure intact.

Detecting malicious intent versus bad tooling

Not every hostile-looking SVG is hostile. Design tools routinely emit empty style blocks, namespace declarations, comments containing the author's username, and references to local font files. A file full of what looks like noise is usually just Illustrator being Illustrator.

Distinguish by behaviour. A script element with an actual payload, an onload attribute defining a function, or an href pointing at an external domain with a query string — those are intentional. A style block with a reset rule is not. Log what your sanitiser removed so you can review the difference in aggregate rather than inspecting every upload by hand.

Safe rendering of untrusted files

When you must display a user's SVG and cannot guarantee it has been sanitised, rasterise it server-side. Rendering the image to a PNG means the output is pixels, and pixels cannot execute. This is the approach large platforms use for avatar and logo uploads. Do the rasterisation in an isolated process with memory and CPU limits, with no network access.

The same principle makes SVG to PNG a useful security control, not just a format conversion. If your pipeline produces a PNG preview, serve that preview and never serve the original file from your main origin.

If the rasteriser runs in a sandbox with no egress, the SSRF class disappears entirely. If it also has a hard memory cap, the resource exhaustion class disappears. Both are configuration, not code.

A practical hardening checklist

  1. Parse SVG with an XML library configured to forbid DTDs and external entities.
  2. Cap input file size before parsing.
  3. Run the sanitiser against an element and attribute allowlist.
  4. Reject or strip all on* attributes and non-fragment hrefs.
  5. Serve user content from a distinct origin, with Content-Disposition: attachment on download routes.
  6. Do all rasterisation in a network-isolated sandbox with memory limits.
  7. Store the sanitised copy, and treat the original as untrusted forever.

If you accept customer artwork as a matter of course, handling bulk customer artwork covers the intake side of the same problem, and what print shops ask customers shows the file requirements that reduce surprise uploads.

For background on what the format legally contains, see what an SVG actually is. If your concern is cleanup for machinery rather than security, the SVG optimisation guide covers stripping extraneous markup, and batch conversion workflows covers running the same treatment across a queue of files.

faqs.question: Can an SVG file contain malware?
faqs.answer: It can contain script, event handlers and external references, because SVG is XML markup that browsers execute. A well-known SVG can carry cross-site scripting payloads that run when served from your domain. It cannot infect an operating system the way a binary executable does, but it can steal sessions and pivot through your application.

faqs.question: Is loading an SVG in an img tag safe?
faqs.answer: Much safer than inlining it. When an SVG loads through an img element, browsers disable scripting and block most external resource loads. The danger returns if you inline the markup into your page's DOM, embed it in an iframe, or navigate directly to it on your own origin.

faqs.question: What is XXE and does it apply to SVG?
faqs.answer: XXE is XML External Entity injection: a DTD defines an entity pointing at a local file or URL, and the parser expands it into the document. SVG is XML, so it applies wherever an SVG is parsed by a server-side library that has not disabled external entities. The fix is to disallow DTD processing entirely.

faqs.question: How do I sanitise an SVG before serving it?
faqs.answer: Parse it with an XML parser that rejects DTDs, then rebuild the document using an allowlist of safe elements and attributes. Drop script, foreignObject, style and all on* event attributes. Reject any href that is not a same-document fragment. Then serve the rebuilt file from a separate origin.

faqs.question: Why rasterise untrusted SVGs instead of cleaning them?
faqs.answer: Rasterisation reduces the output to pixels, which cannot execute or make network requests. It closes every markup-based attack class at once, including ones you did not anticipate. The cost is that the result is no longer vector, so keep the original quarantined and regenerate if needed.

title: Screen Print Color Separations: Manual vs Automatic
seoTitle: Screen Print Color Separations: Manual vs Automatic Workflow
seoDescription: Separations decide whether your screen print registers. Compare manual and automatic methods, and learn the file conditions each one needs.
excerpt: Color separation splits a design into one layer per ink. Manual workflows give total control but take time; automatic RIP software is fast but decides traps and layering for you.
content:
Color separation in screen printing means splitting a design into individual layers, one per ink color, so each screen deposits exactly one color. A four-color design requires four separations, four screens, and four print passes. The separation process determines whether colors register correctly, whether traps prevent gaps, and whether the final print matches the proof.

Two workflows dominate: manual separation, where a designer assigns spot colors and exports one file per screen, and automatic separation, where RIP software or a plugin reads the artwork and generates separations based on algorithms. Each approach has tradeoffs in control, speed, file requirements, and the skill level needed to execute it correctly.

What a Color Separation Is

A separation is a single-color layer. If your design has red, yellow, and black, you create three separations: one file showing only the red areas, one showing only yellow, and one showing only black. Each separation becomes a film positive, which is burned onto a coated screen. When you print, you register the screens so each color lands in the correct position, building the full-color image.

Spot color separations print solid ink—no halftone dots, no blending. If the design contains gradients or photographic elements, you must either convert those to halftone screens (covered in halftone and simulated process) or flatten them into spot regions. Spot separations work best for vector art, logos, and designs with flat color fills.

Registration marks—crosshairs or circles printed on every screen—let you align each layer. Without registration marks, even a 1mm shift between screens produces visible gaps or color fringing. Most screen printers add marks automatically in their RIP, but manual workflows require you to place them in the source file before separating.

Manual Separation Workflow

Manual separation gives you complete control. You assign each design element to a named spot color in Illustrator, Inkscape, or CorelDRAW, then export one file per color. This workflow suits simple designs (2–4 colors), specialty inks (metallic, glow-in-the-dark), and shops that want to optimize ink layering order or trap width by hand.

The steps: open the design, select all objects that should print in the first color (e.g., red), assign them a spot color named "Red" in the swatches panel, then hide or delete all other colors and export that layer as a PDF or EPS. Repeat for each color. Each exported file contains only the geometry for one screen. File format matters: spot colors must remain as named swatches, not converted to CMYK or RGB process colors, or the RIP will not recognize them.

Trapping and choking compensate for misregistration. A trap expands the lighter color slightly so it overlaps the darker color beneath it, preventing white gaps if the screens shift. A choke shrinks the top color so the bottom color shows through a thin border. Trap width typically ranges from 0.5pt to 1pt (0.18mm to 0.35mm), depending on press precision and substrate texture. You apply traps manually by duplicating a shape, offsetting the path, and assigning it to the underlying color layer.

Manual separation is slow—each color requires selection, export, and proofing—but it gives you pixel-level authority over what prints. If a design has overlapping transparency effects or live blends, manual separation forces you to flatten or rasterize those areas first, which can be a benefit (you control how effects render) or a burden (more steps).

Automatic Separation Workflow

Automatic separation uses RIP software (AccuRIP, Separation Studio, SimSep) or a plugin (Spot Process Separation for Illustrator) to analyze artwork and generate separations in seconds. The software reads colors, groups similar hues, and outputs one file per screen. This workflow suits high-volume shops, designs with many colors, and print operators who prefer speed over manual tweaking.

The tradeoff: less control. The algorithm decides how to handle gradients, transparency, and overlapping objects. If the design has a soft drop shadow, the RIP may rasterize it and add a halftone screen, or it may flatten it into the nearest spot color, depending on settings. You must inspect the separations before burning screens to ensure the software made the choices you wanted.

File requirements differ. Automatic separation works best with flattened RGB or CMYK artwork where all effects are rasterized and all text is outlined. If you hand the RIP a file with live blends, spot colors, and vector effects, results vary by software. Some RIPs preserve spot colors and separate them as-is; others convert everything to process colors first, then separate by channel. Check your RIP's documentation and run test files to understand its behavior.

Automatic trapping is built into most RIPs, but it applies a uniform trap width to all edges. If you need custom traps—thicker traps for rough substrates like burlap, or no trap on fine detail—you may still need to pre-trap the file manually before handing it to the RIP.

Separation MethodControl LevelSpeedFile RequirementBest For
Manual (Illustrator/Inkscape)Total—every trap, every overlapSlow—minutes per colorSpot colors, no live effects2–4 color designs, specialty inks, fine art prints
Automatic (RIP software)Limited—algorithm decidesFast—seconds for all colorsFlattened RGB/CMYK, effects rasterizedHigh-volume shops, photo-realistic prints, simulated process
Hybrid (manual pre-trap + RIP)High—trap by hand, separate by softwareModerateSpot colors with manual traps appliedComplex designs needing custom traps but fast output

Common Separation Failures and Fixes

White gaps between colors signal misregistration or missing traps. If you printed a two-color design and see a thin white line where red meets blue, either the screens shifted during printing (mechanical issue) or you did not apply a trap (file issue). Re-export the file with a 0.5pt trap on the lighter color, or adjust press registration if the gap width varies across the print.

Colors printing in the wrong order cause muddy results. Lighter colors should print first, darker colors last, so each layer sits on top of the previous one without obscuring it. If you print black first and yellow second, the yellow may not fully cover the black, producing a greenish tint. Reorder the screens in your press setup or relabel the separations so the print operator knows the correct sequence.

Halftone moiré appears when automatic separation generates overlapping halftone screens at the same angle. This happens when the RIP converts a gradient or photo to CMYK halftones without adjusting screen angles. Fix it by setting each halftone screen to a different angle (cyan at 15°, magenta at 75°, yellow at 0°, black at 45°), or by using a stochastic (random dot) halftone that eliminates angle-dependent moiré. The halftone and simulated process guide covers this in detail.

For general information on preparing print-ready files across different processes, see print-ready artwork requirements. If you are separating for DTF instead of screen printing, the DTF white underbase guide explains how alpha channels replace manual trapping.

File Export Settings for Separations

Export each separation as a high-resolution PDF (300 DPI minimum for rasterized elements) or EPS with spot colors preserved. If your RIP accepts TIFF, export at 600 DPI bitmap with one file per color channel. Do not export separations as JPG—JPEG compression introduces artifacts that show up as jagged edges on screen.

Embed fonts or convert all text to outlines before separating. If the file contains live text and your RIP does not have the font installed, characters will reflow or disappear. Use Type → Create Outlines in Illustrator or Path → Object to Path in Inkscape.

Include crop marks and registration marks on every separation. Most RIPs add these automatically, but if you are burning screens manually, place crosshairs at each corner of the design in your source file, assign them to every color layer, and ensure they export with each separation. This guarantees consistent alignment across all screens.

If you are working with SVG files for web-to-print workflows, convert them to PDF or EPS before separating—most screen print RIPs do not process SVG directly. Use SVG to PDF conversion or SVG to EPS conversion to prepare files for separation software.

When to Use Simulated Process Instead

Spot color separation works for designs with distinct, flat color regions. If the design has photographic content, gradients, or more than six colors, simulated process (CMYK halftone separations over a white or highlight-color underbase) is faster and more cost-effective than printing ten or twelve spot color screens.

Simulated process uses four to six screens (white underbase, cyan, magenta, yellow, black, and sometimes a highlight color like red or blue) to reproduce a full-color image. The trade-off: halftone dots are visible up close, and color matching is less precise than spot colors. For apparel printing on dark garments, simulated process is the standard. For logo work and brand-critical color matching (Pantone requirements), stick with spot separations.

Read the halftone and simulated process guide for a full comparison of line screen settings, underbase strategies, and when to use index separations instead of full CMYK.

faqs.question: What is the difference between spot color separation and simulated process?
faqs.answer: Spot color separation prints one solid ink per screen, ideal for logos and flat-color designs with 2–6 colors. Simulated process uses CMYK halftone screens over a white underbase to reproduce photographic images and designs with many colors. Spot colors give precise color matching; simulated process gives full-color range with fewer limitations but visible halftone dots.

faqs.question: How wide should traps be in screen print separations?
faqs.answer: Trap width typically ranges from 0.5pt to 1pt (0.18mm to 0.35mm). Use narrower traps (0.5pt) for smooth substrates and high-precision presses. Use wider traps (1pt or more) for textured fabrics or manual presses with lower registration accuracy. Test on your specific press and substrate to find the minimum trap that prevents white gaps.

faqs.question: Can I use RGB artwork for screen print separations?
faqs.answer: Yes, but convert RGB to spot colors first if you want manual control over each screen. Automatic RIP software accepts RGB and converts it during separation, but the algorithm decides how to map RGB values to spot channels. For predictable results, assign spot colors (named swatches) in your design software before exporting separations.

faqs.question: Why do my separations have white gaps after printing?
faqs.answer: White gaps indicate either misregistration (screens shifted during printing) or missing traps (no overlap between adjacent colors in the file). Check press alignment first—if gaps are consistent, add a 0.5–1pt trap to the lighter color in your separation file. If gaps vary across the print, the press needs mechanical adjustment.

faqs.question: Do I need registration marks on every separation?
faqs.answer: Yes. Registration marks (crosshairs or circles) printed on each screen allow you to align layers precisely. Without them, even small shifts produce visible misregistration. Most RIP software adds marks automatically, but manual workflows require you to place them in the source file and export them with each color layer.

title: Halftone and Simulated Process: Printing a Gradient
seoTitle: Halftone Screen Printing: Simulated Process for Gradients
seoDescription: Screen printing cannot print a continuous gradient. Halftone dots turn tone into printable pattern. Here is how line frequency and angle decide quality.
excerpt: Halftone dots create tone in screen printing by varying size, not ink transparency. Line screen frequency, dot angle, and dot gain determine whether your simulated process print looks smooth or shows moiré and banding.
content:
Screen printing cannot reproduce continuous tone the way a photograph does. Instead, it uses halftone dots—tiny ink spots arranged in a grid—where dot size and spacing create the illusion of tonal variation. Simulated process printing applies this principle to full-color images by layering CMYK halftone screens over a white or colored underbase, letting screen printers reproduce photographic artwork on garments without needing a separate screen for every color.

Halftone quality depends on three variables: line screen frequency (LPI), dot angle, and dot gain. Get these wrong and you see visible moiré patterns, loss of detail, or colors that print darker than the proof. Understanding how each parameter affects the final print lets you optimize separations for your press, mesh count, and substrate.

How Halftone Dots Create Tone

A halftone screen divides an image into a grid of cells. Each cell contains one dot. In light areas, the dot is small; in dark areas, the dot is large. Your eye blends the white space between dots with the ink color, perceiving a continuous gradient. This technique dates to 19th-century printing but remains the only way to print grayscale or color photos with spot-color inks.

Line screen frequency, measured in lines per inch (LPI), determines how fine or coarse the halftone appears. A 45 LPI screen has 45 rows of dots per inch, producing large, visible dots. An 85 LPI screen has 85 rows per inch, producing smaller, finer dots. Higher LPI gives smoother gradients but requires finer mesh screens and more precise press registration.

For screen printing on fabric, LPI typically ranges from 35 (coarse, for rough textiles) to 65 (fine, for smooth garments). Offset printing uses 150–300 LPI because paper holds finer detail than fabric. If you apply a 150 LPI halftone to a 110-mesh screen, the mesh cannot resolve the dots—ink bleeds through multiple openings, and the image turns muddy.

Simulated Process vs. CMYK Process

Simulated process is not true CMYK. True process printing (like offset or digital press) uses transparent cyan, magenta, yellow, and black inks that blend optically where dots overlap, producing a full spectrum of colors. Screen print inks are opaque, so overlapping dots do not blend—they stack. A cyan dot over a magenta dot does not produce blue; it produces whichever ink layer is on top.

To work around this, simulated process adds a white underbase (or a highlight color underbase, like red or yellow) printed first, then layers CMYK halftone screens on top. The white base gives the CMYK inks something bright to sit on, preventing the dark fabric from showing through and dulling colors. Some printers add a fifth or sixth screen (spot red, spot blue) to boost colors that CMYK cannot hit accurately—this is called index separation or UltraSep.

Index separations use spot colors for key elements (skin tones, brand colors) and halftone screens for less critical areas (backgrounds, shadows). This hybrid approach gives better color accuracy than pure CMYK halftones but requires more screens. A six-color simulated process job might use white underbase, cyan, magenta, yellow, black, and spot red.

ParameterEffect on PrintAdjustment Guidelines
Line screen (LPI)Higher LPI = finer dots, smoother gradients; lower LPI = coarser dots, more visible texture35–45 LPI for 110-mesh, 55–65 LPI for 156-mesh, 65–85 LPI for 230-mesh on smooth substrates
Dot angleIncorrect angles cause moiré (overlapping grids create interference patterns)Use 30° offsets: cyan 15°, magenta 75°, yellow 0°, black 45°
Dot gainDots spread during printing, darkening the image and filling in highlightsCompensate by reducing dot size 5–15% in prepress, or underexpose screens slightly to shrink dots
Underbase opacityThinner underbase saves ink but lets fabric color show through; thicker underbase gives brighter CMYK but adds hand (stiffness)Print white underbase at 100% opacity in highlight areas, 70–80% in shadows to reduce hand

Mesh Count and LPI Relationship

Mesh count is the number of threads per inch in the screen fabric. A 110-mesh screen has 110 threads per inch; a 230-mesh screen has 230. Higher mesh counts allow finer detail and smaller halftone dots, but they also reduce ink deposit, which can cause incomplete coverage on dark fabrics.

The rule of thumb: mesh count should be at least 4× the LPI. For a 55 LPI halftone, use a 220-mesh screen minimum. For a 35 LPI halftone, 140-mesh is sufficient. If you try to print a 65 LPI halftone on a 110-mesh screen, the mesh openings are too large relative to the dot size—ink floods through, dots merge, and fine details disappear.

White underbase screens use lower mesh counts (110–156) because you need thick ink deposit to block the fabric color. CMYK halftone screens use higher mesh counts (200–230) because you want thin, precise dots that do not obscure each other. This is why simulated process requires multiple screens with different mesh specifications—you cannot use the same mesh for every color.

Dot Angle and Moiré Prevention

Each halftone screen has an angle—the direction the grid of dots tilts. If you stack two halftone screens at the same angle, the grids align and create a visible pattern called moiré. Moiré looks like wavy lines or rosettes and ruins the print. To prevent it, rotate each color screen to a different angle, offset by at least 30°.

The standard angles: cyan at 15°, magenta at 75°, yellow at 0°, and black at 45°. Yellow is least visible, so it tolerates a 0° angle without causing moiré. Black is most visible, so it gets the 45° angle—the eye perceives 45° diagonals as softer than vertical or horizontal lines. These angles are not arbitrary; they are mathematically spaced to minimize interference between overlapping grids.

Some RIP software (AccuRIP, Separation Studio) applies these angles automatically. If you are generating halftones manually in Photoshop, you must set the angle for each channel individually. In Photoshop, convert the image to Grayscale, then Image → Mode → Bitmap, choose Halftone Screen, and enter the LPI and angle for each separation.

Stochastic (random dot) halftones eliminate moiré entirely by randomizing dot placement instead of using a fixed grid. This works well for fine-detail images, but stochastic screens are harder to burn (they require higher-resolution films or direct-to-screen imaging) and are less common in garment printing. Most screen printers stick with angled halftones.

Dot Gain Compensation

Dot gain is the tendency for halftone dots to spread during printing. A 50% dot in your file may print as a 60% dot on fabric because ink soaks into the weave and expands beyond the mesh opening. This makes the entire image darker and can fill in highlight details (light areas where dots should be small).

Compensate for dot gain by reducing dot size in the prepress file. If you expect 10% dot gain, reduce all dot values by 10% before burning screens. Most RIP software has a dot gain compensation setting—enter the expected gain percentage, and the software shrinks dots proportionally. Alternatively, underexpose screens slightly during burning, which produces smaller mesh openings and smaller dots.

Dot gain varies by substrate. Smooth, tightly woven fabrics (performance polyester, dress shirts) have less dot gain (5–10%) because ink sits on the surface. Coarse, open-weave fabrics (canvas, fleece) have more dot gain (15–25%) because ink soaks in. Run test prints on your target fabric and measure dot gain with a densitometer or by visual comparison to the proof, then adjust compensation settings for that substrate.

Underbase Strategy for Dark Garments

On white or light-colored garments, you can skip the underbase and print CMYK halftones directly—the fabric itself acts as the white base. On dark garments (black, navy, dark gray), you must print a white underbase first, or the CMYK inks will not be visible. The underbase blocks the fabric color and gives the halftones a bright foundation.

Two underbase approaches: full-coverage (print white everywhere the design appears) or highlight-only (print white only in light areas, let the fabric color serve as the black in shadows). Highlight-only underbases save ink and reduce hand (stiffness), but they require precise registration—if the white underbase shifts, you see white edges around dark areas.

Some printers use a colored underbase instead of white. For a sunset image, a yellow or orange underbase printed first can warm the entire palette, reducing the amount of yellow and magenta halftone ink needed on top. This technique is common in high-end simulated process and requires custom color profiling to predict how the underbase affects the CMYK layers.

For general screen print file preparation, see screen print color separations. For other apparel printing processes, compare sublimation, DTF, and UV DTF. If you are preparing vector artwork for screen printing, use PNG to SVG conversion or logo vectorization to ensure clean edges before applying halftones.

When to Use Simulated Process

Simulated process suits photographic images, designs with gradients or shading, and artwork with more colors than you want to print as spot colors. It is the standard for full-color T-shirt printing on dark garments. If the design has ten distinct colors, simulated process (six screens) is cheaper and faster than printing ten spot color screens.

Simulated process does not suit logos or text that require exact Pantone matching, because halftone dots introduce visible texture and color shifts. For brand-critical color matching, use spot color separations (covered in manual and automatic separation workflows). For print-ready file requirements across all processes, see print-ready artwork checklists.

faqs.question: What LPI should I use for screen printing on T-shirts?
faqs.answer: Use 45–55 LPI for standard garment printing with 156-mesh screens. Lower LPI (35–45) works for coarse fabrics or 110-mesh screens. Higher LPI (55–65) requires 200–230 mesh and smooth, tight-weave substrates. Going above 65 LPI on fabric usually causes dot gain and loss of detail.

faqs.question: Why do my simulated process prints have wavy patterns (moiré)?
faqs.answer: Moiré happens when two halftone screens have the same or similar angles, causing the dot grids to interfere. Fix it by setting each color to a different angle: cyan 15°, magenta 75°, yellow 0°, black 45°. Most RIP software applies these angles automatically. If separating manually, check your halftone settings for each channel.
