faqs.answer: After tracing, use Path → Simplify (Ctrl+L) to reduce nodes by 20–50% with minimal shape change. Before tracing, increase the Optimize value to 0.4–0.6 and set Smooth Corners to 1.2–1.33. Run Simplify twice if the first pass leaves jagged curves.

faqs.question: Can I batch-process Trace Bitmap on multiple files?
faqs.answer: Inkscape does not expose Trace Bitmap in its command-line interface, but you can call Potrace directly. Install Potrace and run a shell loop: for f in *.png; do convert "$f" bmp:- | potrace -s -o "${f%.png}.svg"; done to process an entire directory.

faqs.question: Why does my traced logo have gaps and open paths?
faqs.answer: Gaps appear when pixel edges don't form closed loops in the source. Clean the scan first: open it in GIMP, use Colors → Levels to make backgrounds pure white (255) and lines solid black (0). Check "Invert image" in Trace Bitmap if needed.

faqs.question: Is Inkscape Trace Bitmap as good as Illustrator Image Trace?
faqs.answer: For line art and technical drawings, Inkscape offers finer control over corners and smoothing because it exposes Potrace parameters directly. For complex color artwork, both perform similarly. Inkscape is free and better for scripted batch workflows; Illustrator integrates with Adobe Creative Cloud.

title: Rhino: Tracing a Scanned Drawing Into Clean Curves
seoTitle: Rhino Tracing Guide: Scanned Drawing to Curves
seoDescription: Rhino's curve tools outperform automatic tracing on technical drawings. Here is a repeatable workflow for turning a scan into one spline per stroke.
excerpt: Rhino reads SVG, AI, DXF but doesn't trace internally. Prepare scans at 300–600 DPI, clean in GIMP, trace in Illustrator or Inkscape, import via Rhino Import command. Use ReduceCrv, CloseCrv, Join to clean paths. For accuracy, redraw with PictureFrame reference.
content:
Rhinoceros does not include a built-in raster-to-vector tracer. When you need to convert a scanned architectural elevation, a hand-drawn plan, or a reference sketch into editable curves, the workflow moves through an external tracing tool — typically Illustrator, Inkscape, or a dedicated tracer — then imports the resulting vector paths into Rhino as curves. The challenge is maintaining scale, handling layer organization, and deciding when to trace automatically versus redrawing manually with Rhino's curve tools.

This guide explains how to prepare scanned drawings for tracing, which tools integrate cleanly with Rhino, and how to import traced SVG or DXF files while preserving accuracy and layer structure.

Why Rhino Doesn't Trace Internally

Rhino is a NURBS modeler, not a pixel editor. Its strength is precise geometry — curves defined by control points, not pixel boundaries. Tracing is fundamentally a pixel-to-vector conversion, and embedding that into Rhino would duplicate functionality already handled by dedicated tools. The Rhino development team chose integration over duplication: Rhino reads SVG, DXF, AI, and DWG, so you trace elsewhere and import the result.

This separation has an advantage. External tracers offer preview modes, threshold adjustment, and speckle suppression tuned for raster input. Rhino's curve tools (Curve, InterpCrv, Polyline, Arc, Circle) let you refine traced paths or redraw them from scratch with dimension-driven precision.

Preparing the Scanned Drawing

Before tracing, clean the scan to remove noise, correct skew, and set proper resolution. A poorly prepared scan produces traced paths that require hours of manual cleanup.

Resolution and Format

Scan line art at 300–600 DPI in grayscale or black-and-white mode. Higher DPI does not improve trace quality beyond 600 DPI and increases file size. Save as TIFF or PNG (lossless). Avoid JPEG — compression artifacts become traced as small jagged paths.

Cleaning the Scan

Open the scan in GIMP or Photoshop. Use Image → Auto → Levels to make whites pure (255) and blacks solid (0). Run Filters → Enhance → Unsharp Mask at 80% strength, 1-pixel radius to crisp up faded lines. Rotate the image if skewed using Image → Transform → Arbitrary Rotation and set the canvas background to white before rotating.

Apply Filters → Noise → Median with a 1-pixel radius to remove scanner dust and JPEG artifacts. Check that dimension lines, text, and fine details are still readable. Save the cleaned version and close the original.

Tracing the Drawing

Three workflows: auto-trace in Illustrator or Inkscape, manual trace in a vector editor, or manual redraw directly in Rhino. Choose based on drawing complexity and accuracy requirements.

Auto-Trace in Illustrator (Fast, Moderate Accuracy)

Import the cleaned scan into Illustrator. Select it and open Object → Image Trace → Make. In the Image Trace panel, choose the "Technical Drawing" preset for architectural plans or CAD exports, or "Black and White Logo" for clean line art.

Expand the Advanced section. Set Paths to 80–85%, Corners to 75–85%, and Noise to 4–8 pixels. Click Trace. Once tracing finishes, click Expand in the top toolbar to convert the trace result to paths. Ungroup all layers and delete any unwanted background regions.

Save as SVG (File → Export → Export As, choose SVG, uncheck "Responsive" in the SVG Options dialog). Use SVG 1.1 profile and set Decimal Places to 3 for dimension accuracy.

Auto-Trace in Inkscape (Free, More Control)

Import the scan into Inkscape (File → Import, embed the image). Select it and open Path → Trace Bitmap. Choose "Brightness cutoff" mode and set the threshold to 0.45–0.50. Enable "Suppress speckles" with a size of 4–8, and set "Smooth corners" to 1.0–1.2.

Click Update to preview. If lines are broken or missing, lower the threshold to 0.35–0.40. If too much noise appears, increase speckle suppression to 8–12. Once satisfied, click OK. Inkscape creates a new path group above the original image. Delete the original image and ungroup the paths.

Save as Plain SVG (File → Save As, choose "Plain SVG" format). This removes Inkscape-specific metadata that Rhino cannot parse.

ToolBest ForOutput FormatRhino Import Command
Illustrator Image TraceMixed line weights, shaded regionsSVG, AI, DXFImport or _Open
Inkscape Trace BitmapClean line art, architectural plansPlain SVGImport
AutoCAD (manual redraw)Dimensioned plans with exact measurementsDWG, DXFImport or _Open
Rhino (manual redraw)Organic shapes, 3D reference sketchesNative .3dmDirect drawing

Importing Traced Paths into Rhino

Rhino reads SVG via the Import command. The paths arrive as curves in model space at a scale determined by the SVG viewBox attribute. If the traced drawing was scanned at an unknown scale, you will need to measure and rescale after import.

Using the Import Command

In Rhino, type Import and select your SVG or DXF file. Rhino places all paths as curves in the active layer. The import dialog does not expose scale or unit options — these are inferred from the file. SVG paths import at 1 unit = 1 SVG user unit (typically 1 pixel or 1/96 inch).

After import, type SelCrv to select all curves. Type BoundingBox and note the dimensions. If the drawing represents a building facade 30 meters wide but the bounding box shows 3000 units, the import scale is 100:1. Use Scale to correct it: select the curves, type Scale, pick a base point, and type 0.01 as the scale factor.

Preserving Layers

If your SVG was organized into layers (Illustrator or Inkscape), Rhino imports each layer as a separate Rhino layer. Check the Layers panel (Panels → Layers) after import. Rename layers to match your project naming conventions (e.g., "Floor Plan," "Elevations," "Sections").

If all paths imported into a single layer, open the SVG in a text editor and check that each group has an id or inkscape:label attribute. Rhino uses these to generate layer names. Re-export from your vector editor with layer names intact.

Refining Traced Paths in Rhino

Traced paths rarely need no adjustment. Curves may overshoot, have excessive control points, or fail to close where they should. Three Rhino commands clean up common issues.

Simplifying Curves (ReduceCrv)

Traced curves often have dozens of control points where five would suffice. Select a curve and type ReduceCrv. Set the tolerance to 0.01–0.1 units (depending on your model scale). Rhino removes unnecessary control points while keeping the curve within the tolerance distance of the original shape.

For batch simplification, type SelCrv to select all curves, then run ReduceCrv once. Check the result at full zoom — if fine details are lost, undo and reduce the tolerance.

Closing Open Curves (CloseCrv)

If a region that should be a closed polyline has a small gap, select the curve and type CloseCrv. Rhino connects the endpoints with a straight segment. For gaps larger than 0.1 units, use CurveBoolean or manually draw a connecting line with Line, then use Join to merge all segments.

Joining Polylines (Join)

Traced line art often arrives as many short segments. Select all segments that should form one polyline and type Join. Rhino merges touching curves into a single curve. If Join fails, check that endpoints overlap exactly — use PointsOn (F10) to show control points and Move endpoints to snap them together.

When to Skip Tracing and Redraw

For dimensioned architectural plans or technical drawings where accuracy matters more than speed, redraw the geometry manually in Rhino rather than tracing. Use the scanned image as a reference underlay.

Loading a Scan as a Background Image

Type PictureFrame and select your scan. Rhino inserts the image as a plane in model space. Scale the plane to match known dimensions: measure a reference line on the scan (e.g., a 10-meter wall), measure the corresponding distance in Rhino, and use Scale to correct the plane.

Lock the picture frame layer so you don't accidentally select it. Set the layer color to gray or reduce its transparency to 50% so your drawn curves stand out.

Drawing Over the Reference

Use Polyline, InterpCrv, Arc, and Circle to trace over the image. Enable Ortho (F8) for straight lines and Snap (F9) to snap to drawn geometry. For curved walls or organic shapes, use InterpCrv with as few points as possible — you can edit control points later.

Manual redrawing is slower (expect 1–3 hours for a detailed plan) but produces dimension-accurate geometry with minimal cleanup. The result is ready for 3D modeling, section cuts, and export to fabrication without further adjustment.

Export Formats for Downstream Tools

Once traced paths are refined in Rhino, export them for use in other CAD tools or fabrication machines.

DXF for AutoCAD and CNC

Select the curves to export and type Export. Choose DXF and set the version to "2018 Lines & Arcs" or "2013 Polyface Mesh" depending on the target tool. DXF export flattens all curves to the active CPlane — if your geometry is 3D, set the CPlane to the desired view (Top, Front, Right) before exporting.

SVG for Web and Print

Rhino's native SVG export (File → Save As → SVG) works for simple line art but lacks control over stroke width, fill, and viewBox. For better results, export to AI (Illustrator format) and open it in Illustrator or Inkscape to adjust styling and re-export as SVG.

PDF for Documentation

Type Print and choose "Print to PDF." Set the page size to match your layout and adjust line weights in the print dialog. PDF export is vector-based and scales cleanly for client presentations or construction documentation.

faqs.question: Can Rhino trace scanned drawings natively?
faqs.answer: No. Rhino is a NURBS modeler and does not include raster-to-vector tracing. Trace the scan in Illustrator, Inkscape, or another tool, export as SVG or DXF, and import into Rhino. Use Rhino's curve tools (ReduceCrv, Join, CloseCrv) to refine the result.

faqs.question: What DPI should I scan architectural plans for Rhino import?
faqs.answer: Scan at 300–600 DPI in grayscale or black-and-white mode. Higher DPI does not improve tracing beyond 600 DPI. Save as TIFF or PNG (lossless). Clean the scan in GIMP or Photoshop with Levels and Unsharp Mask before tracing.

faqs.question: How do I scale imported SVG paths correctly in Rhino?
faqs.answer: After import, type SelCrv to select all curves, then BoundingBox to check dimensions. Measure a known reference (e.g., a 10-meter wall). If the bounding box shows 1000 units, the scale is 100:1. Use Scale with factor 0.01 to correct it.

faqs.question: Why do imported paths have so many control points?
faqs.answer: Traced curves follow pixel edges and produce excessive nodes. After import, select all curves and type ReduceCrv. Set tolerance to 0.01–0.1 units. Rhino removes unnecessary control points while keeping the curve within tolerance. Check the result at full zoom.

faqs.question: Should I trace a scanned plan or redraw it manually in Rhino?
faqs.answer: For dimension-critical work (architectural plans, technical drawings), redraw manually. Use PictureFrame to load the scan as a reference, scale it to known dimensions, lock the layer, and trace over it with Polyline, Arc, InterpCrv. Manual redrawing is slower but produces exact geometry.

title: CorelDRAW SVG Workflow: Export Settings That Survive
seoTitle: CorelDRAW SVG Export: Settings and Common Failures
seoDescription: CorelDRAW can export SVG well or badly. Learn which options preserve text as paths, keep units, and stop effects from flattening into images.
excerpt: CorelDRAW exports clean SVG but requires preparation: convert text to curves (Ctrl+Q), rasterize bitmap effects at 150–300 DPI, choose SVG 1.1 profile, set decimals to 2–3. Post-process with SVGO or SVGOMG to reduce file size 30–60%. Export PDF/X-4 for print, not SVG.
content:
CorelDRAW writes SVG files with cleaner geometry than most vector editors, yet the format it exports is not always web-ready. Embedded fonts break rendering in browsers, proprietary color spaces produce incorrect fills, and multi-page documents export as single massive SVG files with inline raster previews. The workflow from CorelDRAW to web, print, or fabrication tools requires understanding which export options to enable, how to simplify complex artwork, and when to clean the SVG afterward in a text editor or optimizer.

This guide walks through CorelDRAW's SVG export dialog, explains each setting and its effect on file size and compatibility, and shows how to prepare artwork before export to avoid common failures.

Why CorelDRAW SVG Export Differs

CorelDRAW's native format (CDR) is proprietary and feature-rich — it stores bitmap effects, lens effects, PowerClips, and text-on-path with fidelity no other tool matches. When you export to SVG, CorelDRAW must decide what to preserve, what to simplify, and what to rasterize. The export dialog offers three profiles: SVG (web-optimized), SVG 1.1, and SVG Tiny. Each makes different tradeoffs between fidelity and compatibility.

The SVG profile embeds non-standard attributes to preserve CorelDRAW-specific features. SVG 1.1 strips those attributes and produces standard-compliant output. SVG Tiny omits gradients, filters, and masks for mobile compatibility. For web use, choose SVG 1.1. For print workflows, export to PDF or EPS instead.

Preparing Artwork for SVG Export

Before opening the export dialog, simplify the artwork to remove effects that don't translate cleanly to SVG.

Convert Text to Curves

Select all text objects and choose Object → Convert to Curves (Ctrl+Q). This converts text to vector paths, preventing font embedding issues and ensuring the design looks identical on any system. The downside is the text becomes non-editable — save a copy of the original CDR file before converting.

For large amounts of body text (paragraphs, legal copy), leave the text as text and export to PDF with fonts embedded. SVG is not a document format; it is a graphics format.

Rasterize Bitmap Effects

Lens effects, drop shadows, transparency blends, and bitmap color adjustments do not export to SVG directly. CorelDRAW either ignores them or embeds a raster fallback. To preserve the visual appearance, rasterize effects before export.

Select the object with effects applied and choose Bitmaps → Convert to Bitmap. Set resolution to 300 DPI for print, 150 DPI for web. Choose RGB color mode for screen, CMYK for print. The object becomes a raster image embedded in the vector file. For cleaner results, redraw the effect using gradients and transparency instead of bitmap effects.

Break Apart PowerClips

PowerClips (CorelDRAW's clipping masks) export as SVG <clipPath> elements, which work correctly in most tools. However, complex nested PowerClips can produce invalid SVG. Break apart PowerClips that don't need to remain editable: select the PowerClip, choose Object → Break Apart, and manually delete the clipping frame.

CorelDRAW FeatureSVG Export BehaviorRecommended Fix
Text with custom fontsEmbedded or converted to pathsConvert to curves (Ctrl+Q) before export
Bitmap effects (lens, shadow)Ignored or rasterized inlineConvert to Bitmap at 150–300 DPI before export
PowerClips (clipping masks)Exported as <clipPath>Works in most tools; break apart if export fails
Mesh fillsRasterized as embedded PNGRedraw with gradients or export as PDF
Fountain fills (gradients)Exported as <linearGradient> or <radialGradient>Works correctly; verify colors in web browser

Using the SVG Export Dialog

With the artwork prepared, choose File → Export (Ctrl+E) and select SVG from the format list. Name the file and click Export. The SVG Export dialog opens with four sections: General, Advanced, HTML, and Maintain Layers.

General Settings

The Profile dropdown offers three options. Choose SVG 1.1 for maximum compatibility. The "SVG" option adds CorelDRAW-specific attributes that other tools ignore. "SVG Tiny" omits features most web workflows need (gradients, transparency, filters).

Set Text to "Convert text to curves" if you haven't already done so manually. If you leave text as text, enable "Embed fonts" only if the target system has the same fonts installed — embedded fonts increase file size and break rendering in some browsers.

Enable Embed bitmaps if your artwork includes placed raster images. CorelDRAW encodes them as Base64 data URIs inside the SVG. For large images, this bloats file size — consider linking images externally instead (uncheck "Embed bitmaps" and place images in the same directory).

Advanced Settings

The CSS dropdown controls how styles are written. "Inline" writes style attributes directly on each element (fill="#FF0000"). "CSS properties" writes a <style> block at the top. For web use, choose "Inline" — it produces larger files but avoids CSS specificity conflicts. For print workflows where you will edit the SVG in a text editor, choose "CSS properties" for easier bulk edits.

Set Decimal places to 2–3. Higher precision (4–6 places) increases file size with no visible improvement. Lower precision (1 place) causes rounding errors in small artwork.

Enable Responsive if the SVG will be used in a web layout where it needs to scale fluidly. This removes fixed width and height attributes and adds viewBox only. Disable it for icons or logos that should display at a fixed size.

Maintain Layers (Optional)

If your CorelDRAW file is organized into layers, enable Export layers as SVG groups to preserve that structure. Each layer becomes a <g> element with an id attribute matching the layer name. This is useful if you will edit the SVG later in Inkscape, Illustrator, or a text editor.

Post-Export Optimization

CorelDRAW SVG export produces valid but unoptimized files. Path coordinates are verbose, unused definitions remain, and inline styles repeat across every element. Two tools clean this up: SVGO (command-line) and SVGOMG (web-based GUI).

Using SVGO

Install SVGO via npm: npm install -g svgo. Run it on your exported file:

svgo input.svg -o output.svg

SVGO removes unused definitions, merges paths, rounds coordinates, and collapses redundant groups. File size typically drops 30–60% with no visual change. Add --pretty to keep the output human-readable for manual editing.

Using SVGOMG (Web GUI)

Open SVGOMG in a browser. Drag your SVG into the window. Toggle optimization passes in the left panel. Disable "Remove viewBox" if your SVG is responsive. Disable "Remove hidden elements" if your file includes layers meant to be shown/hidden via CSS. Download the optimized version when satisfied.

Fixing Common Export Failures

Three problems appear frequently: embedded fonts breaking web rendering, incorrect colors in gradients, and massive file sizes due to embedded rasters.

Font Rendering Failures

If text displays incorrectly or not at all in a browser, the font is either not embedded correctly or uses a format browsers don't support. Open the SVG in a text editor and search for <defs>. If you find <font> or <font-face> elements, delete the entire <defs> block. Convert the text to curves in CorelDRAW and re-export.

Incorrect Gradient Colors

If a gradient appears washed out or oversaturated, the color space is wrong. CorelDRAW sometimes exports CMYK gradients as RGB without conversion. Open the SVG in a text editor, search for <linearGradient> or <radialGradient>, and check the stop-color values. If they are named colors (e.g., DarkRed), replace them with hex codes (#8B0000). Re-open the original CDR file, convert all objects to RGB color mode (Edit → Find and Replace → Replace Objects → Color Model), and re-export.

Bloated File Size

If your SVG is over 5 MB, it likely has embedded raster images or mesh fills. Open the SVG in a text editor and search for data:image. Each occurrence is a Base64-encoded image. Extract these to separate files and reference them with <image href="filename.png"> instead. Alternatively, export the vector artwork only and place raster images separately in your layout tool.

Exporting Multi-Page Documents

CorelDRAW's multi-page feature does not translate to SVG. If you export a document with three pages, CorelDRAW creates a single SVG with all pages stacked vertically. Each page becomes a group offset by the page height.

For web use, export each page individually: delete all but one page, export, undo, delete a different page, export again. For print workflows, export the entire document to PDF (which supports multiple pages natively) instead of SVG.

SVG vs. EPS vs. PDF for Print

For print workflows, SVG is rarely the best choice. SVG does not support CMYK color, spot colors, overprint, or bleed. If your artwork is going to a commercial printer, export to PDF/X-4 or EPS with fonts embedded.

Use SVG for print only when the target tool cannot read PDF or EPS (rare) or when the recipient needs to edit the artwork in a vector editor. In that case, convert colors to RGB, convert text to curves, and warn the recipient that spot colors and overprint are not preserved.

Using CorelDRAW SVG in Fabrication Tools

Laser cutters, vinyl plotters, and CNC routers typically require vector paths with no fills, no strokes, or specific stroke colors to indicate cut/engrave layers. CorelDRAW exports filled shapes and stroked paths as-is, so you must prepare the artwork first.

For laser cutting, convert all shapes to hairline outlines: select all objects, remove fills (Fill Tool → No Fill), set outline width to "Hairline," and assign colors to layers (red = cut, blue = engrave). Export to SVG or DXF. For CNC, export closed paths only — open paths cannot be machined. Use Arrange → Shaping → Weld to merge overlapping shapes before export.

faqs.question: Should I convert text to curves before exporting SVG from CorelDRAW?
faqs.answer: Yes. Select all text and press Ctrl+Q to convert to curves. This prevents font embedding issues and ensures the design looks identical on any system. The downside is text becomes non-editable — save a copy of the CDR file before converting.

faqs.question: Which SVG profile should I choose in CorelDRAW export?
faqs.answer: Choose SVG 1.1 for maximum compatibility. The "SVG" option adds CorelDRAW-specific attributes that other tools ignore. "SVG Tiny" omits gradients, transparency, and filters. For web use, SVG 1.1 is the best choice.

faqs.question: Why is my exported SVG file over 10 MB?
faqs.answer: It likely has embedded raster images or mesh fills encoded as Base64 data URIs. Open the SVG in a text editor, search for data:image, and extract those to separate files. Alternatively, export vector artwork only and place rasters separately.

faqs.question: How do I reduce SVG file size after exporting from CorelDRAW?
faqs.answer: Use SVGO (command-line: svgo input.svg -o output.svg) or SVGOMG (web GUI at jakearchibald.github.io/svgomg). Both remove unused definitions, merge paths, round coordinates, and collapse groups. File size typically drops 30–60% with no visual change.

faqs.question: Can I export multi-page CorelDRAW documents to SVG?
faqs.answer: CorelDRAW exports all pages as one SVG with pages stacked vertically. For web use, export each page individually: delete all but one page, export, undo, repeat. For print workflows, export to PDF (which supports multiple pages natively) instead of SVG.

title: Canva to SVG: Why Exporting Directly Does Not Work
seoTitle: Canva to SVG: Export Options and What Each Keeps
seoDescription: Canva does not offer SVG on every plan, and its PDF export is not always vector. Compare the paths to a real SVG and what each one preserves.
excerpt: Canva SVG is hybrid vector with rasterized effects, embedded fonts, and Base64 images. Export to PDF Print, open in Illustrator/Inkscape, delete rasters, keep text and shapes. For complex designs, redraw manually using PNG as reference. Use Figma or Affinity Designer for clean vector workflow.
content:
Canva is a raster-first design tool — every element you place becomes pixels when you export. The PNG download is 72–300 DPI raster, the PDF is vector-wrapped raster, and the "SVG" option (available only on Canva Pro) produces a hybrid file with rasterized effects, embedded fonts, and proprietary markup that breaks compatibility with standard SVG tools. If you need true vector output — scalable, editable paths with no pixel fallback — the workflow requires exporting to PDF, converting in Illustrator or Inkscape, and cleaning the result.

This guide explains why Canva SVG is not actually vector, how to extract vector elements from Canva PDF exports, and when to redraw the design manually in a proper vector editor instead.

Why Canva SVG Export Is Misleading

Canva markets its SVG export as "vector format," but the output is closer to an HTML document with embedded rasters. Text remains as <text> elements with specific fonts (which break if the font is not installed), photos and uploads are embedded as Base64 PNG data, and effects like shadows, blurs, and gradients are rasterized into inline images. Only basic shapes (rectangles, circles, straight lines) remain as true vector paths.

Open a Canva SVG in a text editor and search for <image. You will find dozens of data URIs, each encoding a rasterized region at 72 DPI. This approach works for Canva's internal rendering but fails in tools that expect clean vector paths: vinyl cutters ignore rasters, laser cutters cannot engrave them, and screen printers need spot-color separations that Canva SVG cannot provide.

Exporting from Canva

Canva offers three export paths: PNG (raster, any plan), PDF (vector-wrapped raster, any plan), and SVG (hybrid, Canva Pro only). Each has different characteristics.

PNG Export (Raster Only)

Click Share → Download → PNG. Set DPI to 300 if the output will be printed, 150 for web. Canva rasterizes the entire design at the chosen resolution. The result is a flat image with no vector data. Use PNG when the final deliverable is a web graphic, social media post, or email banner. Do not use PNG if you need to scale, edit shapes, or separate colors.

PDF Export (Vector-Wrapped Raster)

Click Share → Download → PDF Print. Canva writes a PDF with vector text and rasterized everything else. Photos, effects, and complex shapes become 300 DPI embedded images. The PDF opens in Illustrator or Inkscape, but when you select an object, you find it is a raster image clipped to a vector bounding box, not an editable path.

This format works for print shops that need CMYK output and bleed settings. It does not work for laser cutting, vinyl plotting, or any workflow that requires true vector paths.

SVG Export (Hybrid, Canva Pro Only)

Canva Pro users see an SVG option in the download menu. The file it produces is valid SVG but not editable vector. Text uses embedded fonts (which break in browsers if the font is unavailable), gradients are rasterized, and shadows become inline Base64 images.

This format is acceptable for web embedding when you do not need to edit the content. It is not suitable for fabrication, print production, or workflows where you need to recolor or modify shapes.

Export FormatVector TextVector ShapesEditable in IllustratorWorks in Vinyl Cutters
PNGNoNoNoNo (raster only)
PDF PrintYesNo (rasterized)Limited (text only)No (requires vector paths)
SVG (Pro only)Yes (with fonts)Partial (basic shapes)Limited (cleanup needed)Partial (shapes only)

Extracting Vector Elements from Canva PDF

If you have Canva Pro and need true vector output, the cleanest workflow is: export to PDF Print, open in Illustrator or Inkscape, select and delete rasterized regions, and manually redraw complex shapes using the PDF as a reference.

Opening Canva PDF in Illustrator

Open the PDF in Illustrator (File → Open). Illustrator imports the PDF as a multi-layered document with text, raster images, and clipping masks. The artboard size matches the Canva design dimensions.

Unlock all layers (Object → Unlock All) and ungroup everything (Object → Ungroup, repeat until nothing ungroups). Select a shape. If it is raster, you will see a pixelated bounding box when you zoom in. Delete it. If it is vector, the outline remains crisp at any zoom level — keep it.

Text remains editable but references the original font. If you don't have the font installed, Illustrator substitutes a default. Convert text to outlines (Type → Create Outlines) to preserve the exact appearance.

Opening Canva PDF in Inkscape

Open the PDF in Inkscape (File → Open → PDF Import Settings). Choose "Internal import" and select the page to import. Inkscape places all elements on the canvas.

Select all (Edit → Select All) and ungroup (Object → Ungroup, repeat). Click individual objects to identify rasters. If the status bar shows "Image," the object is raster — delete it. If it shows "Path" or "Text," it is vector — keep it.

Convert text to paths (Path → Object to Path) to avoid font substitution issues.

Manual Redraw Workflow

For designs with many effects, gradients, or complex shapes, extracting vector from Canva PDF is impractical. The faster approach is to redraw the design manually in Illustrator or Inkscape using the Canva PNG export as a reference underlay.

Loading the Reference Image

Export the design from Canva as PNG at 300 DPI. Open Illustrator or Inkscape and create a new document matching the design dimensions. Import the PNG (File → Place in Illustrator, File → Import in Inkscape) and lock the layer so you don't accidentally select it.

Reduce the image opacity to 40–50% so drawn shapes stand out. If the design has multiple pages, export each page as a separate PNG and redraw them in separate artboards or layers.

Tracing Shapes

Use the Pen tool (P) to trace over shapes. Draw one closed path per region. For circles and rectangles, use the Ellipse (L) and Rectangle (M) tools rather than tracing freehand. For text, retype it with the Text tool (T) using the closest available font, then adjust size and tracking to match.

For complex organic shapes, use the Pencil tool (N in Illustrator) or Bezier tool (B in Inkscape) with smoothing enabled. Draw with as few anchor points as possible — you can add nodes later if needed.

Matching Colors

Sample colors from the reference PNG using the Eyedropper tool (I). For precise matching, note the hex codes in Canva before exporting and type them into the Fill color panel in your vector editor. If the design uses gradients, recreate them manually with the Gradient tool (G).

Alternative: Recreate in Figma or Affinity Designer

If the Canva design is simple (logo, icon, flat illustration), consider recreating it in Figma or Affinity Designer rather than extracting from Canva. Both tools export clean SVG by default, with no rasterized fallbacks or embedded fonts.

Figma Export

Recreate the design in Figma using vector shapes and text. Select the entire frame and choose Export → SVG. Figma produces standard-compliant SVG with no embedded rasters. Convert text to outlines before export if the design uses custom fonts (Flatten Selection in Figma).

Affinity Designer Export

Affinity Designer reads Canva PDF imports better than Illustrator or Inkscape — it preserves more vector data and separates rasters more cleanly. Open the Canva PDF in Affinity Designer, delete rasterized regions, and export as SVG (File → Export → SVG). Set "Flatten transforms" and "Convert text to curves" for maximum compatibility.

When to Use Image Tracing

If the Canva design is a logo or simple flat illustration with hard edges, use auto-tracing instead of manual redraw. Export the design as PNG at 300 DPI and trace it in Illustrator or Inkscape.

Tracing in Illustrator

Import the PNG into Illustrator. Select it and open Object → Image Trace → Make. Choose the "High Fidelity Photo" preset for complex artwork or "3 Colors" for simple logos. Expand the result (Object → Expand) and clean up stray paths with the Direct Selection tool (A).

Tracing in Inkscape

Import the PNG into Inkscape. Select it and open Path → Trace Bitmap. Choose "Brightness cutoff" for line art or "Colors" for multi-color logos. Set the number of scans equal to the number of distinct colors. Click OK, delete the original PNG, and simplify paths (Path → Simplify, Ctrl+L).

Canva Alternatives for Vector Work

If you regularly need vector output, switch to a tool designed for vector editing. Illustrator and Affinity Designer are professional-grade. Inkscape and Figma are free alternatives with nearly the same feature set.

Canva is optimized for speed and ease of use, not precision or editability. It excels at social media graphics, presentations, and quick mockups. For logos, print production, and fabrication, use a dedicated vector editor from the start rather than trying to extract vectors from Canva output.

faqs.question: Is Canva SVG export true vector?
faqs.answer: No. Canva SVG is hybrid: text uses embedded fonts, photos and effects are rasterized as Base64 images, only basic shapes (rectangles, circles, lines) remain vector. Open a Canva SVG in a text editor and search for <image to see rasterized regions.

faqs.question: How do I get clean vector output from Canva?
faqs.answer: Export to PDF Print, open in Illustrator or Inkscape, unlock and ungroup all layers, delete rasterized regions (check if objects are images or paths), keep vector text and shapes. Convert text to outlines to avoid font substitution.

faqs.question: Can I use Canva designs for laser cutting or vinyl plotting?
faqs.answer: Not directly. Canva exports rasterize effects and shapes, which vinyl cutters and laser cutters cannot process. Export to PDF, open in Illustrator, delete rasters, redraw shapes as vector paths, set strokes to hairline, and export as SVG or DXF.

faqs.question: Should I redraw a Canva design manually or extract vector from PDF?
faqs.answer: For simple logos and flat illustrations, extract vector from PDF. For designs with many effects, gradients, or photos, redraw manually: export as PNG at 300 DPI, place as reference in Illustrator/Inkscape, reduce opacity to 40%, trace over with Pen and shape tools.

faqs.question: What Canva alternatives produce clean SVG?
faqs.answer: Figma (free, web-based) and Affinity Designer (paid, desktop) export standard-compliant SVG with no rasterized fallbacks. Inkscape is free and open-source. Illustrator is industry-standard but subscription-based. All produce cleaner vector output than Canva.

title: Figma to SVG: Export Settings and What Gets Flattened
seoTitle: Figma SVG Export: Settings, Outlines and Flattening
seoDescription: Figma exports SVG cleanly until effects, images or masks get involved. Learn the settings that keep artwork vector and what cannot survive.
excerpt: Figma exports clean, standard-compliant SVG with no embedded rasters or metadata. Enable 'Outline strokes' for fabrication, flatten selection for final assets, outline text for consistent rendering. Use SVGO/SVGOMG to optimize further. For print, export PDF instead of SVG.
content:
Figma exports SVG more cleanly than any other design tool — no embedded rasters, no proprietary markup, and minimal path bloat. Yet the way Figma organizes layers, applies constraints, and handles text can produce SVG files that are awkward to edit in other tools or that break when embedded in web pages. The difference between a Figma SVG that works everywhere and one that fails in production is understanding what "Flatten Selection" does, when to outline strokes, and how to structure frames before export.

This guide explains Figma's SVG export pipeline, shows which settings to enable for web versus fabrication workflows, and demonstrates how to prepare designs to avoid common failures.

How Figma SVG Export Works

When you export a frame or selection to SVG, Figma converts every vector node, text span, and effect into standard SVG elements. Rectangles become <rect>, circles become <circle>, arbitrary shapes become <path>, and text becomes <text> with font attributes. Strokes are preserved as stroke attributes, not separate paths. Masks become <clipPath> or <mask> elements. Effects (shadows, blurs) become <filter> elements.

This direct mapping produces compact, standard-compliant SVG. The file size is typically 40–70% smaller than an equivalent export from Illustrator or Sketch because Figma does not embed previews, multiple resolution variants, or editor metadata.

The Export Panel

Select a frame, group, or individual layer and open the Export panel (lower-right, or right-click → Export). Click the + button and choose SVG from the format dropdown. Figma shows two settings beneath the format: Outline strokes and Include 'id' attribute.

Enable "Outline strokes" if the target tool does not support stroke attributes (laser cutters, vinyl plotters, some web renderers). This converts strokes into filled paths. Disable it if you need to edit stroke widths later in Illustrator or Inkscape.

Enable "Include 'id' attribute" if you will manipulate the SVG with JavaScript or CSS. Figma generates IDs from layer names ("Rectangle 5" becomes id="Rectangle_5"). Disable it to reduce file size when IDs are not needed.

Use CaseOutline StrokesInclude 'id' AttributeAdditional Steps
Web icon (static)NoNoNone
Web icon (animated)NoYesName layers descriptively before export
Print logoYesNoFlatten selection, outline text
Laser cuttingYesNoRemove fills, set strokes to hairline
Editable in IllustratorNoYesKeep layer structure intact

Flatten Selection vs. Export As-Is

Before exporting, decide whether to flatten the selection. Flattening merges overlapping shapes, resolves boolean operations, and converts effects into static paths. It produces simpler SVG but removes editability.

When to Flatten

Flatten when the SVG will be used as a final asset with no further editing: web icons, print logos, app resources, or fabrication files. Select the frame or group and choose Object → Flatten Selection (Ctrl+E on Windows, Cmd+E on Mac). Figma merges all layers into a single flattened group.

Export the flattened group. The resulting SVG has fewer elements, no nested groups, and no boolean operations — just paths. This format is more compatible with edge-case renderers (Android VectorDrawable, older browsers, some laser cutter software).

When to Keep Layer Structure

Keep layers when you or someone else will edit the SVG in Illustrator, Inkscape, or Figma again. Export the frame without flattening. The SVG preserves groups, named layers, and mask relationships. Strokes remain as stroke attributes, not expanded paths. Boolean operations (unions, subtracts) remain as separate overlapping paths — the target editor must resolve them.

Handling Text in SVG Export

Figma exports text as <text> elements with font-family, font-size, and other attributes. This works in browsers if the font is web-available (Google Fonts, system fonts). It fails in tools that don't load fonts (Android Studio, Inkscape on headless servers, some fabrication software).

Outlining Text (Convert to Vector)

To ensure text renders identically everywhere, convert it to vector paths before export. Select the text layer and choose Object → Flatten Selection, or right-click → Outline Stroke (this works on text too). Figma converts the text into path geometry. The downside is the text becomes non-editable — you cannot change the wording or font after conversion.

For body text or text that will be translated, keep it as <text>. For logos, headings, and decorative text, outline it.

Font Subsetting and Embedding

Figma does not embed fonts in SVG exports. If the font is not available on the target system or in the browser's font stack, the text displays in a fallback font (usually Arial or sans-serif). To prevent this, either outline the text before export or host the font as a web font and reference it in CSS.

Exporting Multiple Artboards or Frames

Figma does not batch-export multiple frames into a single SVG. Each frame exports as a separate file. To export many frames at once, select all frames in the layers panel (Shift+click), add SVG to the export settings (one setting applies to all selected frames), and click Export. Figma generates one SVG per frame and downloads them in a ZIP archive.

If you need all frames in one SVG (rare, typically for sprite sheets), manually copy-paste frames into a single master frame before export. Use a plugin like "Combine Artboards" or script it via the Figma API.

Optimizing Figma SVG for Web

Figma SVG is already lean, but two tools make it leaner: SVGO (command-line) and SVGOMG (web GUI).

Using SVGO

Install SVGO via npm: npm install -g svgo. Run it on your exported file:

svgo input.svg -o output.svg

SVGO removes unused definitions, merges paths, rounds coordinates, and collapses redundant groups. For Figma exports, the size reduction is typically 10–30% (smaller than the 40–60% reduction on Illustrator exports, because Figma already produces clean SVG).

Using SVGOMG (Web GUI)

Open SVGOMG in a browser. Drag your SVG into the window. Toggle optimization passes in the left panel. Disable "Remove viewBox" if your SVG is responsive. Disable "Remove hidden elements" if your file includes layers meant to be shown/hidden via CSS. Download the optimized version when satisfied.

Preparing Figma Designs for Fabrication

Laser cutters, vinyl plotters, and CNC routers require vector paths with specific stroke or fill configurations. Figma's default export produces filled shapes and stroked paths, which fabrication software may interpret incorrectly.

Laser Cutting Workflow

For laser cutting, convert all shapes to hairline outlines with no fills. In Figma, select all objects in the frame, set fill to "None," and set stroke to 0.01px (the smallest allowed). Assign different stroke colors to different layers: red for cut, blue for engrave, green for marking (standard conventions vary by shop).

Enable "Outline strokes" in the export settings. This converts the strokes into filled paths that laser cutters can interpret. Export as SVG or DXF (use a plugin like "DXF Export" for native DXF output).

Vinyl Plotting Workflow

Vinyl plotters need closed paths with no strokes. Select all shapes, set stroke to "None," and ensure all paths are closed (no open endpoints). Export with "Outline strokes" disabled. Open the SVG in Inkscape or Illustrator to verify paths are closed (Path → Close Path if needed).

Figma SVG vs. Illustrator SVG

Figma SVG is cleaner, smaller, and more standards-compliant than Illustrator SVG. Illustrator embeds editor metadata, preview images, and multiple coordinate systems that bloat file size. Figma strips all metadata and writes minimal markup.

The tradeoff is that Illustrator SVG preserves more editability — layers, adjustment layers, and appearance attributes remain when you re-open the file in Illustrator. Figma SVG is optimized for final output, not round-tripping back to the editor.

For web use, Figma is superior. For print workflows where you will re-edit the file in Illustrator, export from Figma to PDF (which Illustrator opens cleanly) rather than SVG.

Common Figma SVG Failures and Fixes

Three problems appear frequently: missing text (font not available), clipping masks not working, and bloated file sizes due to unnecessary complexity.

Missing or Wrong Fonts

If text displays in the wrong font, outline it before export: select the text layer, choose Object → Flatten Selection. The text becomes vector paths. For editable text, host the font as a web font and reference it in your page's CSS.

Clipping Masks Not Working

If a clipping mask fails in a browser or Illustrator, the mask geometry may be invalid. In Figma, masks must be closed paths. Check that the mask layer is a closed shape (no open endpoints). If the mask is a group, flatten it before export.

Bloated File Size

If your SVG is over 1 MB, the design is too complex. Simplify it: merge overlapping shapes (Union boolean operation), delete hidden layers, and reduce the number of nodes in curves (use the Simplify plugin or redraw curves with fewer points). Flatten the selection before export.

faqs.question: Should I enable 'Outline strokes' when exporting SVG from Figma?
faqs.answer: Enable it for laser cutting, vinyl plotting, or tools that don't support stroke attributes. This converts strokes into filled paths. Disable it if you need to edit stroke widths later in Illustrator or Inkscape. For web icons, leave it disabled to keep file size small.

faqs.question: How do I prevent Figma text from displaying in the wrong font?
faqs.answer: Outline the text before export: select the text layer, choose Object → Flatten Selection (Ctrl+E / Cmd+E). The text becomes vector paths and renders identically everywhere. The downside is text becomes non-editable. For editable text, host the font as a web font.

faqs.question: What does 'Flatten Selection' do in Figma before SVG export?
faqs.answer: Flatten merges overlapping shapes, resolves boolean operations, and converts effects into static paths. It produces simpler, more compatible SVG but removes editability. Flatten when the SVG is a final asset (web icon, print logo, fabrication file). Keep layers for files you'll edit again.

faqs.question: Can I export multiple Figma frames as one SVG file?
faqs.answer: Figma exports each frame as a separate SVG. To combine frames, copy-paste them into a single master frame before export, or use a plugin like 'Combine Artboards.' For sprite sheets, manually arrange frames in one frame and export that.

faqs.question: Is Figma SVG smaller than Illustrator SVG?
faqs.answer: Yes. Figma SVG is 40–70% smaller than Illustrator SVG for the same design because Figma does not embed editor metadata, previews, or multiple coordinate systems. Illustrator SVG preserves more editability; Figma SVG is optimized for final output and web use.

title: Bulk Vectorizing Customer Artwork: A Process for Shops
seoTitle: Bulk Vectorizing Customer Artwork: Shop Workflow and QA
seoDescription: When customers send a pile of screenshots and JPGs, consistency beats craft. Build a batch process with intake rules and a pass/fail check.
excerpt: Bulk vectorization needs triage (easy/medium/hard/impossible), batch processing with consistent settings, a QA gate with pass/fail criteria, and a rework loop. Systematize or waste time on files that fail late.
content:
Bulk vectorization workflows turn dozens or hundreds of customer-supplied raster images (logos, drawings, clipart) into production-ready vector files. The challenge is consistency: each source file has different resolution, background, and complexity, and each output file must meet the same quality standard for downstream use (printing, cutting, embroidery). A systematic workflow with triage, batch processing, QA gates, and rework loops prevents bottlenecks and ensures no low-quality file reaches production.

Ad-hoc vectorization—opening each file one at a time, tracing it by hand, and hoping for the best—does not scale. You need rules: which files can be auto-traced, which need manual cleanup, what simplification settings to use, and how to check output before it moves to the next stage. For shops handling 50+ customer files per week, a repeatable process saves hours and reduces rework.

Intake and Triage by Difficulty

Not all raster images vectorize equally. A clean, high-contrast logo on a white background auto-traces cleanly in seconds. A low-res JPG with JPEG artifacts, gradients, and no clear edges requires manual tracing or redrawing. Triage separates files into categories—easy (auto-trace), medium (auto-trace + cleanup), hard (manual trace), and impossible (contact customer for better source)—before batch processing begins.

Easy files: high resolution (300+ DPI at final size), solid colors, clean edges, white or transparent background, no gradients or photos. These go straight to batch auto-tracing with minimal supervision. Examples: vector logos exported as PNG, scanned ink drawings, simple clipart.

Medium files: moderate resolution (150–300 DPI), some noise or JPEG artifacts, soft edges, or busy backgrounds that need removal. These auto-trace, but the output needs manual cleanup—deleting stray nodes, simplifying paths, fixing gaps. Examples: low-res logos, photos of drawings on textured paper, clipart with compression artifacts.

Hard files: low resolution (under 150 DPI at final size), complex details, gradients, or photos. Auto-tracing produces poor results (thousands of nodes, jagged edges, no recognizable shapes). These require manual tracing with the Pen tool, or redrawing from scratch. Examples: blurry phone photos of hand-drawn sketches, heavily compressed social media profile pictures, images upscaled from thumbnails.

Impossible files: resolution is so low or quality so poor that even manual tracing cannot produce usable output. Contact the customer and request a higher-resolution source, or offer to redraw the artwork for a fee. Examples: 50×50 pixel favicon, screenshot of a screenshot, image saved and re-saved as JPG ten times.

StageAutomation LevelHuman CheckPurpose
Intake & triageLow—visual inspection by operatorEvery file—sort into easy/medium/hard/impossiblePrevents wasting time auto-tracing files that will fail
Batch auto-traceHigh—run all easy files through vectorization toolSpot check 10% of outputs for node count, gaps, stray pathsHandles bulk of simple files with minimal labor
Manual cleanupMedium—use software tools (simplify, smooth, delete stray nodes)Every medium file—verify output matches sourceFixes auto-trace artifacts without full redraw
QA gateNone—human review every output100% inspection before releasing to productionCatches errors before they reach printing, cutting, or embroidery
Rework loopLow—return failed files to cleanup or triageRe-check after fixesEnsures rework meets standard before final release

Batch Vectorization Settings

Consistency is key. Use the same vectorization settings for all easy files in a batch, so outputs have uniform node counts, path simplification, and color handling. If you change settings per file, QA becomes harder—you cannot compare outputs to a known baseline.

Common settings: color mode (full color, limited palette, or black and white), noise reduction (threshold for ignoring small specks), path simplification (how aggressively to reduce nodes), and corner detection (whether to preserve sharp angles or smooth them). For most logo vectorization, use limited palette (6–12 colors), moderate noise reduction (ignore specks under 5 pixels), high simplification (reduce nodes by 50–70%), and preserve corners.

For tools like PNG to SVG conversion or logo vectorization, adjust threshold and simplification until the output matches the source visually without excessive node count. A good vectorized logo has 100–500 nodes for simple shapes, 500–2000 for complex artwork. If a simple logo produces 5,000+ nodes, simplification is too low—increase it.

Export format: SVG for web use and cutting machines, EPS or AI for print shops, DXF for CNC and laser cutters (covered in SVG to DXF conversion). For batch processing, export all files to the same format first, then convert to other formats as needed for specific jobs.

Naming Convention

Use a consistent file naming scheme so you can trace outputs back to source files and customer orders. Example: CustomerName_OrderID_FileName_v1.svg. If rework is needed, increment the version number (_v2.svg, _v3.svg). Avoid spaces and special characters in filenames—some software and web servers choke on them.

For large batches, include a date stamp or batch ID in the filename or folder name (2026-11-06_Batch23/). This makes it easier to track which files were processed when, and to re-run a batch if settings need adjustment.

QA Gate: Pass/Fail Criteria

Every vectorized file must pass QA before moving to production. Define objective pass/fail criteria so different operators make consistent decisions. Subjective judgments ("looks good enough") lead to inconsistent quality.

Pass criteria: (1) output matches source visually (same colors, same shapes, no missing details); (2) node count is reasonable (under 2,000 for simple logos, under 5,000 for complex artwork); (3) no stray paths or disconnected fragments outside the design; (4) no gaps in closed shapes (a circle should be one closed path, not an arc with endpoints); (5) colors are solid fills or gradients, not raster textures embedded in vector shells.

Fail criteria: (1) jagged edges or stair-stepping on curves; (2) missing details (text illegible, fine lines disappeared); (3) excessive nodes (5,000+ for a simple logo); (4) colors shifted significantly from source; (5) file too large (over 5 MB for a logo suggests embedded raster data or too many nodes). Failed files return to cleanup or triage for rework.

Spot-check tools: zoom to 400% and inspect curves for smoothness. Check node count (most vector software displays this in the status bar or Document Info panel). Overlay the vector output on the source raster image at 50% opacity to verify alignment and detail accuracy.

Rework Loop and Escalation

Files that fail QA enter a rework loop. Minor issues (stray nodes, small gaps) go back to cleanup with specific notes ("delete nodes in lower-right corner," "close path on letter O"). Major issues (output does not resemble source, wrong colors) go back to triage—maybe the file was miscategorized as easy when it should have been manual trace.

Track rework rate: if more than 20% of auto-traced files fail QA, your triage or settings are wrong. Either tighten triage criteria (move more files to medium/hard), or adjust batch settings (lower noise threshold, increase simplification). If rework rate stays low (under 10%), the process is working.

Escalate impossible files to the customer immediately. Do not waste time trying to vectorize a 72 DPI phone photo when the customer has a high-res original on their computer. Send a polite message: "The file you provided is too low resolution for vectorization. Can you send the original logo file (AI, EPS, PDF, or high-res PNG)?" Most customers have better files; they just did not know which one to send.

Automation Tools and Scripts

For shops processing hundreds of files, automation reduces manual labor. Use command-line tools (Potrace, AutoTrace, ImageMagick) or scripting (Python with PIL, Node.js with sharp) to batch-process files overnight. The operator triages files in the morning, runs the batch script, then QA checks outputs in the afternoon.

Example workflow: customer uploads a ZIP of 100 logos. Operator downloads ZIP, extracts files, visually sorts them into /easy, /medium, /hard folders. A script runs Potrace on all files in /easy with preset settings, outputs SVGs to /output. Operator spot-checks 10 outputs, finds they pass QA, releases the batch. Medium files get auto-traced with different settings, then manually cleaned. Hard files go to a specialist for manual tracing.

For online workflows, some SaaS tools (Vector Magic, Vectorizer.ai, Vectorr) offer API access for batch uploads and downloads. The shop uploads files via API, the service processes them, and the shop downloads results. This offloads compute load but costs per file (typically $0.50–$2.00 per image). For high-volume shops, self-hosted tools are cheaper long-term.

Customer Communication and Expectations

Set clear expectations during intake. If the customer uploads a 72 DPI JPG, warn them before processing: "This file may not vectorize cleanly due to low resolution. We recommend providing a higher-res source, or we can manually redraw the artwork for an additional $X." This prevents disputes after delivery when the customer complains the output does not look perfect.

Offer tiered pricing: automatic vectorization (cheap, fast, works for clean files only), cleanup included (moderate price, handles most files), and manual redraw (expensive, slow, but perfect for any artwork). Most customers choose the middle tier—they want quality but do not want to pay for full custom illustration.

faqs.question: What is the difference between auto-trace and manual trace?
faqs.answer: Auto-trace uses software algorithms to convert raster pixels into vector paths. It is fast and works well for clean, high-contrast images, but produces poor results on low-res or complex artwork. Manual trace uses the Pen tool to draw paths by hand, which is slow but gives perfect control. Use auto-trace for easy files, manual trace for hard files.

faqs.question: How do I know if a file is too low resolution to vectorize?
faqs.answer: Divide pixel dimensions by final print size. If the result is under 150 DPI, the file is likely too low. Example: a 600×600 pixel image printed at 6×6 inches is only 100 DPI. Auto-tracing will produce jagged edges and excessive nodes. Request a higher-res source from the customer, or offer to redraw the artwork.

faqs.question: What node count is too high for a vectorized logo?
faqs.answer: Simple logos should have under 500 nodes; complex artwork under 2,000; very detailed illustrations under 5,000. If a simple logo has 10,000+ nodes, simplification is too low or the source file has noise/artifacts. Increase path simplification, or manually trace instead of auto-tracing.

faqs.question: How can I batch-process files faster?
faqs.answer: Triage first—do not waste time auto-tracing files that will fail. Use command-line tools (Potrace, AutoTrace) or scripts (Python, Node.js) to run batch conversions overnight. Spot-check 10% of outputs during QA instead of inspecting every file individually. Failed files return to rework; passed files release immediately.

faqs.question: What should I do when a customer sends an unusable file?
faqs.answer: Contact them immediately and request a better source: original logo file (AI, EPS, PDF, SVG), high-res PNG or JPG (300 DPI at final size), or a photo taken in good lighting against a plain background. Most customers have better files but did not know which one to send. Do not spend hours trying to fix a 72 DPI phone screenshot.

title: What Print Shops Should Ask Customers for, and Why
seoTitle: Print Shop Artwork Intake: The Questions That Prevent Reworks
seoDescription: Most reprints start with a missing answer at intake. Use a short form that captures the constraints each job type actually depends on.
excerpt: Intake forms that capture final size, substrate, process, color expectations, text changes, brand assets, and deadlines prevent rework. Missing context forces shops to guess, and guesses cause reprints and delays.
content:
Intake forms that capture final reproduction size, substrate details, print process, color expectations, text changes, brand assets, and delivery deadlines prevent 80% of rework. When customers submit artwork without this context, print shops make assumptions—wrong assumptions lead to reprints, delays, and disputes. A structured intake form forces customers to answer the questions that matter before files enter production, reducing back-and-forth and ensuring the first proof matches expectations.

Most print shops ask the same core questions, but many do so informally (email threads, phone calls, vague order notes). A formal intake form—web form, PDF checklist, or order management system—makes answers visible to everyone on the production team and creates a record for quality control and dispute resolution.

Final Reproduction Size

Customers often submit files at the wrong size. They send a 2×2 inch logo and expect it printed at 12×12 inches, or they send an 8×11 inch flyer and expect it scaled down to a business card. Without knowing the final reproduction size, the shop cannot check resolution, set up the press, or quote accurately.

Ask: "What is the final printed size? (width × height in inches or cm)." If the customer is unsure, ask for the intended use: "Will this be a T-shirt chest print (10–12 inches wide), a business card (3.5×2 inches), a large banner (4×8 feet)?" Provide examples with common sizes so the customer can pick the closest match.

For apparel, ask garment size and print placement. A full-chest print on an adult large T-shirt is typically 12–14 inches wide, but a youth small only accommodates 8–10 inches. Placement matters too: center chest, left chest (pocket print), full back, sleeve. A design sized for center chest will not fit on a sleeve without scaling down, which may make text illegible.

For signage and large-format, ask viewing distance. A banner hung 20 feet high can use 150 DPI resolution and 2-inch text; a poster viewed at arm's length needs 300 DPI and 0.5-inch text. Knowing viewing distance lets the shop validate resolution and recommend text size adjustments if needed.

QuestionWhy It MattersFailure If Missing
Final reproduction size (width × height)Determines resolution requirements, press setup, material cost, and whether design fits substrateFile printed at wrong size, requiring reprint; or resolution too low, causing pixelation
Substrate/garment colorAffects ink choices (white underbase for dark fabrics), color matching (RGB/CMYK), and whether design will be visibleDesign is invisible (white ink on white shirt), colors are dull (no underbase on dark fabric), or ink does not adhere
Print process (screen, DTF, sublimation, offset, etc.)Each process has different file requirements (spot colors, transparency, CMYK vs RGB, resolution)File is incompatible with process, requiring separation, color conversion, or manual cleanup before printing
Color expectations (exact Pantone, close match, or flexible)Determines whether spot colors are needed, whether a proof is required, and what color space to useCustomer rejects print because colors do not match brand guidelines or proof
Text or content changesText edits require access to live text (outlined text cannot be edited); knowing changes up front prevents file reworkText is already outlined in customer file, making edits impossible without redrawing; or edits happen after proofing, delaying production
Brand assets (logo files, fonts, color codes)Ensures design uses correct logo version, approved fonts, and brand colors; prevents using low-res logos pulled from websiteShop uses wrong logo or guesses brand colors, customer rejects proof
Deadline and turnaround expectationDetermines production priority, whether rush fees apply, and whether proofs can be sent for approval before printingCustomer expects 24-hour turnaround when shop schedules 5-day standard; or rush order disrupts production queue without premium pricing

Substrate and Garment Details

Print processes are substrate-dependent. Sublimation only works on polyester; DTF works on cotton and blends; screen printing works on any fabric but requires different inks for light vs dark garments. If the customer does not specify substrate, the shop guesses, and the guess is often wrong.

Ask: "What are you printing on? (garment color, fabric content, product type)." For apparel, include a dropdown with common options: white cotton, black cotton, heather gray 50/50 blend, navy 100% polyester, etc. For hard goods, list options: ceramic mug, stainless steel tumbler, acrylic sign, glossy paper, etc.

Fabric content affects process selection. A customer orders 100% cotton shirts and submits a design expecting sublimation—sublimation does not work on cotton. The shop must contact the customer, explain the issue, and recommend DTF or screen printing instead. If the intake form had asked fabric content up front, this would have been caught before artwork submission.

Garment color affects white underbase requirements. For DTF or screen printing on dark fabrics, the shop must print a white underbase first, then layer colors on top. If the customer submits a file with no transparency and expects it printed on black fabric, the shop must clean up the file to add transparency (covered in DTF white underbase issues). Knowing garment color up front lets the shop request transparent PNGs during file submission, not after review.

Print Process Selection

Many customers do not know the difference between screen printing, DTF, sublimation, offset, and UV DTF. They submit artwork and expect the shop to pick the right process. The shop can do this, but it requires asking substrate, quantity, and turnaround first—if those details are missing, the shop cannot recommend a process.

Ask: "How many pieces are you printing?" Small runs (1–50) usually go to DTF or direct-to-garment. Medium runs (50–500) often use DTF or screen printing. Large runs (500+) use screen printing for apparel, offset for paper goods. If quantity is missing, the shop cannot quote accurately—setup costs for screen printing are high but per-unit costs are low, so pricing changes dramatically between 10 units and 1,000 units.

Ask: "What print process do you prefer, or would you like a recommendation?" If the customer has no preference, the shop chooses based on substrate, quantity, and turnaround. If the customer specifies a process (e.g., "I want sublimation"), the shop can immediately flag incompatibilities ("sublimation only works on polyester; your garments are cotton, so we recommend DTF instead").

For process comparisons, see sublimation, DTF, and UV DTF. For screen print file requirements, see color separation workflows.

Color Expectations and Matching

Color disputes are common. The customer submits an RGB file, the shop prints it in CMYK, and the customer complains the colors are wrong. Or the customer expects an exact Pantone match but did not specify a Pantone code, so the shop guesses. Clear color expectations during intake prevent these issues.

Ask: "Do you need exact color matching (Pantone), close match, or are you flexible?" If exact match, ask for Pantone codes or brand color specifications (PMS 186, HEX #FF5733, CMYK 0/100/100/0). If close match, clarify tolerance ("colors should be recognizably red, but exact shade does not matter"). If flexible, the shop has freedom to adjust colors for printability.

Ask: "Do you have brand guidelines or a style guide?" Many businesses have PDF brand guides that specify logo colors, fonts, and usage rules. If the customer provides this up front, the shop can match colors exactly and use approved logo files, preventing rework when the customer rejects a proof because "that is not our red."

For RGB vs CMYK issues, explain during intake: "Offset and commercial digital printing use CMYK inks. If your design has bright RGB colors (neon blues, oranges, greens), they may shift during CMYK conversion. We can provide a proof before printing if color accuracy is critical." This sets expectations and gives the customer a chance to request a proof.

Text and Content Changes

Customers often submit final artwork, then request text changes after the shop has outlined fonts or started production. If the shop knows changes are coming during intake, they can request editable source files (AI, INDD, PSD with live text layers) instead of flattened PDFs or rasterized PNGs.

Ask: "Will there be any text or content changes? (names, dates, phone numbers, etc.)" If yes, ask for a list of changes or a note that "text will be provided later." Request source files with live text, or offer to make edits for a fee if only flattened files are available.

For variable data (e.g., 100 shirts with different names on each), ask for a CSV or spreadsheet during intake. If the customer submits one design and then emails a list of 100 names two days later, production is delayed while the shop sets up variable data printing. Knowing this requirement up front allows scheduling and proper file setup.

Brand Assets and Logo Files

Customers frequently submit low-res logos pulled from their website (72 DPI favicon, screenshot of their social media profile picture) and expect high-quality prints. The shop either has to contact the customer for a better file, or vectorize the logo (covered in bulk vectorization workflows), which adds time and cost.

Ask: "Do you have a high-res logo file? (AI, EPS, PDF, SVG, or PNG at 300 DPI)." If no, ask: "Can you request the logo from your designer or marketing team?" Most businesses have vector logos somewhere; they just do not know where. If the customer truly has no high-res logo, offer vectorization as a service.

Ask: "What fonts are used in your design?" If the design contains live text, the shop needs the fonts installed to edit or proof the file. If fonts are not provided, the shop must either outline the text (making edits impossible) or substitute a similar font (which may not match exactly). Request font files during intake, or ask the customer to outline text before submission if no edits are expected.

Deadline and Turnaround Expectations

Customers assume fast turnaround without asking. They submit an order on Monday and expect it shipped by Wednesday, when standard turnaround is 7–10 business days. Clear deadline expectations during intake prevent disputes and allow the shop to charge appropriately for rush orders.

Ask: "When do you need this? (date, or standard/rush turnaround)." Provide standard turnaround times in the intake form: "Standard: 7–10 business days. Rush: 3–5 business days (+30% fee). Same-day: available for orders under 10 units (+100% fee)." If the customer needs rush, the shop can prioritize production and charge accordingly.

Ask: "Do you need a proof before production?" If yes, add proof review time to the schedule (1–2 business days for digital proof, 3–5 days for physical sample). If no, the shop can proceed directly to production after file check, saving time but increasing risk of customer rejection after printing.

Sample Intake Form Checklist

Here is a complete intake checklist for apparel printing. Adapt it for other print processes (signage, packaging, promotional products) by swapping substrate/garment fields with product-specific questions.

  • Contact Information: Name, email, phone
  • Order Details: Quantity, garment sizes (S/M/L/XL breakdown), garment color(s), fabric content (cotton, polyester, blend)
  • Design Specifications: Final print size (width × height), print placement (center chest, full back, left chest, sleeve), number of colors in design
  • File Information: File format (PNG, PDF, AI, etc.), resolution (DPI), color space (RGB, CMYK, spot colors), transparency (yes/no for DTF)
  • Print Process: Preferred process (screen print, DTF, sublimation, or "recommend one"), or auto-select based on quantity and substrate
  • Color Matching: Exact Pantone match required (list codes), close match acceptable, or flexible
  • Text/Content Changes: No changes expected, minor edits needed (list them), or variable data (attach CSV)
  • Brand Assets: High-res logo provided (yes/no), fonts provided or outlined (yes/no), brand guidelines attached (yes/no)
  • Deadline: Needed by (date), or turnaround (standard/rush/same-day)
  • Proofing: Digital proof required before production (yes/no), physical sample required (yes/no)
  • Shipping: Shipping address, delivery method (ground/express), packaging requirements (individual poly bags, bulk box, etc.)

For file requirements across different processes, see print-ready artwork checklists. For handling bulk customer artwork, see bulk vectorization workflows. For DTF-specific intake questions, see DTF transparency requirements.

faqs.question: Why do print shops need to know final print size up front?
faqs.answer: Final size determines resolution requirements (300 DPI at that size), press setup, material cost, and whether the design fits the substrate. If a customer submits a 2-inch logo expecting it printed at 12 inches, resolution may be too low. Asking up front prevents reprints and allows accurate quoting.

faqs.question: What happens if I do not specify garment or substrate color?
faqs.answer: The shop guesses, and the guess is often wrong. For example, if you submit a design with no transparency expecting it printed on black fabric, the shop must add transparency to prevent white box issues (DTF) or add a white underbase (screen printing). Specifying color up front lets the shop request the correct file format during submission.

faqs.question: Why does the print shop ask about color matching?
faqs.answer: To know whether you need exact Pantone matching (which requires spot color separations or color profiling), close matching (CMYK conversion is acceptable), or flexible colors (shop can adjust for printability). Without this info, the shop guesses, and you may reject the proof because colors do not match your brand.

faqs.question: Should I outline fonts before sending files to a print shop?
faqs.answer: Only if you are certain no text changes are needed. Outlined text cannot be edited—if you later want to change a date or phone number, the shop must redraw the text or ask for the source file with live text. During intake, tell the shop if changes are expected, so they can request editable files or charge for manual edits.

faqs.question: What is the difference between standard and rush turnaround?
faqs.answer: Standard turnaround (typically 7–10 business days for custom apparel, 3–5 days for digital printing) allows the shop to schedule production efficiently and proof designs before printing. Rush turnaround (3–5 days or same-day) requires prioritizing your order, often with premium pricing (+30–100%). Specify your deadline during intake to avoid surprises.
